title: Stenographic Services
one_liner: A litigation-adjacent service industry where court reporting, deposition transcription, and legal real-time recording are pressured by staffing shortages and courtroom digitization.
overview: US stenographic services are a specialized legal support activity serving courts, attorneys, and firms through real-time transcript capture, deposition reporting, and closed-caption/captioning services. Demand is sensitive to judicial staffing, court budgets, and process rules, while technology is making alternative capture methods more practical in many settings without fully replacing certified human recorders.

key_stats.market_size: $2.8bn (projected 2026, from prior IBIS trend-based baseline)
key_stats.growth: -0.4% CAGR projected (declining trajectory from prior near-term baseline)

baseline_2022.growth: -0.4% annualized (industry decline trend signal from prior filings and projections)

how_it_makes_money: Court and deposition coverage billed as in-court reporting/recording services, daily or hourly based engagement and retainers
Transcript production and expedited turnaround services for depositions, trials, hearings, and appeals
Transcript copy/sale and distribution fees; ancillary legal documentation and captioning services
Private court reporting contracts (including higher per-event rates than salaried court-paid reporting in some jurisdictions)
cost_structure: Labor-dominant costs: certified reporters, proofing/scopist workflow, and retention/compliance requirements
Moderate-to-high technology overhead for secure stenotype hardware, playback/real-time systems, and managed storage/distribution
Low fixed-cost footprint relative to many professional services, but volatile utilization and scheduling costs
Copy-sale revenue leakage risk when e-filing and digital distribution increase and reduce paid transcript handling
major_players: American Association of Electronic Reporters and Transcribers (AAERT)
U.S. federal and state court systems
Court-reporting firms and freelance reporting networks
Law firms and legal departments using deposition/live-court reporting
current_dynamics: The U.S. market is experiencing a dual shift: operational pain from workforce stress and policy-driven compensation/retention pressure, while courts and legal teams increase use of structured digital capture and AI/ASR-supported workflows where permitted. Policy activity is intensifying around oversight and the role of AI/ASR in official records.
whats_growing: Digital and real-time reporting workflows for speed and scheduling reliability
Use of transcript workflows tied to judicial technology modernization and accessibility requirements
Regulatory attention to AI/ASR governance in court records and transcript integrity
whats_shrinking: In-person stenographic pipeline depth due to workforce aging and entry decline
Relative share of purely manual capture in lower-priority or recordable court settings
Freelancer margin pressure from compression of copy-sale and transcript handling economics
recent_developments: 2025-04-10: AAERT released a 2025 industry trends release citing workforce shortage and stronger digital reporting adoption.
2025-04-14: Arkansas Act 499 was implemented, and NCRA pushed SB628 to improve competitiveness for freelancers and small court-reporting businesses.
2026-03-19: Congress introduced the Research and Oversight of AI in Courts Act targeting AI/ASR impacts on judicial records.
2026-01 to 2026-04: NCRA and related associations continued to emphasize that certified human oversight remains required for official records where accuracy and integrity are critical.
outlook: Short term outlook is cautious: steady institutional demand for accurate legal records should keep the industry viable, but growth is constrained by declining traditional staffing capacity, so firms that scale with certified digital workflows and quality assurance will gain share versus legacy-only models.
themes: Workforce replacement pressure
AI/ASR integration with strict human-authenticated record standards
Court-budget and access-to-justice policy shaping procurement and pay
Higher value placed on speed, reliability, and digital-ready transcript delivery
one_sentence: The industry remains essential for official legal records but is in structural transition, balancing shrinking on-site stenographic capacity against growing demand for speed, continuity, and accessible court records.

title: Stevedoring & Marine Cargo Handling in the US
one_liner: US marine cargo handling is operating with resilient throughput, persistent alliance concentration, and still-high cost pressure from labour and infrastructure intensity.
overview: In 2023, US ports moved 2.6 billion short tons of waterborne cargo, and port cargo mix remained heavily concentrated in large gateways. A 2025-2026 outlook from industry filings shows carrier alliances and shipping agreements continuing to dominate trade governance, while US trade data in 2026 still shows mixed demand signals: a narrower trade deficit alongside a heavy commodity flow profile. U.S. gateway-level operational data shows both rebound and moderation, with Los Angeles port activity holding above 1.0 million TEUs in June 2026 but annualized throughput still sensitive to front-loading and tariff cycles.

market_size.2023_total_tonnage: 2.6 billion short tons through top U.S. ports (BTS, 2023)
market_size.2026_la_volume: LA container total reached 1,002,734 TEUs in June 2026

growth.2025_to_2026_la_june: +12.37% total TEUs in June 2026 vs June 2025

growth.value: 3.2% annualized growth to about USD 12.9 billion

revenue_sources: Stevedoring and cargo handling fees (loading/unloading, break-bulk and container operations)
Port service charges and terminal handling income (shipping line/shipper billed services)
Storage, berth, gate, and ancillary logistics service revenues
Equipment handling and yard throughput fees linked to container turnover
how_it_makes_money.contract_model: Volume-driven service contracts and carrier/terminal operating agreements tied to vessel schedules and throughput.

labour_intensity.description: High labour content in dock operations and cargo movement
labour_intensity.data: Waterborne transportation and support activities employed 145,680 workers with $12.7B payroll in 2023 (BTS/USCG-linked methodology context)

capital.description: Large fixed-cost base in cranes, yard systems, berth infrastructure, and rail/yard interface
capital.example: Port of Los Angeles FY2024/2025: 85 ship-to-shore cranes and 1,985 cargo-handling equipment; $799M operating revenue vs $346M operating expense

other_cost_drivers: Energy and bunker-linked costs (carrier and terminal-side)
Port congestion drag (idle berth time, detention/demurrage risk exposure)
Regulatory compliance, safety, and security enforcement costs
cost_structure.profitability_implications: The model is highly leveraged to throughput cycles; productivity and congestion management materially drive margins.

current_dynamics: Trade flows remain globally stressed but not collapsing: June 2026 U.S. goods and services balance narrowed to a $73.3B deficit.
Major alliances continue to structure global and trans-pacific capacity deployment; Ocean/Gemini/Premier remain the main alliance frameworks for US service trade.
US port operators are balancing mixed momentum: LA June 2026 volume was above prior-year monthly levels while FY 2025/26 is still in progress with slight early-year softness.
whats_growing: US trade balance improved in June 2026: goods and services deficit narrowed to $73.3B from $77.6B in May 2026.
Port of Los Angeles monthly total TEU handling in June 2026 rose to 1,002,734 (+12.37% y/y vs June 2025).
Alliance monitoring focus expanded in 2025-2026 with multiple VSA structures, indicating sustained structured capacity coordination.
whats_shrinking: US top-25 US container terminals showed 2023 loaded TEUs down about 11% versus 2022 (indicating correction after prior peak years).
Port of Los Angeles FY2025/26 (in progress) showed a -1.10% drop versus FY2024/25, suggesting normalization after earlier front-loading.
recent_developments: 2026-04-01: FMC filed its FY-2025 Annual Report noting continued intensive review of VSA/alliances in major US trade lanes.
2025-01: The 2M structure was replaced by Gemini (Maersk + Hapag-Lloyd); THEA was replaced by Premier (YML, HMM, ONE), reflecting major alliance transitions.
2025-01: CMA CGM/COSCO/OOCL/OOCL alliance filing with FMC and MSC/ZIM cooperative arrangement reported, affecting Atlantic/Panama-style trade routings.
2026-06: US carriers/ports context shifted with LA data showing 10.11% rise in June total loaded TEUs and 16.93% rise in total empty TEUs vs June 2025.
2026-08-04: U.S. Census and BEA June 2026 release recorded exports of $314.7B and imports of $388.0B (seasonally adjusted, BOP basis).
outlook: Near-term outlook is mixed: demand appears steadier than in crisis conditions, but the industry is unlikely to regain pre-2022 expansion rates quickly. Profitability should improve on operational efficiency and route diversification only if congestion and alliance capacity management keep reliability stable. Continued tariff and trade-policy shifts are likely to cause periodic front-loading/re-routing rather than smooth volume growth.
themes: Carrier alliance concentration and alliance governance remain the main competitive dynamic
Tariff-led cargo front-loading continues to cause cyclical volume spikes and volatility
Port-level productivity investments (on-dock rail, berth utilization, crane productivity) remain the key competitiveness lever
Labour and infrastructure costs keep margins sensitive to throughput timing and reliability
one_sentence: The US stevedoring ecosystem in 2025-2026 is seeing modest recovery in trade fundamentals while carrier consolidation and tariff-driven cargo shifts keep capacity use and rates volatile.

title: Stock & Broth Production
one_liner: The U.S. stock and broth production industry is a small, low-growth packaged-food segment under pressure from fresh and cleaner-food preferences, but dominant national brands still preserve profitability through scale, packaging, and category management.
overview: Stock and broth producers make shelf-stable liquid and dried soup/base products used as pantry and cooking ingredients, historically sold through grocery and foodservice channels. The category is structurally mature, with brand trust and shelf presence concentrated in a few national players. Since 2025-26, manufacturers have leaned into cooking-use occasions, reformulation, and broader 'better-for-you' narratives to slow demand erosion rather than reverse it.

key_stats.market_size: US$936.0 million (2026, projected)
key_stats.growth: -0.1% CAGR (2021–2026 projected decline)
key_stats.profitability: ~11.7% profit margin cited in baseline profile; category still above many ultra-processed peers despite volume pressure
key_stats.concentration: More than 70% revenue share historically concentrated in top four operators

baseline_2022.market_size: US$942.0 million (historical baseline line in provided file, closest prior reference point to 2022)
baseline_2022.growth: Industry demand had already shown weak trend before 2026 (about -1.2% average annual over 2016–2021 path in baseline framing)

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell brand-name and private-label stock, broth, and related soup/seasoning base products primarily to grocery retailers and, to a lesser extent, foodservice users; revenue comes from volume plus mix shift toward higher-value packs, stronger private-label contracts, and premium positioning through cleaner ingredient claims.
cost_structure: Raw proteins and flavor inputs (especially poultry and meat components), packaging formats (including pouch/carton conversion), manufacturing labor, and logistics are the largest cost blocks; in 2026, tariffs, commodity/input inflation, and transport cost volatility were explicitly cited as margin pressure points.
major_players: The Campbell's Company (Swanson, Campbell, Pacific Foods; reported in category remarks and segment disclosures)
General Mills / Progresso (soup and broth brand family under the GIS portfolio)
Private-label producers serving major grocery and mass retail networks (notably through retailer contracts)
current_dynamics: Broth demand is not collapsing as fast as long-forecasted dry formats and remains tied to at-home cooking frequency.
Private-label shares remain meaningful, with retailers using competitive pricing and promotions to defend shelf space.
2026 producer commentary shows branded recovery efforts in selected subcategories despite headline net sales declines.
Ingredient cost inflation and logistics pressure remain a core margin drag in the 2026 period.
whats_growing: Brand-level broth consumption in 2026 showed consecutive-quarter growth momentum in at least one major packaged-food operator's Q2 remarks.
Health-forward and convenience-led positioning (cleaner ingredients, better-for-you messaging) is still attracting incremental trial.
Organic and natural positioning across the food market strengthened in 2025, expanding premium pull for cleaner pantry solutions.
whats_shrinking: Overall category growth remains weak; broader demand for traditional soup-and-broth formats is still declining over medium horizon.
Dry bouillon and lower-margin packaged SKUs face faster share erosion versus differentiated liquid/cooking-use formats.
Price-sensitive, volume-driven grocery spending is limiting share gains for higher-priced branded broth and soup SKUs.

outlook: For 2026–2027, the industry is more likely to remain in mild contraction than to reaccelerate, with growth concentrated in selected branded broth formats, improved recipes, and private-label competitive execution; downside remains cost inflation persistence and continued consumer migration toward fresher alternatives.
themes: Category reformulation toward cleaner labels
Shift from purely canned units to convenient liquid and meal-cooking formats
Private-label and promotion intensity in grocery channels
Ingredient and logistics inflation management
Niche growth in organic/health-positioned alternatives despite category-level decline

title: Stock & Commodity Exchanges in the US
one_liner: U.S. stock and commodity exchanges in 2025-2026 remain a high-concentration, high-compute market where network effects, derivatives growth, and recurring data monetization drive profitability.
overview: The U.S. market is led by a few globally connected exchange groups and is best read as a platform economy: exchange participation scales with flow, while fixed infrastructure and regulatory obligations dominate cost structure. 2025 was a solid year across headline exchange operators, with commodity and equity derivatives activity and data subscriptions offsetting pressure on some legacy listing and liquidity channels. The long-run winners are firms that can combine exchange access, clearing, market data, and analytics into sticky product bundles that remain defensible under higher scrutiny and volatility cycles.

market_size.basis: Estimated from major U.S. listed exchange operators' 2025 reported totals: ICE $12.640bn (consolidated), Nasdaq $5.249bn net revenue, CME $6.5206bn, and Cboe $4.7142bn

growth.2025_vs_2024_operator_mix: ICE +7.0%, CME +6.4%, Cboe +15.2%, Nasdaq +13.0% in 2025 year-over-year, with high growth concentrated in market data and derivatives-linked lines
growth.macro_note: 2022-2027 slower-growth outlook in prior IBIS baseline has been partially offset by elevated derivatives activity in 2025

Listing and market access fees across equities and futures channels
Market data, reference data, analytics, and terminal/venue distribution bundles
Ancillary technology and post-trade infrastructure tied to venue operations
how_it_makes_money.2025_specific_pattern: 2025 filings show continued contribution from market services, exchange/clearing platforms, and data-driven enterprise solutions, with derivatives and market data being the strongest incremental revenue anchors

dominant_cost_drivers_2025: High fixed costs for low-latency matching, co-location, risk monitoring, and surveillance
Variable settlement and transaction-related expense that scales with volume
Regulatory, cyber, and compliance staffing/legal spend tied to SEC and global market-regulatory obligations
Technology and data-center capex to sustain uptime, speed, and cross-venue redundancy
cost_structure.pricing_pressure: 2025-2026 competition from ATSs and OTC routing keeps pure execution fee increases structurally difficult while market-data bundling and software value-add improve stickiness

current_dynamics.2026_market: Execution and data monetization stayed resilient through 2025 while participants continued reallocating toward multi-venue, automated, and derivatives-heavy workflows.
current_dynamics.competition: Liquidity continues to split across lit exchanges, ATSs, and broker internalization, pushing visible execution fees lower and increasing the value of bundled data and clearing services.
current_dynamics.regulation: Market structure and product approval cycles in 2025-2026 remain a major constraint, especially on trading hours, transparency, and market-risk controls.

whats_growing: 2025 and 2026 data indicate strong exchange economics from derivatives and data-driven revenue lines in the majors.
Exchange network scale effects improved as major operators absorbed fixed costs and expanded product sets (including futures, AI/analytics, and tokenized infrastructure planning).
Market-making and hedging flow supported by volatility cycles kept transaction throughput structurally higher than 2024 trough periods.
whats_shrinking: Margins in conventional listing/vanilla order-routing channels remain vulnerable to internalization and ATS substitution (2025-2026 competitive pressure).
The share of pure transaction growth unconnected to premium data and solutions appears under pressure versus the higher-value software/data bundles.
Regulatory frictions in both equities and derivatives markets add incremental operational and compliance cost loadings in 2025-2026.

2026-07-23: Nasdaq reported 2026 Q2 net revenue of $1.5bn, continuing 2025-to-2026 momentum into mid-year.

outlook.2026_to_2027: The near-term outlook is constructive but uneven: high-capacity derivatives and data monetization should remain supportive, while fee compression and market-structure regulation likely cap headline multiples and make selective innovation the key differentiator.
outlook.risk_to_revenue: Any easing of volatility, stricter margin/capital requirements, or slower product adoption in advanced venue models could reduce incremental flow-dependent upside.

Derivatives-led revenue resilience
24x5 and session extension
Tokenization and exchange digitization
Regulatory-cost drag with high fixed cost base
one_sentence: The industry in 2026 is supported by strong 2025 results from major operators, persistent volatility demand, and infrastructure-led expansion, while margin headroom is pressured by regulation and competition from internalization and ATSs.

title: Stone Mining in the US
one_liner: Stone mining in the US remains a stable, infrastructure-sensitive heavy materials industry with consolidation accelerating.
overview: USGS survey data show the industry’s core business remains strong despite cyclical variability: in 3Q 2025 crushed stone sold or used reached 441 million metric tons (+7% QoQ vs 2024), while first-9-month crushed-stone consumption was 1.10 billion metric tons versus 1.12 billion in 2024. Sand-and-gravel consumption in 3Q 2025 was 262 million metric tons (+5% QoQ), but YTD 2025 was 657 million metric tons versus 673 million in 2024. Public information from 2026 USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries indicates crushed stone was the leading U.S. nonfuel mineral by value in 2025, with an estimated annual output value around $27 billion and about 1.5 billion metric tons, showing continued scale leadership as domestic infrastructure, roadbase, and concrete inputs remain the primary demand drivers.

key_stats.market_size: $27.0 billion (2025 US crushed stone value, USGS 2025 estimate context)
key_stats.growth: 3Q 2025 crushed stone was +7% year-on-year vs 3Q 2024, but YTD 2025 crushed-stone consumption declined versus YTD 2024; construction aggregates growth is uneven across quarters and regions.

baseline_2022.market_size: $19.4 billion (IBIS baseline period reference from provided file, 2021-2022 era)
baseline_2022.growth: IBIS baseline shows industry revenue CAGR of 2.22% in 2003-2021 and 1.74% projected for 2021-27; baseline industry projection in that period was to grow to about $21.2 billion by 2026.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily from selling quarried and processed stone (especially crushed stone) into road construction, concrete/construction materials, and infrastructure supply chains, with supporting sales of asphalt/concrete-related products and specialty stone/calcium-based products; pricing power is driven by tonnage sold, regional spread, and fuel/haulage pass-through.
cost_structure: Major cost blocks are energy and fuel (drilling, crushing, hauling), labor/safety compliance, blasting and maintenance, heavy equipment utilization, freight/rail/trucking logistics, mine development and environmental permitting/rehabilitation, and cost volatility in raw material inputs and labor.
current_dynamics: Demand remains concentrated in infrastructure and construction-linked end-markets, while USGS quarterly releases show strong quarter-to-quarter rebounds (weather effects) but weaker first-nine-month cumulative volumes versus 2024. Company disclosures show both high-volume execution and pricing discipline are central: major players reported 2025 results with improved margin and pricing, even as macro demand in single-family and nonresidential starts stayed below post-COVID peaks in parts of the market.
whats_growing: Public infrastructure and resilient roadbase demand as agencies rebuild and maintain transport networks
Mix-adjusted aggregates pricing, with several large players reporting multi-year margin expansion
Strategic consolidation, including the Martin Marietta–Lhoist North America combination, reinforcing scale
Vertical/logistics integration and high-volume footprint optimization by major operators
whats_shrinking: Year-to-date 2025 aggregate-volume growth is softer in cumulative terms due to quarter volatility and weather
Some regional markets show weaker building-activity intensity, especially in private nonresidential and select housing segments
High transport dependence keeps net realizations exposed to freight and fuel shocks
recent_developments: 2025-09-01: USGS reports aggregates in 3Q 2025 with crushed stone up 7% and first-9-month crushed-stone consumption at 1.10 Gt.
2026-02-11: Martin Marietta reported 2025 aggregates revenue $5.0B, ASP $23.11/ton, and 2026 low-single-digit shipment guidance.
2026-02-17: Vulcan Materials reported 2025 results with strong full-year earnings growth and reported mix-adjusted 2026 optimism.
2026-06-29: Martin Marietta announced a definitive agreement to combine with Lhoist North America, expanding U.S. aggregates and limestone platform scale.
outlook: Near-term demand is expected to remain supportive from infrastructure, transport renewal, and public construction, but growth is likely to be moderate and uneven across regions due to macro cyclicality. The most likely path is steady volume recovery with continued M&A and productivity-focused cost discipline as key value drivers.
themes: infrastructure-led demand
quarterly weather volatility
consolidation and strategic combinations
pricing resilience through mix and footprint optimization
lower-margin segments under pressure when weather and demand weaken
one_sentence: U.S. crushed stone output is still large and demand-linked to construction, while short-term volume swings are weather and capital-cycle driven.

title: Stone, Concrete & Clay Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: Demand remains tied to construction activity, with infrastructure and logistics channels supporting shipments even as financing-sensitive housing demand softens.
overview: The industry supplies construction aggregates, cement-related materials, and related stone/clay products to contractors, builders, and builders’ supply channels; buyers are concentrated in residential renovation and repair, private commercial projects, and public infrastructure. Distribution economics are highly location-sensitive due to material weight and short shelf-life constraints in some products, making proximity to end markets and transport efficiency critical.

market_size.source_note: Derived from 2022 IBIS baseline near 25,755 with the published weak-growth trajectory.

how_it_makes_money: Gross margin comes from wholesaling spreads between purchased product cost and sell-through price to contractors and distributors.
Delivery is a material part of revenue economics; freight, handling, and terminal/service charges are commonly built into pricing.
Additional value comes from value-added mix-and-match inventory management, pre-dispensed lots, and local fulfillment services that reduce customer stockholding and downtime.
cost_structure: Fuel and transport costs are a major exposure; for example, U.S. on-highway diesel climbed from 4.578 to 5.348 dollars per gallon in June 2026 (U.S. weekly).
Input and energy exposure remains material across cement- and aggregate-linked supply chains, with suppliers citing coal, diesel, electricity, and gas volatility.
Labor and equipment utilization pressures persist in excavation, quarrying, hauling, and yard operations, especially near metropolitan demand centers.
Environmental and permitting compliance adds operating burden as emissions and land-use standards tighten in major aggregates corridors.
current_dynamics: Construction spending remains highly mixed: total construction (SAAR) was 195,927 million in June 2026, while private construction was 144,547 million and public construction was 51,381 million.
Private activity weakened (June 2026 private construction showed a 4.7% year-to-date decline), while public spending and highway-related activity remained comparatively firmer.

Housing permits and starts in June 2026 remained sensitive to rates: permits 1,367,000 SAAR (-3.0% vs revised May 2026 and -2.3% vs June 2025), while starts were 1,427,000 SAAR (+19.0% vs revised May 2026 but still volatile month-to-month).
Financial conditions remain tight for end users as 30-year mortgage rates stayed elevated (6.69% on Aug 6, 2026, weekly), supporting a cautious affordability outlook.

Industry consolidation activity continues: Martin Marietta announced a US$13.5 billion combination with Lhoist North America (June 29, 2026), showing strategic emphasis on vertically integrated, infrastructure-linked footprints.
whats_growing: Public highway and transit-related demand channels supported by federal funding and grant pipelines.
Consolidation and network-scale moves by large aggregates specialists to build Sun Belt and high-growth market coverage.
Infrastructure-ready distribution investments and integrated logistics to reduce haul distance and response time.
Environmental substitutions and efficiency upgrades (including fuel and kiln/cement process adjustments) in supplier portfolios.
whats_shrinking: Rate-sensitive standalone residential demand intensity versus peak-cycle years.
Near-term price realization when material competition increases in regional construction downturn pockets.
Small regional wholesalers with narrower truck-ratio and slower permitting support under higher operating leverage.

2026-08-03: Census construction spending showed June 2026 total at 195,927 million SAAR; private was 144,547 million SAAR and public was 51,381 million SAAR.
2026-07-17: Census reported June 2026 permits 1,367,000 SAAR and starts 1,427,000 SAAR.
2026-07-10: DOT IIJA funding status reported $545,691,946 enacted budget authority, $392,472,231 grants announced, and $237,219,512 outlays.

outlook: The market is likely to remain structurally demand-constrained in residential and cyclical nonresidential segments when financing is expensive, while public infrastructure and strategic replacement work keep part of the demand base supported. Winners in 2025-26 are expected to be operators with dense regional footprints, integrated supply networks, disciplined freight strategy, and strong balance sheets. Margin outlook is mixed: pricing power can recover in tighter regional supply zones, but high fuel and energy costs continue to pressure operating leverage.
themes: Public infrastructure as a stabilizer
Rate-sensitive housing and financing drag
Consolidation through strategic acquisitions
Logistics intensity and local delivery windows
Decarbonization and emissions-related cost pressure

title: Storage & Warehouse Leasing in the US
one_liner: US storage and warehouse leasing in 2025-26 shows resilient unitized demand and a shift toward modern, faster logistics facilities while legacy industrial supply and price pressure persist.
overview: The market combines two connected segments: self-storage rental for households and businesses, and modern warehousing for logistics and distribution. Demand is still supported by relocation, e-commerce, and shorter cycle supply-chain strategies, but macro uncertainty, rising borrowing costs, and older-space overhang keep pricing subdued and keep vacancy elevated in many submarkets.
how_it_makes_money: Income is earned mainly from monthly storage and warehouse leases, plus ancillary charges and service revenue (moving supplies, access upgrades, insurance/loan products), with REITs emphasizing same-store operating performance and development/acquisition pipelines for growth.

major_cost_drivers_2025_2026: Property operating costs and labor intensity (same-store NOI pressure was evident at major REITs in 2025).
Debt servicing costs remained elevated: CubeSmart reported weighted average debt interest at 3.34% in 2025 versus 2.97% in 2024; Public Storage reported 3.2% weighted average debt rate in 2025.
Development and expansion spending continued: Public Storage disclosed 2.1m new NRSF built/expanded in 2025 and 3.5m NRSF under construction/expansion pipeline.
cost_structure.pricing_power_constraint_2025_2026: CBRE and Cushman both flagged subdued rent growth in much of the industrial segment, with selective resilience in newer/modern logistics product.

title: Street Cleaning Services
one_liner: Street and parking lot cleaning in the US is a niche service industry where private commercial contracts dominate and municipal outsourcing remains the largest source of growth risk and opportunity.
overview: The US market is small and mature, but still grows with road and lot use. IBISWorld’s latest baseline shows street cleaning services at about US$1.884B in 2021 and projected to reach about US$2.1B by 2026, with parking-lot and garage cleaning as the largest revenue segment. Demand is most resilient where cleaning is tied to private commercial operations and industrial dust-control obligations, while pure street-sweeping contracts for municipalities are more sensitive to local fleet strategy and public procurement rules. FHWA motor-vehicle-miles data show 2024 total vehicle-miles at 3,294,031 million, up from 3,246,817 million in 2023, confirming ongoing base demand for surface cleaning and contamination control. June 2026 US construction spending data also show continued public highway and street spending (US$150,909 million SAAR) and strong nonresidential activity, supporting construction-site cleaning demand at least through 2026.

baseline_2022.market_size: US$1.884 billion (latest detailed near-2022 benchmark in baseline report, in 2021 dollars)
baseline_2022.growth: 5.5% rebound in 2021 after 2020 contraction of 7.1%

how_it_makes_money: Recurring monthly/weekly sweeping and wash contracts for parking lots, garages, and commercial real-estate lots.
Municipal or county outsourcing contracts for supplemental or full public-road sweeping windows.
Project-based construction and industrial site contracts tied to dust/sediment control and site compliance needs.
Contract pricing by cleaned area, frequency, required service level, and traffic/contamination intensity.
Upsell services such as pressure washing, surface decontamination, and pre/post construction cleanup.

cost_structure.labour: Labor is structurally the largest cost (about 48.4% of 2021 revenue in baseline analysis); median wage pressure aligns with BLS janitorial/buildings-cleaning labor benchmark (median $17.27/hour in May 2024).
cost_structure.fleet_and_equipment: Vehicle and sweeper fleets are capital intensive, with ongoing maintenance, sweeper wear, replacement cycles, and fuel/energy exposure.
cost_structure.pricing_competitiveness: High competition from fragmented operators compresses margins, especially on price-led bids.
cost_structure.compliance_costs: Stormwater/erosion-control documentation, wash-water handling, and permit-related operating requirements increase overhead for construction-linked contracts.

current_dynamics.demand_mix: Commercial parking-lot/garde and construction/industrial work remain steadier than pure municipal road sweeping.
current_dynamics.competition: The sector remains highly fragmented with local operators competing on route coverage and price.
current_dynamics.policy_pressure: EPA stormwater construction requirements continue to tighten operational standards for contractors tied to development activity.

whats_growing: Parking-lot-focused recurring maintenance contracts due to higher utilization pressure on commercial and retail surfaces.
Demand for construction-site and industrial lot cleaning where runoff and sediment controls are enforced.
Municipal contracts that package street cleaning with broader public works maintenance.
whats_shrinking: Pure municipal street-only cleaning as more cities improve in-house sweeper coverage or receive fleet upgrades.
Room for large independent price increases because fragmentation sustains aggressive bidding.
recent_developments: 2026-08-03: EPA posted updates on construction stormwater permits and issued a notice for proposed 2027 CGP with comment period through 2026-09-02.
2026-08-03: Census reported June 2026 total construction spending at US$2,166.5 billion SAAR and highway and street spending at US$150.909 billion.
2026-08-03: EPA page showed continued stormwater compliance framing including required controls for wash-water, fuel/oil runoff, and site stabilization in construction activity.
2025-05-20: Orange County, FL awarded street sweeping service bids including USA Services of Florida LLC and TransPremier LLC contracts around US$668k–US$1.7M.
2026-03-24: Muskegon MI public package showed 2026–2028 street sweeping contract bidding with incumbent Tri-Us Services, Inc. and SCA of MI.
outlook: For 2026 and beyond, the industry is likely to grow slowly but remain steady, supported by commercial lot maintenance and construction activity while facing continued price compression from fragmented local competition and public-sector budget/technology swings.
themes: Regulation-led cleaning demand
Commercial real-estate dependency
Fragile municipal contract economics
Vehicle activity remains a long-cycle demand floor
Labor intensity and service continuity pressure
one_sentence: In 2026, US street-cleaning demand is stable-to-slow-growing as parking-lot maintenance remains essential, while tighter stormwater compliance and local budget cycles reshape contract dynamics.

title: Street Vendors in the US
one_liner: Street vending remains a low-barrier food-service subsector where policy capacity, mobility economics, and event-driven demand determine winners.
overview: 2022 baseline conditions still define the structure: mobile food-service operators were concentrated in small enterprises and high-turnover models, with IBIS reporting around 2022 US revenue of $2,487m and about 72,624 people employed. The latest government-linked indicator shows a structural rise in scale over time, with BLS noting mobile food services employment at 44,119 in 2024 (2000: 4,383; +906.6%). In 2026, public reporting also confirms municipal permitting changes rather than demand collapse as the strongest near-term constraint, especially where license caps are being lifted. Industry-facing demand remains linked to convenience and outdoor/late-day consumption, while cost pressure from energy and compliance continues to limit margin expansion.

revenue_model: Immediate-consumption food and beverage sales from carts/trucks
Corporate, university, and high-traffic location contracts
pricing_characteristics: High itemized pricing with rapid menu turns
Premium menu differentiation offsets part of cost pressure
Low capital footprint enables fast cash-cycle businesses

core_costs.note: 2022 reporting cited elevated commodity and protein costs as a recurring squeeze on margins
Fuel and vehicle operations remain major operating expenses for trucks/carts
Food-service labor plus tax and payroll obligations remain fixed and rising as regulations tighten
Municipal licensing is a fixed operating cost and can bind expansion in high-demand markets

selected_2026_inputs.item: Max SE earnings subject to SS tax

major_players: Independent operators (about 85.60% of 2025 food-truck market by ownership share)
current_dynamics: Regulation is now a demand limiter in major metros. New York City is adding supervisory license pathways and more general-vendor slots under 2026 reforms, while also maintaining category-based permit requirements and waiting-list sequencing. At the same time, operators are shifting toward predictable contracts (events, workplaces, university contexts) to reduce weather and daily footfall risk.
whats_growing: Legal capacity expansion in 2026, higher share of independent operators entering structured channels, and stronger demand for convenience dining during transit, event, and evening windows are likely to grow vendor counts and sales mix complexity.
whats_shrinking: Margin expansion is difficult where energy and ingredient costs remain elevated and enforcement/compliance burdens rise; lower-income discretionary spending remains vulnerable to inflation, especially when fuel and CPI pressures persist.
recent_developments: 2024: NYC baseline law framework and permit structure for mobile food vendors remains structured around category-specific licenses and inspections (mobile food vendor license + permit requirement).
2025-07-14: BLS reported 2024 mobile food services employment at 44,119, up from 4,383 in 2000 (+906.6%), showing sustained long-horizon expansion.

2026-07-01: NYC licensing framework under Local Law 54/18 increases mobile food permit capacity through expanded supervisory-license allocation (1,500 non-Manhattan + 500 citywide + 200 veteran/disabled supervisory licenses annually).
2026-07: New York City DCWP page notes 10,500 additional General Vendor licenses starting after 2027 while accepting new 2026 waitlists, reflecting ongoing municipal capacity expansion.

2026-05-21: National Restaurant Association economic outlook projected 2026 GDP growth at 2.3% and noted persistent inflation pressure, which raises traffic and food-cost risk for small format dining.
2026-01-13: Mordor food truck data portal reported 2026 U.S. food truck market size at USD 1.16b (up from USD 1.09b in 2025).
outlook: Near term (2026-2028), industry structure is likely to tilt toward higher-formality operators with better compliance capacity, especially in cities with permit reforms. The sector should keep gaining from experiential and convenience demand, but profitability will depend on operational discipline: tighter menus, route efficiency, fleet/vehicle productivity, and disciplined tax and labor compliance.
themes: Regulatory capacity expansion
Low-cost entry vs compliance burden
Urban convenience and outdoor dining demand
Labor and food-cost inflation drag
Shift to contract-based, repeatable sales channels
one_sentence: From a 2022 baseline of about $2,487m in revenue, the sector has continued to show strong long-tail growth through 2025-2026, with legal supply expanding in key cities as digital ordering, campus/event contracts, and municipal reform reshape unit economics.

title: Strip Clubs
one_liner: U.S. strip clubs remain a compact, cash-intensive nightlife segment where physical social experience and alcohol-led spending still anchor revenue.
overview: Recent 2025 disclosures show the sector is still dominated by a few large operators amid many regional private clubs, and growth is constrained by licensing intensity rather than broad consumer demand collapse. Industry structure continues to be experience-led (cover, beverage, room, and VIP packages) with persistent sensitivity to local permitting regimes.

market_size.2022: US$7.2B (near-2022 proxy from baseline strip-club file)

growth.2025_2026_major_public_operator: RCI Hospitality FY2024 to FY2025: -5.5% (US$295.6M to US$279.4M)

baseline_2022.market_size: US$7.2B (closest available baseline figure used as 2022 proxy)
baseline_2022.growth: Industry baseline path showed post-COVID recovery, with a 2.1% annualized projected rebound through 2026 from the early-2020s trough

how_it_makes_money: Cover/entry charges and membership-style patron spending.
Alcohol sales remain the largest revenue engine (historically ~44.6% of venue revenue).
Private dances, VIP room packages, and bottle-service are high-margin add-ons.
Food and non-alcoholic amenities support length of stay and spending per visit.
Brand repositioning toward premium dining and hospitality formats is used to reduce stigma and capture higher-ticket guests.
cost_structure: License and regulatory costs are structural: many jurisdictions require special permits and restrict dancing, operating hours, and adult entertainment operations.
Texas-style excise style rules raise variable cost per admitted patron where applicable (US$10 per entry rate in Texas as of 2025-09-01).
Labor complexity is high because dancers/performers are explicitly treated as tipped occupations, adding payroll/tax treatment risk.
Venue fixed costs remain high from lease, security, insurance, and compliance obligations, especially in central city markets.
major_players: RCI Hospitality Holdings (public): 71 establishments in 15 states, US$279.4M revenue in FY2025 (Sept 30, 2025 basis).
Sizable private regional chains remain a major share of the market (fragmented local ownership plus legacy brands).
Deja Vu-affiliated club networks remain cited in labor/compliance filings and are frequently treated as one of the largest private operator footprints in this segment.
current_dynamics: Consolidation and scale are concentrated in a few large operators, while long-tail city/metro clubs remain the majority by number.
Demand remains discretionary and cyclical, with stronger performance tied to higher-income leisure spending and nightlife activity.
Alcohol-first economics remain critical; changes in local beverage licensing or permit status materially affect viability.
Regulatory risk remains place-specific and non-uniform, with some municipalities reversing restrictions after industry pushback.
whats_growing: In 2026, operators reported that physical experience demand can coexist with abundant online adult content, especially for social-nightlife formats.
Premiumized club formats that blend dining, nightlife, and controlled VIP experiences are expanding.
Municipal policy windows can open quickly after short-lived moratoria reversals, as seen in New Orleans in early 2026.
whats_shrinking: Same-store traffic and margin stability weakened for listed peers in 2025 (RCI quarter-over-quarter same-store deterioration in 2025 was notably negative).
Small and non-compliant operators are more exposed to permitting friction, enforcement, and legal cost under rising adult-entertainment oversight.
Purely performance-driven, low-differentiation strip-venue formats are under pressure versus branded hospitality-style models.
recent_developments: 2025-09-01: Texas sexually oriented business fee increased to US$10 per admitted patron, effective Sept. 1, 2025, versus US$5 before.
2025-09-17: RCI Hospitality leadership and company named in a federal indictment-related report on alleged tax fraud/bribery allegations in public business coverage.
2026-01-27: New Orleans City Council lifted a newly passed French Quarter moratorium that would have restricted new strip clubs.
2026-03-19: RCI filed FY2025 results showing 71 club assets across 15 states and FY2025 consolidated revenue of US$279.4M.
2026-05-07: PR coverage from a major club operator highlighted stronger in-person attendance sentiment despite unlimited digital adult content availability.
outlook: Short to medium term, the segment is likely to stay small but resilient, with upside tied to tourism, higher discretionary spend in hospitality, and legal predictability; downside remains tied to local anti-vice/land-use actions, rising compliance cost, and workforce/legal scrutiny.
themes: Experiential resilience versus digital substitution
Labor and tipped-income classification risk
City-level zoning volatility
Alcohol-permit dependency
Brand-led premiumization of nightlife format
one_sentence: The industry is in slow recovery, with major operators showing mixed 2025 performance, while zoning, alcohol permitting, and labor/taxed compensation issues keep operating risk elevated.

title: Subprime Auto Loans
one_liner: Subprime auto lending in the U.S. has returned as a larger share of financing but remains a high-delinquency, tightly priced segment in 2025–2026.
overview: The industry mainly serves borrowers with weak credit profiles in auto purchase and refinance transactions, delivered through banks, captive finance arms, credit unions, and buy-here-pay-here (BHPH) specialists. The market is being pulled by persistent mobility needs and still-high credit costs, while being constrained by delinquency risk, tighter inquiry behavior, and stricter credit qualification.

key_stats.market_size: 2026-01: auto loan balances reached $1.69T (NY Fed CMD Household Debt & Credit, Q1 2026), implying roughly $0.26T if subprime share at 15.31% in 2025-12 is applied; 2025-12: auto loan originations were $69.9B across 2.2M loans (CFPB).
key_stats.growth: 2025-12: total auto-loan originations +1.8% year-over-year (CFPB); 2026-01: auto loan balances +$18B quarter-over-quarter (NY Fed, Q1 2026); 2025Q3: auto loans 30+ DPD was 3.88% (Fed/NY Fed CCP, via FRB note).
key_stats.delinquency: 2025Q3: auto loan delinquency at 30+ days was 3.88%; 2026-01: auto late-delinquency transitions were reported as flat versus 2025Q4 (NY Fed, Q1 2026).
key_stats.pricing: 2026-05: 60-month new-auto finance rate at commercial banks was 7.14% (FRED, G.19 series RIFLPBCIANM60NM).

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 (closest comparable from provided baseline): no separate 2022 value shown; IBIS baseline in source shows $14.4B industry revenue estimate for 2021 and projects 2021-2027 growth.
baseline_2022.growth: Baseline forecast context: 2021-2027 CAGR of 3.82% in IBIS baseline snapshot.

how_it_makes_money: Revenues come from elevated interest margins on higher-risk borrower books, origination fees, insurance/ancillary products sold at point of sale, and credit-related servicing economics; returns are supported when default losses are managed through tighter screening and pricing.
cost_structure: Major costs are funding (warehouse lines, ABS markets, and balance-sheet liquidity), credit loss provisioning, delinquency management (collections/repossessions), underwriting/servicing infrastructure, and compliance with expanded consumer-protection monitoring.
major_players: Large bank auto-loan programs and captives
current_dynamics: The segment shows demand recovery with elevated risk: subprime financing share improved while credit conditions remain selective. BHPH channels remain important for weaker-credit borrowers but carry materially higher delinquency and are increasingly concentrated in riskier borrower cohorts.
whats_growing: 2025-12: subprime borrowers reached 15.31% of total vehicle financing in Q4 2025, up from 14.54% in Q4 2024 (Experian).
2026-01: total auto debt expanded to $1.69T (+$18B QoQ) (NY Fed Q1 2026).
2026-01: auto-loan demand showed stability in delinquency transitions, supporting continued credit supply at higher prices.
whats_shrinking: 2026-04: CFPB shows inquiry activity down 5.6% year-over-year (tighter funnel conversion pressure).
2025-2026: deep reliance on the weakest subprime borrowers is constrained by higher payment burdens and elevated delinquency sensitivity.
2025-2026: traditional high-risk channels remain stressed versus bank-backed underwriting (BHPH delinquency materially above traditional lenders).
recent_developments: 2025-12: CFPB auto-loan dashboard reported 2.2M originations and $69.9B in new loan volume, +1.8% YoY.
2025-12: CFPB credit tightness was 2.7% lower year-over-year; inquiries were down 5.6% by Apr 2026.
2026-01: NY Fed Household Debt & Credit reported auto loan balances at $1.69T, with auto balances up $18B quarter-over-quarter.
2026-01: NY Fed noted auto late-delinquency transitions held steady versus 2025Q4 while broader aggregate delinquency was flat.
2025-12 to 2026-03: Experian’s Q4 2025 analysis showed subprime financing share rose to 15.31% of vehicle financing and average loan amounts rose for both new and used vehicles.
2025-12: Fed note on auto-loan delinquencies reports 2025Q3 auto loan 30+ DPD at 3.88%, with low-income segments remaining above higher-income cohorts.
outlook: Near-term outlook is mixed: moderate asset growth from persistent vehicle financing need is likely, but valuation depends on labor and rate persistence, underwriting standards, and whether delinquency continues to plateau rather than worsen. The sector should remain profitable at scale if lenders maintain disciplined underwriting and pricing.
themes: Higher interest rates keep APRs high for subprime borrowers and pressure payment resilience.
Subprime share has rebounded but borrower risk remains elevated in downturn-sensitive segments.
Concentration in BHPH and other direct-risk channels remains a key source of delinquency volatility.
Large lenders are likely to retain subprime exposure through tighter risk-based pricing rather than broad expansion.
Data-driven credit scoring and tighter approvals are central to profitability in late-cycle consumer credit.
one_sentence: By 2026, demand for subprime auto credit remained resilient as prices and vehicle replacement needs persisted, while lenders kept underwriting tight because delinquency risk stayed elevated.

title: Sugar Processing in the US
one_liner: U.S. sugar processors convert beet and cane output into refined/raw sugar under a quota- and allotment-driven system that keeps most production domestic and sold for food use.
overview: US sugar processing in 2026 is operating in a policy-managed market where domestic production, imports, and distribution are shaped by USDA loan, allotment, and trade-allocation rules. USDA ERS projects FY2026/27 total sugar use near 12.389 million short tons raw value (STRV), up from 12.364 million STRV in FY2025/26, while ending stocks remain elevated but manageable at 1.673 million STRV (stock-to-use 13.5%, per USDA ERS outlook updates). U.S. sugar imports remain heavily constrained by WTO/FTA TRQ structure and Mexico’s suspension-era limits, while domestic food and beverage demand has shown pockets of resilience (especially beverages), and downstream restaurants remain a smaller and more volatile channel than packaged goods channels.

notes: FY2026 through Apr (monthly SMD): domestic human consumption deliveries 7.137 million STRV, up 2.1% from FY2025 through Apr.
FY2025/26 to FY2026/27 outlook revisions lifted total supply to 14.268 million STRV in one monthly revision cycle.

baseline_2022.growth: 1.25% CAGR (2005-2022); projected 0.84% CAGR (2022-2028), with 2022 revenue baseline.

how_it_makes_money: Convert domestic and imported raw sugar streams into refined and raw sugar for food, beverage, confectionery, baking, and grocery channels.
Sell bulk crystalline and packaged sugar via wholesalers, retailers, and ingredient buyers.

Capture additional margin through re-export-eligible channels, sugar-containing products programs, and byproducts such as molasses and syrup streams; some domestic cane beets can be diverted through CCC/Flex feedstock channels.
cost_structure: Raw input materials dominate cash cost: farm-gate sugar content from sugar beet and sugar cane and inbound/raw import sugar.
Processing is energy- and maintenance-intensive (evaporation, crystallization, refining, packaging, and logistics).
Compliance with commodity, allotment, and trade-allocation mechanics is a meaningful structural overhead and working-capital cost driver.
current_dynamics: Policy remained the main market stabilizer in 2026, but not the growth driver: domestic harvest and deliveries stayed above last year’s pace early in FY2026, while exporters stayed weak and refined sugar prices eased. Domestic use stayed near flat year-over-year in aggregate, with channel dispersion (beverages up, foodservice weak, confectionery mixed). Import allocations remained constrained by TRQ and suspension rules, and monthly USDA market data revisions narrowed uncertainty but reinforced a competitive domestic margin environment.
whats_growing: Domestic human-consumption deliveries in FY2026 YTD were above FY2025 YTD, showing continuing packaged-food demand strength.
Cane output in FY2026 YTD was reported above FY2025 YTD in USDA monthly SMD tables (higher cane production through Apr 2026).
Beverage-channel deliveries were notably stronger in FY2026 YTD (+11.3% vs FY2025 YTD in USDA SMD category table).
whats_shrinking: FY2026 YTD total exports dropped sharply versus FY2025 YTD, indicating limited international outlet growth.
FY2026 YTD total imports from non-program and program channels were lower than prior-year YTD levels after the 2025 production/shortage cycle and ongoing TRQ constraints.
Hotels/restaurants/institution deliveries were down in FY2026 YTD vs FY2025 YTD.
recent_developments: 2025-07-17: USDA ERS monthly outlook language reflected an upward revision in U.S. FY2026/27 sugar supply to 14.268 million short tons raw value (STRV).

2025-12-15: USDA ERS December 2025 outlook reported lower refined sugar price support conditions, citing mid-2025/26 bulk refined beet sugar spot around 41 cents per pound and high-tier refined world sugar around 45–46 cents per pound.
2026-02-10: USDA-FSA reassigned 315,464 short tons, raw value, of FY2026 Florida cane sugar allotment to Louisiana processors.
2026-06-11: USDA FSA published April 2026 Sweetener Market Data with FY2026 YTD deliveries and use; total deliveries were 7,188,423 STRV and domestic human-consumption deliveries were 7,137,384 STRV.
2026-07-16: USDA ERS released Sugar and Sweeteners Outlook: July 2026 (SSS-M-455), updating FY2025/26 and FY2026/27 outlook assumptions.
2026-07-17: USTR published FY2026 WTO TRQ allocations, confirming 1,117,195 MTRV raw cane in-quota for FY2026 and no added specialty sugar to the refined sugar TRQ.
outlook: Near-term outlook is modestly constructive but not expansive: domestic use is expected to remain near-flat to mildly higher, while heavy policy management likely keeps market conditions stable relative to prior years. Key upside in FY2026/27 comes from stable food-grade demand and any substitution toward real sugar by branded food and beverage producers; downside risk is export weakness, import-competition pressure, and pricing softness when stock levels rise.
themes: Protected domestic sugar regime (allotments, loans, TRQs)
Input and policy sensitivity
Channel drift toward packaged consumption
High inventory/price pressure phases
Slow channel recovery in restaurants vs packaged retail and beverage strength
one_sentence: The U.S. sugar processing market remains stable at roughly 12.4 million short tons in FY2026/27 with tight policy-managed imports, high-cost legacy supports, and uneven demand by end-use channel.

title: Sugarcane Harvesting in the US
one_liner: US sugarcane harvesting in 2026 is policy-bound, mechanized, and increasingly concentrated in Florida-Louiana operations.
overview: US sugarcane production remains concentrated in Florida and Louisiana, with Texas at or near zero output in 2025/26. USDA’s February 2026 Crop Production forecast put the 2025 crop at 35.9 million tons for sugar and seed on 949,000 harvested acres (up 1% from January and up 4% from last season). ERS reported a strong 2025/26 rebound (4.162 million short tons raw value) but revised the 2026/27 cane outlook down to 4.088 million STRV, with total US sugar supply projected at 14.062 million STRV.

key_stats.market_size: US sugarcane and seed production: 35.9 million tons in the 2025 crop year (NASS February 2026); US cane sugar forecast: 4.162 million STRV in FY 2025/26 and 4.088 million STRV in FY 2026/27.
key_stats.growth: 2025 crop production +1% from January 2026 estimate; +4% from prior season. FY 2025/26 cane sugar output +64,000 STRV from FY 2024/25; FY 2026/27 cane sugar output -130,000 STRV from FY 2025/26. FY 2025/26 imports reduced 25% from FY 2024/25 in ERS outlook framing.

baseline_2022.market_size: IBIS baseline revenue 2022: R$1,398 million (source report: March 30, 2022).
baseline_2022.growth: IBIS baseline CAGR 2005-2022: 1.41%; projected 2022-2028: 0.63%.

how_it_makes_money: Growers earn through sugarcane sale contracts to processors, typically priced via by-product-adjusted formulas and minimum grower payment rules tied to sugar recovery. Processors convert cane to sugar under a tightly managed domestic price-support framework (marketing allotments, loan rates, and tariff-rate quota mechanics), which helps sustain domestic price levels relative to world sugar. Revenue also benefits from policy-protected domestic market structure and byproduct revenue streams in some operations (notably molasses and energy co-products).

cost_structure.field_and_harvest: Mechanized harvest labor, fuel, fertilizer, and crop establishment/maintenance are largest variable costs.
cost_structure.post_harvest_and_transport: Quick transport and milling within the narrow sucrose window is critical; logistics costs rise with longer transport distances and congestion.
cost_structure.policy_and_compliance: Compliance with loan, allocation, and reporting frameworks; water, environmental, and land-use constraints in South Florida.
cost_structure.seasonality_risk: Weather-driven yield swings increase downside risk on fixed overheads, especially in hurricane or flood-prone zones.

major_players: Florida Crystals (FY 2026 revised Florida allocation: 863,521 STRV)
Growers Co-op. of FL (FY 2026 revised Florida allocation: 439,888 STRV)
U.S. Sugar Corp (FY 2026 revised Florida allocation: 997,696 STRV)
Sugar Growers and Refiners (FY 2026 Louisiana allocation: 1,621,172 STRV)
M.A. Patout & Sons (FY 2026 Louisiana allocation: 718,502 STRV)
Amalgamated Sugar Co (major beet/cane-integrated player in Federal Register allotment disclosures)
current_dynamics: The sector is operating under a managed-supply regime: USDA set FY 2026 OAQ at 10,166,000 STRV and reassigned cane allocations from Florida to Louisiana (315,464 STRV) in February 2026; ERS now projects a softer 2026/27 supply path, while acreage and yield improvements in Louisiana offset Florida softness.
whats_growing: Florida-to-Louisiana share shift continues: Louisiana surpassed Florida in consecutive recent years and absorbed 315,464 STRV of FY 2026 cane allotment in reassignment.
2025/26 Louisiana campaign strength improved with record-or-near-record production (ERS August 2025 state split increase to about 2.154 million STRV).
Policy support remains active through CCC loan-rate floors and active marketing-allotment administration.
whats_shrinking: US federal loan and policy revisions show tightening relative to prior years: 2026/27 total sugar supply forecast is lower than 2025/26.
2025/26 U.S. cane sugar rose slightly, but FY 2026/27 US cane sugar is forecast lower at 4.088 million STRV.
Texas remains non-producing for FY 2025/26 in official reallocation tables.
recent_developments: 2025-09-26: USDA raised FY 2026 raw cane loan rates (Florida: 24.00 cents/lb; Louisiana: 25.11 cents/lb raw cane sugar loan-rate context in 2025/26 CCC guidance).
2025-09-26: USDA announced minimum grower payment references (Florida: $34.62/net ton; Louisiana: $39.29/gross ton) and no Feedstock Flexibility actions for FY 2024/25 reporting period.
2025-08-18: ERS August 2025 outlook showed US 2025/26 cane sugar up to 4.162 million STRV with Florida slightly down and Louisiana rising.
2026-02-10: NASS Crop Production forecast sugar and seed at 35.9 million tons, 949,000 acres, 37.8 tons/acre (up 0.3 ton from January).
2026-02-10: USDA reassigned 315,464 short tons raw value of Florida FY 2026 cane allotment to Louisiana.
2026-05-18: ERS May 2026 outlook forecast FY 2026/27 US sugar supply at 14.062 million STRV, with cane sugar at 4.088 million STRV (lowest since 2019/20).
outlook: Near-term supply in 2026/27 looks constrained versus 2025/26, so concentration risk and policy execution risk (allotments, loan program details, and TRQ use) dominate earnings variability. The most likely trajectory is continued Louisiana momentum, flat-to-lower total sugar output, and ongoing consolidation around large processor groups with mechanized harvesting.
themes: Policy-managed domestic sugar market
Regional production concentration
Weather- and climate-driven yield variation
Shift in harvested area and productivity by state
Strategic reallocation rather than structural price liberalization
Competition from alternative sweetener and processed-sugar market exposure
one_sentence: US sugarcane output held near record levels in 2025/26, but government allotment reallocations and lower 2026/27 production expectations are tightening sector economics.

title: Summer Camps
one_liner: The U.S. summer camp market is a tuition-led recreation industry for children, teens, families, and growing adult retreat segments that is shifting toward premium specialty and experiential programming.
overview: The IBIS baseline shows this industry reached about USD 3,005M in 2021 after a 2020 shock, with recovery expected to continue as demand for organized child supervision and structured enrichment rises. In 2025, broader vacation/recreational camp analyses estimate total US market size around USD 24.26B with overnight-heavy segments estimated near USD 4.6B, showing re-expansion of high-value spending. At the same time, cost inflation, staffing constraints, and stronger competition from substitute daytime programs are increasing pressure on entry-level operators and lower-margin offerings.
how_it_makes_money: Overnight and program tuition/fees (primary revenue line).
Food, lodging, and bundled activity charges.
Ancillary add-ons: specialty trip fees, excursions, and program extensions.
Associated merchandise and optional premium services (wellness sessions, transport, extended stays).
Corporate and group bookings for retreats, team-building, and branded sessions.

cost_structure.labor: Recreation workers are core to operations; BLS reports median annual wages for recreation workers were USD 35,380 in May 2024 with 327,700 jobs.
cost_structure.facilities: Housing, meals, transport, grounds, utilities, and maintenance are fixed-to-variable hybrids tied to season length and capacity utilization.
cost_structure.safety_and_compliance: Background checks, medical screening, insurance, and incident prevention create recurring costs that are higher in overnight youth environments.
cost_structure.acquisition_and_admin: Seasonal marketing, registration infrastructure, and customer support are increasingly digital and price-sensitive.
cost_structure.pricing_pressure: Rising operating labor and facility costs are forcing camps to rebalance mix toward premium add-ons and higher-margin niche offerings.

current_dynamics: Specialty and outcomes-driven camps (sports, STEM, leadership, wellness) are outpacing generic volume models.
Competition from day-camp and other structured alternatives continues to compress pricing power in core overnight segments.
Costs are rising, so operators are emphasizing higher-ARPPU packages, repeat-family retention, and occupancy management.
Labor-market structure remains seasonal and concentrated in recreation-worker roles, creating recurring staffing risk.
Family willingness to spend has increased, but parents are increasingly selective on value and ROI of each program.
whats_growing: Overnight, specialty, and skill-focused programming (sports, educational, adventure, wellness).
Regional and family-adjacent demand in higher-capacity markets and adult-focused retreat overlays.
Use of online discovery/registration and program bundling for conversion across session types.
whats_shrinking: Low-complexity mass overnight camps that do not differentiate on skill outcomes.
Purely discretionary volume expansion without retention levers; many operators report more capacity held static or maintained rather than rapidly growing.
Net margin headroom as wage and safety-related costs rise faster than generic session pricing.
recent_developments: 2026-02: Jewish camp census report noted 2025 overnight/day sector waitlists declined and many camps reported maintained or lower-than-full capacity in more weeks.
2026-02: FJC 2025 field data showed average overnight capacity remained near 301 beds per camp and day-camp average around 386 spots, indicating selective scaling rather than broad expansion.
2025-01: Mordor/industry trackers estimated 2025 market size at USD 24.26B and 2024 at USD 23.05B, with 2025-2030 CAGR above 5%.
2025-05: Morning Brew cited ACA-based pricing that in 2024 average day camp cost was USD 87/day and overnight was USD 173/day; 25% of parents expected to spend over USD 2,000 on summer camp.
2026-06: Morning Brew reported the youth camp sector at roughly USD 4.6B (IBIS-based estimate) and described a premium premiumization trend with tuition rising.
2025-07: BLS recreation workers profile showed 327,700 jobs in 2024 and projected 4% growth 2024-2034 (about 68,100 openings per year).
outlook: Near-term demand remains constructive through 2026 as family income sensitivity, structured youth time, and wellness preferences support participation, but earnings power will depend on operators’ ability to balance safety, staffing, and pricing. Expect slower headline growth in commoditized overnight offerings and stronger growth in differentiated, measurable learning/outcomes and family-adult hybrid formats.
themes: Premiumization toward specialization
Operational resilience through staffing and safety systems
Hybrid portfolio strategy: children + adults + corporate retreats
Digital-first program discovery and pricing intelligence
one_sentence: After a pandemic downturn, camps have rebounded strongly, but inflation-driven cost pressure and substitution from lower-cost day-camp formats are forcing operators toward specialty programming, wellness positioning, and stronger retention playbooks.

title: Sunglasses Stores
one_liner: Single-location and chain retailers selling non-prescription sunglasses and related accessories remain a mature, service-heavy U.S. niche pressured by digital channels.
overview: The U.S. sunglasses retail segment sells mostly non-prescription and specialty eyewear products; demand is tied to discretionary income, travel and outdoor activity, with premium brand preference concentrated in physical try-on experiences. Industry structure is concentrated among large vertically integrated players, while online-only and mass retailers intensify margin pressure.

key_stats.market_size: $2.1bn (2025, projected)

baseline_2022.growth: +4.8% 2020-2022 (implied from 2.38% CAGR over 2020-2026 path)

how_it_makes_money: Revenues are driven by in-store frame sales, upgrades, premium lens and accessory add-ons, and store-level service fees; Warby Parker-type models also combine physical retail, direct online sales, and eyewear subscriptions/experiences, showing this segment’s viable hybrid format.
cost_structure: Principal costs are inventory acquisition (including freight/portions of optical components), rent and depreciation of physical retail space, retail payroll, marketing, and fulfillment/logistics; in legacy peers, wage costs were about 22.0% of revenue in 2020, while major players report heavy CPG-style marketing and shipping pressure.
major_players: Amazon (online eyewear competitors and traffic capture)
current_dynamics: E-commerce is growing faster than total retail, while standalone specialty sunglasses chains face stronger share pressure despite sustained demand for premium and fashion-oriented eyewear; online and experiential physical formats are converging.
whats_growing: 2026-05: U.S. retail e-commerce in Q1 2026 was $326.7bn, up 9.8% year-over-year, and represented 16.9% of total retail sales.
2026-05: Total U.S. retail sales in Q1 2026 were $1,929.0bn, up 3.9% year-over-year.
2025-12: Warby Parker 2025 total revenue was $871.905m, up 13.0% year-over-year.
2026-06: Warby Parker reported 2025 retail channel revenue of $631.013m and e-commerce revenue of $240.892m.
2025-12: Sunglass Hut’s own locator page lists 1,429 U.S. stores.
whats_shrinking: 2026-05: Q1 2026 e-commerce growth (+9.8% yoy) outpaced total retail growth (+3.9% yoy), highlighting downside pressure on pure physical channel share.
2025-12: In Warby’s 2025 model, advertising spend rose to $113.9m vs $95.8m in 2024 (+19.0%), signaling higher customer acquisition intensity.
2025-12: Shipping-related fulfillment costs in COGS rose from $20.4m in 2024 to $25.2m in 2025 (+23.5%), indicating rising direct-fulfillment burden.
recent_developments: 2026-06: Sunglass Hut store locator listed 1,429 Sunglass Hut stores in the United States.
2026-05: Census Quarterly Retail E-Commerce report (Q1 2026) posted: e-commerce $326.7bn, total retail $1.929T, e-commerce share 16.9%.
2026-07: Census July 16, 2026 monthly report: June 2026 retail sales up 6.7% from June 2025 and up 0.2% vs May 2026.
2025-12: Warby Parker FY2025 report showed revenue growth to $871.905m and disclosed AI-development partnership with Google with up to $75m each side in committed contributions.
outlook: Through 2026-2029, the segment is likely to remain modestly positive in sales but structurally more polarized: stores that combine brand depth, service, and instant availability will likely outperform, while catalog-style or low-service models may lose mix share.
themes: experience-led store conversion
direct-to-consumer + store pick-up
e-commerce penetration and channel share shift
brand-licensed premium positioning
AI-enabled shopping and personalization
