one_sentence: U.S. sunglasses specialists still grow modestly, but sustained e-commerce acceleration and omnichannel competition are reducing reliance on traditional stand-alone store traffic.

title: Sunscreen Manufacturing
one_liner: A mature, brand-led U.S. segment where stronger UV-awareness is offset by tighter ingredient regulation and high standards for efficacy, labeling, and safety.
overview: The industry is a specialized part of personal care manufacturing with concentrated brand control and steady demand from pharmacies, beauty channels, and direct sales. Baseline IBIS data indicate a small but stable category with near-term growth, while 2025–2026 signals show a broader sun care context: the U.S. sun care cosmetics market reached about US$2,149.4 million in 2025, with sunscreen accounting for about 29.20% of that market.

key_stats.market_size: US$574.2 million (2026 IBIS projection) and US$2,149.4 million (2025 U.S. sun care cosmetics market; sunscreen share 29.20% in 2024)
key_stats.growth: IBIS: 2.7% CAGR (2021-2026); GVR: 7.3% CAGR for U.S. sun care cosmetics from 2025-2033
key_stats.demand_context: AAD 2026 survey of 1,132 adults shows 57% regular sunscreen use; 33% sunburned in 2025; and 47% exposed to sunscreen misinformation
key_stats.health_context: CDC notes 6.1 million U.S. people are treated for skin cancer each year (2025) with annual treatment costs of US$8.9 billion

baseline_2022.market_size: ~US$515.8 million (derived from IBIS baseline around 2021 US$502.2 million and IBIS 2021-2026 2.7% trajectory)
baseline_2022.growth: ~2.7% annualized (IBIS projection path to 2026)

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers capture margin through branded sunscreen formulations sold in pharmacies, superstores, grocery, and e-commerce, with premiums for broad-spectrum efficacy, SPF level, water resistance, spray/lotion formats, ingredient positioning (mineral or reef-safe), and multi-benefit combinations like anti-aging or skincare hybrids.

cost_structure.raw_materials: UV actives and petrochemical-linked inputs are the largest variable cost and can swing with chemical feedstock volatility.
cost_structure.formulation_and_compliance: Additional R&D, stability testing, ingredient compatibility work, and expanded safety/evidence packages are required under OTC monograph oversight.
cost_structure.quality_and_liability: Labeling controls, warning language, and lot-level quality requirements add regulatory and quality-assurance cost.
cost_structure.go_to_market: Higher channel costs in pharmacy/drug and beauty retail plus marketing for differentiated positioning.

current_dynamics: Demand remains supported by rising prevention awareness and high perceived sun risk, while FDA has begun enabling filter innovation after long delay (2026 bemotrizinol decision). At the same time, category growth is moderated by stricter ingredient scrutiny and substitution of standalone sunscreen by high-SPF cosmetics and skincare hybrids.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 growth in premium SPF30+ and multi-functional products (broader skincare value bundles)
Demand for mineral, reef-safe, and skin-comfort positioning
R&D-led launches with cleaner and digitally marketed product narratives
Sunscreen usage in beauty-format products such as SPF-mist, tints, and functional cosmetics
whats_shrinking: Commodity sunscreen segments and low-SPF standalone SKUs under stronger price pressure
Some standalone sunscreen demand due to sunscreen-containing makeup/skin formulas
Legacy chemical-filter portfolios that require longer regulatory defensibility and are exposed to public scrutiny
recent_developments: 2025-12-12: FDA announced proposed order OTC000039 to add bemotrizinol (up to 6%) to OTC sunscreen monograph (comment window opened).
2026-01-26: FDA comment period on proposed bemotrizinol order closed (FDA-2025-N-6494).
2026-06-10: Federal Register notice published for final administrative order OTC000039; bemotrizinol added as GRASE ingredient up to 6%.
2026-05-01: AAD released Practice Sun Safety Survey results (1,132 adults, 2026 study period; fewer than three in five Americans use sunscreen regularly; 33% sunburned in 2025).
2025-08-15: CDC updated skin cancer burden messaging, including 6.1 million U.S. patients treated annually and US$8.9B annual treatment costs.
2025-08: Grand View Research updated 2025 sun care report with US$2,149.4 million market size and major players landscape.
outlook: Outlook to 2026 is cautiously positive: base demand remains healthy due to persistent sun-risk messaging, but the industry likely stays structurally mature with modest volume growth and profitability pressure from ingredient validation, litigation-sensitive claims, and low-end competition.
themes: Regulation-led product innovation reset (FDA OTC monograph additions)
Health-risk messaging lifting perceived need for daily and year-round sun protection
Convergence of sunscreen with cosmetics and skin-care categories
Ongoing cost pressure from compliance, testing, and premium channel competition
Shift from pure efficacy products to ingredient-transparency and lifestyle-led formats
one_sentence: U.S. sunscreen manufacturing is a medium-sized mature market that still grows with sun-health demand and premium products, while ingredient approval constraints and substitution into cosmetics keep downside risk elevated.

title: Supermarkets & Grocery Stores in the US
one_liner: US supermarkets and grocery stores remain a high-volume, low-margin necessity sector with modest demand growth and faster gains in digital fulfillment.
overview: US grocery retailing is a mature, scale-driven industry where traffic and spending are relatively stable, but competitive pressure from discount formats, warehouse clubs, and supercenters keeps pricing pressure high. Data in 2025-26 shows grocery sales growing modestly year-over-year while productivity headwinds, labor costs, and inflation pass-through keep margins vulnerable. Leading operators are leaning into delivery, loyalty, private-label, and ad/fee-based earnings to defend returns.

key_stats.market_size: USD 1,025.149B (food and beverage stores gross output, NAICS 445, 2025, not seasonally adjusted annual)
key_stats.growth: +2.4% sector output growth in 2025 versus 2024; March/June 2026 grocery flow growth around +0.9% year-over-year
key_stats.monthly_sales_flow: USD 85.612B (food and beverage stores, May 2026, seasonally adjusted, FRED MRTSSM445USS)
key_stats.labor_base: 3.259M employees in NAICS 445 (all employees, Mar 2026, BLS)
key_stats.wages: $22.57/hour average hourly earnings (all employees, May 2026, BLS)
key_stats.cost_pressure_indicator: unit labor costs +3.3% in 2025; labor productivity -1.7% in 2025 (BLS NAICS 445)

baseline_2022.growth: CAGR 2002-2022: +1.45%; projected 2022-2028 CAGR: +0.84% (IBIS baseline)

how_it_makes_money: Primary economics come from high-turn grocery sales volume with thin merchandising margins, plus upside from private-label assortment, pharmacy, fuel, and services. Larger players increasingly add earnings from e-commerce delivery, in-market advertising, and membership fees to diversify away from pure margin-on-shelf economics.

cost_structure.labor: Labor is a major variable cost; BLS shows 3.259M workers in NAICS 445 and rising unit labor costs of +3.3% in 2025.
cost_structure.sourcing: Commodity and product cost pressure is managed through procurement scale and frequent promotions; smaller format/value propositions remain central.
cost_structure.productivity: Labor productivity declined in 2025, supporting continued focus on automation, labor scheduling, and fulfillment efficiency.
cost_structure.operating_expenses: Digital growth raises handling, delivery, and infrastructure cost; Albertsons cited delivery/handling as a margin headwind in 2026 guidance period.

current_dynamics: 2026 momentum is strongest in omnichannel execution: Walmart reported strong e-commerce acceleration and membership growth, while Albertsons reported rising digital sales and a shift in profit mix despite margin pressure. Smaller assortment and value formats remain active in the channel mix.
whats_growing: Walmart U.S. eCommerce and digital fulfillment remain high-growth levers; Q4 FY26 U.S. eCommerce growth was 27%.
Albertsons reported double-digit digital sales growth (16% Q4, 21% full year FY2025).
Private-label and value-led assortments continue to support basket retention under inflation-sensitive consumer budgets.
Membership and ancillary revenue pools (e.g., Walmart membership fees, Walmart Connect advertising) are expanding as earnings diversification.
whats_shrinking: Pure grocery margin expansion remains constrained; Albertsons reported gross margin softness partly from delivery and handling cost pressure.
Unit labor costs rose faster than labor productivity in 2025, indicating a tighter operating cost environment.
Traditional format share pressure from discount and warehouse club channels remains a structural margin drag.
recent_developments: 2026-07-16: Census advance retail release showed grocery-store sales up +0.9% year-over-year in June 2026 (with a slight -0.4% month-over-month change).
2026-05-01: FRED reported food and beverage stores monthly sales of 85,612 (seasonally adjusted, millions of dollars).
2026-04-23: Walmart reported FY26 grocery sales in Walmart U.S. of 285,482 (vs 276,003 in FY25).
2026-02-19: Walmart Q4 FY26 release said Walmart U.S. eCommerce growth was 27% and noted the eighth consecutive quarter of >20% eCommerce growth.
2025-11-25: Census data for Sep 2025 showed grocery stores with positive annual growth versus Sep 2024 in the latest monthly release.
outlook: Short-term growth is likely modest at the category level, but winners will be operators that scale digital and membership ecosystems while controlling labor and fulfillment cost per unit. A 2026–2028 trajectory is one of modest top-line expansion with selective margin recovery where labor productivity and automation gains outrun cost inflation.
themes: Omnichannel and last-mile fulfillment as core growth engines
Value-led competition intensifying (private label, limited-assortment, discount formats)
Margin diversification into advertising, fees, and services
Labor-cost management and productivity via automation/AI
Consolidation pressure from discount and supercenter scale
one_sentence: In 2026, grocery retailers are holding demand steady while shifting more sales, data, and profit contributions to digital and omnichannel channels.

title: Supply Chain Management Services
one_liner: Demand in the US is shifting toward higher-control, network-wide supply chain execution services as companies redesign trade routes and invest in AI-enabled orchestration.
overview: Supply chain management services support firms across planning, sourcing, transport coordination, inventory control, fulfillment, and returns. In the 2025-2026 period, demand is increasingly tied to tariff-driven network redesign, e-commerce and cold-chain intensity, and tighter operating discipline under volatile transport costs. The market is also pulled between two forces: rising complexity that rewards managed expertise, and cloud software options that let some buyers internalize planning functions.

market_size.scope: US third-party logistics market proxy for supply-chain execution services

how_it_makes_money: Providers charge by project fees for network design and supplier coordination, recurring management contracts for transport and fulfillment execution, transaction-based margins on brokerage/dispatch, and platform subscriptions for visibility, planning, and exception management. Value grows when clients can reduce total landed cost, improve inventory turns, and stabilize service levels across multi-modal networks.
cost_structure: Labor intensity remains a structural cost: warehousing and storage employment in 2026 was about 1.85 million workers with production/nonsupervisory hourly earnings near $26.30 and all-employee hourly around $26.76 in mid-2026. Variable cost pressure is significant from transport economics; BTS data for January 2026 shows truck transportation service costs up 2.0% year-over-year and freight-related service inflation above many other service categories. Software and data-stack costs are rising as firms add AI, visibility, and automation layers faster than before.
current_dynamics: The US is operating in a reconfiguration regime: trade-friction and tariff volatility in 2025 pushed firms toward alternative sourcing geography and more robust network redundancy. Meanwhile, AI is changing procurement and planning workflows, with procurement criteria moving toward agent-enabled and autonomous routing/forecast functions. Service providers are competing on execution reliability and service integration because buyers increasingly expect both cost control and resilience.
whats_growing: 2025-2026: US trucking volumes are projected to recover, with ATA forecasting 1.6% freight tonnage growth in 2025 and long-run freight revenue expansion, reflecting sustained industrial and consumption demand.
2025-2026: US 3PL/fulfillment value continues to expand, with Mordor projecting size from 219.62 in 2025 to 227.69 in 2026.
2026: Life sciences and healthcare logistics workloads are expanding faster than peers in 3PL demand mix because of stricter chain-of-custody and temperature-control requirements.
2026: Life-cycle competition is favoring hybrid models that combine dedicated assets with digital brokerage, as reported by US 3PL service share analysis.
whats_shrinking: 2025: The share of US goods trade growth attributed to the China corridor weakened materially; McKinsey reports much of the 2025 reallocation reduced US import/export flows on that route.
2025-2026: Purely transactional logistics workflows are being commoditized where buyers can substitute direct software tools for low-touch planning functions.
2026: Arrangement of freight and cargo PPI moved -0.4% from Jan 2025 to Jan 2026, showing volatility and pricing competition in parts of the transport services value chain.
recent_developments: 2025-01-16: ATA forecast 2025 truck tonnage +1.6% and trucking remained 72.7% of tonnage and 76.9% of freight revenue in 2024 baselines.
2025-07-02: JPMorgan notes full 2025 tariff scenario could add up to $187.7B in direct import costs for midsize firms; remaining policy framework still implied high residual costs near $82.3B.

2025-04-07: McKinsey trade monitoring shows US effective tariff rate rising to about 22% in early April 2025, then easing near 15% by year-end, while US–China trade displacement reshaped corridor shares.
2025-04-07: McKinsey reports roughly $80B of US sourcing replaced to reroute trade exposure from China in 2025, strengthening near/alternative sourcing flows.
2026-02-27: BTS transportation PPI data show Jan 2026 freight inflation by mode: air +1.7%, truck +2.0%, water +1.0%, arrangement of freight and cargo -0.4%.
2026-04-07: Gartner forecasts SCM software with agentic AI to rise from < $2B in 2025 to $53B in 2030, shifting service expectations toward AI-enabled execution teams.
outlook: Near-term growth in 2026-2028 is likely to stay positive but uneven: service demand should stay supported by reconfigured trade flows, consumer and healthcare fulfillment complexity, and digital visibility adoption, while price competition and software substitution cap margin expansion. Providers that combine domain expertise, labor-flexible operations, and robust AI-enabled execution stacks should outperform commodity providers.
themes: AI-enabled supply chain orchestration
Trade-policy-driven network reconfiguration
Nearshoring, friendshoring, and corridor redesign
Labor intensity vs automation
Hybrid asset/digital logistics model
one_sentence: US supply chain management services in 2025-2026 are growing as a resilience service layer for manufacturing, retail, and healthcare logistics, but margin pressure rises from labor and software competition.

title: Surgical Apparel Manufacturing
one_liner: US surgical apparel is a mature, import-sensitive manufacturing segment with stable procedure demand from aging and obese patient populations but sustained margin pressure from supplier concentration and tariff-driven cost inflation.
overview: IBIS-style baseline data still shows a small, structurally pressured US niche market; recent 2024–26 public signals point to slow volume support from procedure demand and hospital operating continuity, but stronger pressure on pricing from large-volume imports and reimbursement discipline. Demand is now increasingly shaped by outpatient-site surgery policy, while leading firms are defending share via product differentiation and hospital-system-oriented solutions.

market_size.value: US$930.0 million (industry revenue projection in latest IBIS baseline window)

imports_and_supply.value: US$307.9 million for HS 621050 protective surgical/medical garments (World Bank WITS)
imports_and_supply.dominant_supplier_share: China approximately 68.0% of HS 621050 US imports (US$209.4m of US$307.9m)

key_stats.growth: n/a

baseline_2022.market_size: US$893.2 million (industry revenue level reported in the IBIS baseline narrative for the 2021 horizon, nearest benchmark available)
baseline_2022.growth: -1.5% CAGR (five-year 2002-2021 decline profile from baseline)

how_it_makes_money.model: Manufacturers/distributors sell protective apparel (single-use and reusable drapes/gowns, OR apparel, packaging-linked systems) to hospital systems, ASCs, and procedure settings.
how_it_makes_money.revenue_mix_shift: Evidence from Medline and Cardinal shows increasing weight in OR-focused and prime-vendor distribution relationships: Medline's Surgical Solutions line reached US$6,166 million in 2025 (+12.7% y/y), driven by kitting and operating-room product volume.
how_it_makes_money.pricing_dynamics: Most revenue is transactional, contract-based, and exposed to hospital purchasing concentration; premium is increasingly tied to product performance and operational reliability rather than raw commodity price.

cost_structure.material_and_import_costs: Higher import costs are a direct margin risk; Medline reported margin compression from tariffs and sourcing costs (adjusted margin impact in 2025 Surgical Solutions/brand commentary).
cost_structure.manufacturing_and_fulfillment: Labor intensity is moderate, but faster shipment and distribution requirements add meaningful cost exposure (higher outbound freight noted in 2025 filings).
cost_structure.sales_and_admin: SG&A was up 10.1% year-over-year in Medline's 2025 filings, with staffing, distribution and selling costs explicit drivers.
cost_structure.margin_profile: Gross margin moved down in Medline's 2025 filing (Medline Brand gross profit ratio roughly 27.3% to 26.4%), consistent with a price-sensitive, imported-component-heavy environment.

current_dynamics: 2025-02-25 SEC filings and 2026 policy releases show offsetting forces: (1) procedure-site migration and reimbursement rule changes expanding outpatient pathways, and (2) persistent global import competition keeping list pricing pressured; large hospital and distribution relationships remain the key moat in this segment.
whats_growing: Medline's surgical solutions segment reported strong 2025 growth (+12.7% to US$6,166m), indicating sustained OR/operating-room kit demand.
Policy in CY 2026 increased procedural flexibility for outpatient settings (285 procedures moved off inpatient-only list in phase), widening downstream demand for surgery support consumables.
Product development is moving toward workflow-driven OR usability and comfort/ergonomics, with major supplier innovation programs highlighted publicly in 2024.
whats_shrinking: Margin room is constrained by low-cost imported protected apparel; WITS HS 621050 import data in 2024 shows China at ~68% share of this category.
Reimbursement controls in outpatient settings are increasing scrutiny and site-of-service migration pressure on hospital margins, which can suppress discretionary consumables expansion.
Industry participation is structurally downward through consolidation and acquisition by larger healthcare supply ecosystems.
recent_developments: 2024-11-13 — Cardinal Health published an industry-facing update on drape and gown innovation and new design-forward protection features for surgical use.
2024-12 (data release) — CDC BRFSS-based adult obesity prevalence maps were updated, indicating continued high obesity prevalence context for procedure demand.
2025-02-25 — Medline filed its 2025 Form 10-K, reporting Surgical Solutions net sales of US$6,166m (+12.7%) for FY2025.
2025-11-21 — CMS finalized CY 2026 OPPS/ASC rule setting a 2.6% rate update factor for qualifying hospitals/ASCs and adding 289 ASC-covered procedures.
2026-01 — AHA Fast Facts 2026 (using 2024 survey baseline) reported 6,100 US hospitals and 907,216 staffed beds, reinforcing demand breadth across the care system.
outlook: For 2026, this niche remains in mild structural decline if measured in broad commodity terms, but competitive outcomes will be selective: suppliers with stronger OR-system integration, quality credentials, and lower-cost distributed logistics can still grow share even as volume growth stays modest.
themes: Import concentration
Outpatient surgery expansion
Reimbursement discipline
Product differentiation and OR workflow innovation
Consolidation and distributor-led scale
one_sentence: The 2025–26 picture is of a constrained but still growing domestic market for high-compliance OR apparel, driven by outpatient procedure migration and hospital safety spend while globalized low-cost sourcing limits pricing power.

title: Surgical Instrument Manufacturing
one_liner: Surgical instrument demand is lifted by aging populations and outpatient surgery expansion, while payment and cost pressures remain elevated.
overview: The IBIS baseline shows a 2022 U.S. market revenue of USD 40,431m and an expected turnaround from weak prior growth to a projected 2022-2028 growth path above 2% annually. Demand drivers are still concentrated in aging-related surgery demand, minimally invasive workflows, and hospital procedure migration. In 2025-2026, policy changes accelerated site-of-care movement toward ambulatory surgery while also tightening payment assumptions in both ASC and inpatient settings.
how_it_makes_money: Revenue is largely from direct sale of reusable instruments, single-use disposable accessory lines, and recurring service/software/serviceware tied to surgical systems. Major economics are recurring: higher procedure volume drives repeat instrument consumption, upgrades, and service contracts.

drivers: precision-metal and device-grade component procurement costs
quality systems, sterilization and traceability overhead
workforce labor and compliance in heavily regulated manufacturing
warranty, field service, and hospital support obligations
cost_structure.pricing_pressure: CMS payment-rate controls in inpatient and outpatient payment systems constrain device pricing pass-through and push procurement toward total-cost-of-care contracting.

current_dynamics: U.S. population aging: persons 65+ reached 61.2m (Vint. 2024 estimate, Census Office reporting in June 2025).
CMS CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule expanded outpatient flexibility (2.6% update factors, 285 IPO removals, expanded ASC procedure access).
CMS FY 2026 IPPS/LTCH final rule delivered 2.6% inpatient hospital operating update for quality-reporting hospitals and removed the temporary low-wage-index policy.
ASCs remain a core delivery channel: CMS-based ASCA data as of March 2025 shows over 6,500 Medicare-certified ASCs.
whats_growing: Outpatient/Ambulatory delivery growth as procedures shift from inpatient settings toward ASCs under CMS policy updates in 2025-2026.
Robotic and minimally invasive platform usage: Intuitive Surgical reports 2025 U.S. da Vinci procedure growth of roughly 15%.
Hospital infrastructure scale: AHA 2026 Fast Facts sample shows 6,100 hospitals and 35.658.583 total admissions.
Recurring revenue models around disposables, instruments, and service tied to installed system bases.
whats_shrinking: Pure inpatient-volume exposure for standard instrument sets where procedures migrate to outpatient settings.
Margin resilience from standalone capital sales, as reimbursement and site-of-care payment rules increase pressure.
Import competitiveness risk remains meaningful in selected components and low-margin categories amid broader trade regime volatility.
recent_developments: 2025-11-21: CMS CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule set a 2.6% update to qualifying facilities and added 271 IPO-removed codes to ASC coverage pathways.
2025-07-31: CMS FY 2026 IPPS/LTCH rule finalized 2.6% inpatient update for quality-reporting hospitals and projected +$5.0bn operating-payment impact.
2025-07-01: US Census Bureau reported U.S. persons age 65+ at 61.2 million, up 3.1% from 2023 to 2024 vintage baseline.
2026-02 (AHA update): Fast Facts on U.S. Hospitals 2026 showed 6,100 hospitals and 35,658,583 admissions in the latest sample.
2025-12-31: Intuitive Surgical reported 2025 U.S. da Vinci procedures up about 15% year over year and instruments/accessories revenue up 19% to $6.02bn.
2025: ASCA map data (CMS source) showed over 6,500 Medicare-certified ASCs in the United States.
outlook: Short-term direction is constructive (procedural demand and outpatient expansion) but uneven across product lines. By 2026-2027, winning teams are likely those with strong clinical workflow integration, service-backed platform ecosystems, and disciplined operations under tighter hospital reimbursement. Market performance should trend above 2022 baseline but remain vulnerable to policy-induced pricing discipline and input inflation.
themes: Aging-demand tailwind
Outpatient migration
Site-of-care economics
Robotics and minimally invasive consumables
Quality/compliance-linked cost load
one_sentence: The U.S. surgical instrument manufacturing market is in moderate structural growth through higher procedural demand and shift to outpatient settings, but faces margin pressure from payer rules and cost inflation.

title: Surveying & Mapping Services in the US
one_liner: A fragmented geospatial services industry where demand is driven by infrastructure, land development, and digital terrain data modernization.
overview: The industry provides topographic, cadastral, planimetric, and geospatial data services for construction, public works, utilities, real property, and environmental use cases. In 2026 the US market is around $11.0bn and the USGS-backed expansion of high-resolution elevation and hydrography programs is increasing demand for lidar and 3D terrain workflows. IBIS-style data indicates rivalry is high and steady, while no single player has a market share large enough to dominate.

baseline_2022.growth: -0.31% CAGR (projected 2022-2027)

how_it_makes_money: Charging for field-based surveying, mapping, GIS digitization, and geospatial analytics projects
Recurring work from repeat land, utility, and infrastructure clients
Higher-margin custom projects in engineering support, permitting, and compliance
Licensing/usage of processed spatial deliverables and model outputs through subscriptions or project retainers
Professional services integration with design, civil, and environmental workflows
cost_structure: Personnel: survey crews, geomatic technicians, GIS staff, and project managers
Field equipment: GNSS, total stations, lidar, and aerial imaging hardware (including depreciation/lease and maintenance)
Cloud/software stack: GIS platforms, processing tools, data storage, and cybersecurity
Insurance, compliance, quality assurance, and regulatory administration
Travel, mobilization, and field logistics in geographically dispersed jobs
major_players: No single firm has reportable dominant share (fragmented market)
current_dynamics: Demand remains tied to public infrastructure, construction productivity, and geospatial modernization, while automation is reducing repetitive field tasks but increasing dependence on high-quality data interpretation and QA. Market structure is still fragmented, creating strong price pressure in commodity survey scopes and stronger pricing power in integrated 3D/geospatial and data-intelligence offerings.
whats_growing: USGS-supported 3DEP/3DHP expansion and other federal geodata initiatives
Lidar, photogrammetry, and 3D terrain workflows across transportation, utilities, and flood-risk planning
Work tied to IIJA-era transportation and highway modernization spending
Hybrid consulting-plus-data models where mapping firms bundle analytics with surveying deliverables
whats_shrinking: Pure commodity topographic mapping without digital deliverable sophistication
Manual drafting and non-automated processing routines
Low-differentiation jobs in non-technology-upgraded survey capture
recent_developments: 2025-08-06: USGS issued FY26 3DNTM Data Collaboration Announcement to support FY26 3DEP and 3DHP data acquisition.
2025-08-06: USGS 3DNTM FAQ notes the FY26 webinar date and application workflow for project submission partnerships.
2025-10-01: FHWA Notice N4510.909 documented FY2026 apportionment for the NEVI Formula Program within HIP, including $9,454,400,000 appropriation context.
2026-04-10: FHWA IIJA funding page states FY2022-2026 highway apportionment and ~$350bn IIJA period context.
2026-06-29: FHWA Notice N4520.295 released, confirming FY2026 obligation-limitation redistribution mechanics and total annual amount of $62,657,105,821.
outlook: Near-term growth is likely moderate and mixed: demand is supported by transportation, energy, and climate-resilience work, while competition and commoditization keep margins under pressure. Winners are likely firms that combine high-precision field capture with scalable GIS/AI-ready geospatial analytics.
themes: 3D and lidar-first survey modernization
Infrastructure-led demand despite cyclical permitting and project timing
Public-private geospatial partnerships
Automation and digital QA replacing low-value manual collection
Workforce retention in technician and GIS roles
one_sentence: US surveying and mapping services are a moderate-growth, technically intensive niche in professional services, with 2026 market size at about $11.0bn across 16,909 businesses.

title: Sushi Restaurants
one_liner: The U.S. sushi restaurant industry is expanding through urban, convenience-oriented and automation-heavy formats, but rising labor, seafood, and operating costs keep margins under pressure.
overview: Sushi restaurants remain a niche-leaning but durable segment of the U.S. foodservice market, with growth driven by health-conscious eating, ethnic-menu mainstreaming, and increasing demand for fast-casual quality formats. The category is now split between high-ARPU experiential concepts and lower-ticket conveyor/roll-and-go models that compete on throughput and price perception. In 2025–2026, the industry dynamic is less about unit count alone and more about unit economics: lower comparable traffic can be offset by menu mix, automation, and tighter cost discipline.

key_stats.market_size: $27.9bn (2022 cited sector value), $34.9bn (2025 projected); legacy IBIS baseline reported $22.2bn revenue to $32.2bn by 2026 projection.
key_stats.growth: 2021→2022 estimated +23.5%; implied 2022→2025 +25.1% (about 7.8% CAGR); legacy IBIS-style 2021→2026 growth path around 7.7% annualized.

baseline_2022.growth: +23.5% YoY vs 2021 (industry-estimate cited, then used as baseline).

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily from food and beverage sales across dine-in, takeout, and delivery channels, with margin sensitivity tied to average transaction size and menu mix. Higher-margin components include premium rolls, omakase-style programs, and beverage pairings; volume and repeat frequency are supported by loyalty, convenience ordering, and location in dense urban zones.
cost_structure: Food and beverage and labor remain the largest variable costs. Kura Sushi reporting showed food+beverage costs around 29.2% and labor-related costs around 31.9% of sales in FY2024, while ONE Group-linked operations showed pressure from rent, staffing, and general operating support even in expansion periods. Additional pressure points include occupancy, new unit build costs, and increasing G&A as chains scale.
current_dynamics: Urban chain expansion continues, but operator profitability is constrained by high wage and food costs, prompting tighter controls on menu complexity, labor scheduling, and digitalization of ordering/transactions.
whats_growing: Conveyor-belt and quick-service sushi models, technology-led operations (digital ordering, automation, loyalty), and value-oriented premium positioning in high-income metro pockets.
whats_shrinking: Pure dine-in luxury/slow-traffic concepts without strong local demand concentration, and any chain strategy with weak throughput discipline under rising input and labor costs.
recent_developments: 2025-04-08: Kura Sushi reported FY2025 guidance of 14–15 new restaurants and stated food as a major cost driver while adding units.
2025-12-28: ONE Group disclosed 158 total venues, 86 Benihana and 12 RA Sushi units, with 7 new venues opened in 2025 and plans for 6–10 in 2026.
2026-01-2026-02: ONE Group opened one new Kona Grill location and converted a Benihana in 2026 while signalling additional 2026 growth activity.
2026-02-12: NRA’s 2026 industry outlook projected $1.55T restaurant sales with modest 1.3% real sales growth and 42% operators still unprofitable in 2025.
2026-05-08: Sushiro announced its first U.S. Manhattan location, indicating continued global conveyor-belt expansion into the U.S.
outlook: Near-term growth in 2026 should remain positive but uneven: demand is resilient in desirable metro markets, while operators that do not improve labor and food-cost leverage are likely to see sustained margin stress.
themes: Metro-first expansion over broad geographies
Cost-and-compliance resilience on seafood sourcing (labeling, traceability, fraud controls)
Automation and digital channels to lift throughput and reduce per-cover labor drag
Menu and format innovation to capture health, convenience, and value perceptions
one_sentence: Demand is holding up for premium sushi experiences and quick-service sushi formats even as operators balance traffic softness and cost inflation.

title: Sustainable Building Material Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: Demand is shifting from volume growth to performance compliance, with LEED v5 and net-zero programs pushing stronger product differentiation.
overview: The industry builds materials used in energy-efficient and lower-carbon construction, including insulation, wood products, interior finishes, roofing, and structural systems. US demand is increasingly tied to commercial and institutional sustainability standards, while residential projects remain sensitive to incentives and financing cycles. IBIS-style baseline reporting showed early recovery momentum after 2021, but the latest 2025-2026 signals show a more policy- and certification-driven expansion model with stronger compliance content per project.

key_stats.market_size: US$165,619.4 million in 2024, with US$263,727.2 million expected in 2030 (U.S. green building materials forecast).
key_stats.growth: 8.4% CAGR for 2025-2030 (projected), with demand concentration still concentrated in interior finishing and faster growth in insulation.
key_stats.construction_context: Total US construction value was US$544,081.0 million SAAR in June 2026, with total construction up 0.6% from May 2026 and private construction up 6.0% at that release.
key_stats.policy_pull: US energy-efficiency credits remain a major driver in households and retrofit demand through 2025, with implementation and credit mechanics changing in 2026.

baseline_2022.market_size: US$74,186 million revenue (2021 baseline figure in IBIS baseline report, figures in 2021 dollars).
baseline_2022.growth: IBIS projected 0.73% CAGR for 2021-2027 and ~0.6% annualized growth from 2021 to 2026.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell premiumized products marketed on lower energy use, lower emissions, recycled content, and certification compatibility. Revenue is captured through raw material sales, engineered assemblies, and higher-margin specialized lines tied to LEED/energy codes; margins rise when products qualify for high-efficiency or embodied-carbon performance claims and project-spec contracts. Retrofit and new-build spec relationships remain the main route to repeat demand.
cost_structure: Costs are dominated by feedstock inputs (resins, minerals, timber processing, metals), energy, labor quality, certification/admin overhead, and testing/documentation needed for ENERGY STAR, LEED, and embodied-carbon reporting. 2026 regulatory changes add complexity: compliance timelines compress under LEED v5 transition, while appliance/material qualification requirements in federal tax-credit programs increase manufacturer qualification and traceability workload.
major_players: Wood manufacturing and mass timber supply-chain participants (as reflected in WoodWorks project ecosystem)
current_dynamics: 2026 shows two parallel forces: (1) standardization pressure from LEED v5 migration and embodied-carbon reporting, which favors firms with robust digital documentation and product-level performance data; and (2) uneven demand between commercial/public programs, which remain relatively resilient, versus consumer-led segments where incentive timing in 2025-2026 materially affects conversion rates. The market is expanding, but with more emphasis on certification-proof value than pure volume volume growth.
whats_growing: Mass timber and engineered wood use in sustainable applications: 2,833 U.S. projects were in progress or built as of June 2026.
High-performance retrofit materials with insulation and envelope functions as energy-code and efficiency requirements harden.
LEED and LEED Zero adoption breadth is expanding, with 844 LEED Zero programs registered/certified as of March 2026.
whats_shrinking: Consumer-facing retrofit pull tied to 25C-style annual tax-credit behavior is facing timing uncertainty after 2025 annual eligibility windows.
Legacy certification pathways are being sunset, reducing projects built primarily on legacy LEED v4/v4.1 workflows.
Lower-value commodity-grade sustainable materials face pressure as buyers increasingly require full lifecycle and carbon-accounting transparency.
recent_developments: 2025-03-24: DOE postponed implementation of three appliance-related efficiency mandates, influencing near-term compliance and product qualification dynamics.
2025-11-03: USGBC published LEED v5 addenda/tools rollout items and moved implementation content forward toward broader early adopter use.
2026-03-2026: LEED Zero page reported 844 projects registered and certified across LEED Zero categories.
2026-05-28: USGBC LEED-v5 transition page noted July 1, 2027, as the cutoff for new commercial LEED BD+C, ID+C, and O+M registrations in v5.
2026-05-28: GBCI extended LEED v4/v4.1 commercial registration close from 2026-06-30 to 2027-06-30.
2026-08-03: Census reported total construction value at US$544,081.0 million (SAAR) in June 2026.
outlook: Base case for 2026-2029 is continued demand expansion through net-zero retrofit spending, institutional procurement standards, and carbon-accountability in design specs, with stronger preference for mass timber, low-carbon envelopes, and material-level transparency tools. The key constraint is regulatory timing: as LEED v5 and tax-credit documentation requirements mature, players with stronger compliance infrastructure and domestic supply coordination are likely to gain share.
themes: From green product labels to performance claims
Embodied carbon and circularity as procurement criteria
Mass timber and wood-based low-carbon systems
Certification migration and documentation complexity
Policy-driven demand volatility tied to federal credit design
one_sentence: In 2026, US sustainable building materials are benefiting from higher construction activity and stricter performance standards, even as certification timelines and supply costs reshape profitability.

title: Swimming Pool Cleaning Services
one_liner: A recurring, service-heavy U.S. market where household and commercial pool maintenance has become the stability engine as new-pool build activity cools.
overview: The industry is a mature, high-repeat-demand service segment dominated by recurring maintenance visits, chemical management, and seasonal support tasks for private pools and commercial facilities. After the 2020–2021 pool installation surge, growth momentum in 2025–2026 is increasingly coming from service retention and operating discipline rather than pure new-construction expansion. Provider consolidation accelerated in 2026, while labor, chemicals, and pricing pressure remain key constraints.

market_growth.forecast_growth_2026: 69% of survey firms expected revenue growth over next 12 months

key_stats.market_size: n/a
key_stats.growth: n/a

how_it_makes_money: Recurring residential service contracts (often weekly/biweekly routes and monthly billing)
Commercial pool service contracts for hotels, gyms, and multi-family/shared amenities
Chemical testing and balancing plus consumables and replacement parts
Opening, closing, winterization, and seasonal start/stop handling
Repair and retrofit jobs tied to pump/filter/heater maintenance and upgrades
cost_structure: Labor cost intensity remains the largest fixed operating component for route-heavy operators
Chemical and supply costs remain elevated, pressuring pricing and margins
Field operations and customer service are increasingly managed through software; software and tools shifted from optional to essential by 2026
Marketing spend has risen as operators face higher competition and DIY substitution risk
Wage and staffing quality constraints increase training and compliance overhead in 2025–2026
major_players: SPS PoolCare (ranked #1 on 2025 PSN/Jandy Top 50 Service list)
Pool Troopers (acquired by SPS in March 2026)
Amenity Pool Services (operations acquired by SPS in five markets in May 2026)
America’s Swimming Pool Company (large service/repair/renovation franchise footprint)
Fluidra, Hayward, Pentair, and Pool Corporation (large equipment and supply ecosystem partners)
current_dynamics: Service and remodel segments showed stronger resilience than new construction in Q3 2025
55% of service firms reported higher service-call volume in Q3 2025 versus Q3 2024
Provider consolidation moved into a new phase in 2026 through major regional acquisitions
Labor and chemical/material costs remain the primary margin squeeze in 2026
Housing permit/start conditions are stabilizing but remain weak enough to limit installation-led demand pull
whats_growing: Recurring service and maintenance calls and monthly billing model discipline
Acquisitive consolidation among national and regional service networks
Adoption of route and dispatch software for productivity and billing consistency
Hiring with greater use of W-2 technicians for service quality control in 2026
Commercial/resort portfolios where outdoor amenity compliance remains mandatory
whats_shrinking: New pool/spa installation demand cooled versus post-pandemic highs
DIY and price competition compressed gross margins in commoditized service plays
Service-led expansion in some regions is shifting from top-line expansion toward margin efficiency
Single-family housing construction pace has weakened versus prior highs, limiting new household demand tailwind
recent_developments: 2025-12-10: Q3 2025 PHTA survey showed only the service segment had bottom-line profit gains (+1% to +5%), with 55% of service firms reporting higher call volume.
2025-12-10: Q3 2025 survey reported 44% of builders saw higher new-construction revenue while 37% reported decreases, indicating cooling in fresh construction demand.
2026-02-24: State of Pool Service 2026 report cited 10.7 million US pools and a $7.2 billion pool cleaning market, with service companies up 3.6% since 2019.
2026-03-12: SPS PoolCare announced acquisition of Pool Troopers, with combined 2024 revenue of $144 million and 2025 combined revenue of about $157 million.
2026-05-21: SPS PoolCare announced Amenity Pool Services operations acquisition in Phoenix, Tucson, Jacksonville, Orlando, Dallas, and Port Charlotte.
2026-07-17: Census June 2026 update reported housing starts at 1,427,000 SAAR and permits at 1,367,000 SAAR versus 1,379,000 SAAR permits in Jun 2025.
outlook: The 2026–2027 U.S. trajectory is likely to remain positively biased but moderate: service-led demand persists, yet margins improve only for operators that tighten pricing discipline and improve utilization. Near-term growth should come from higher recurring-retention efficiency, route optimization, and selective expansion through acquisitions rather than broad new-market entry.
themes: Recurring revenue over transaction growth
Margin protection through pricing discipline
Operational consistency via software stacks
Shift toward W-2 workforce control in mature operators
Consolidation as the dominant competitive strategy
one_sentence: Across 2025–2026, pool cleaning services show resilient service demand and margin pressure, with consolidation and recurring-contract discipline defining winners.

title: Swimming Pool Construction in the US
one_liner: A labor- and materials-intensive market for building, renovating, and maintaining private and commercial swimming pools, highly dependent on new home construction activity and financing conditions.
overview: IBIS baseline reporting (2022) shows an annual market size near USD 9,343 million with new construction tied strongly to residential building, and commercial projects contributing as a secondary stabilizer. In that baseline, residential/new-home-related activity was about 60% of revenue, with home improvement and maintenance contributing the balance. For 2025, a market tracker reports USD 15.4 billion in U.S. swimming-pool construction spending (up from USD 15.1 billion in 2024), indicating a higher nominal market envelope under broader service definitions and methodology.

baseline_2022.growth: -0.01% annualized (2022-2028 IBIS projection)

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily earned from new pool builds, followed by alterations/reconstruction and maintenance/repair packages; contractors increasingly bundle design, permitting, excavation, concrete shell work, plumbing, finishing, and equipment installations. Commercial customers (hotels, schools, recreation and healthcare facilities) buy through project and maintenance contracts, while residential operators capture add-on upgrades such as spas, heating, safety systems, and filtration upgrades.

main_costs: Skilled labor for concrete, plumbing, electrical, and finish trades
Subcontracted equipment and construction inputs (pumps, concrete, steel, stone, aggregate, filtration and finishes)
Fuel and transport for heavy equipment and materials
Project financing carry and working-capital pressure from seasonal execution
Insurance, licensing, and local permit/compliance costs
margin_pressure: Rising wage rates in construction markets
Input-price volatility in raw materials and pools-and-spa components
Weather and seasonality causing underutilized crews in colder quarters

current_dynamics: The market is in a regime where residential housing starts and mortgage affordability remain the primary swing factor. 2025 Census data showed slight net decline in annual starts versus 2024, which limits broad-based new-home pool volume, while lenders’ mid-6% mortgage conditions in 2026 keep price-sensitive buyers cautious. At the same time, commercial hospitality and athletic/recreation retrofit activity has stayed comparatively steadier where amenities are used as customer acquisition and retention investments.
whats_growing: Maintenance, renovation, and modernization in warm-weather and amenity-led residential zones
Premium residential and commercial pool features (automation, variable-speed systems, energy-efficient upgrades)
Commercial project demand where pools are part of brand, wellness, and amenity strategy
whats_shrinking: New residential pool pipeline during tighter financing windows
DIY-style low-ticket work shifting toward maintenance subcontract models in slower localities
High-friction lead-to-close conversion in markets with elevated all-in borrowing costs
recent_developments: 2025-12-31: Freddie Mac PMMS showed 30-year FRM average 6.15% (2025 baseline reference for cost-of-financing context).
2025-12-31: Census final annual estimates reported 1,358,700 housing units started in 2025, about 0.6% below 2024.
2026-02-18: Census reported privately-owned housing starts at 1,404,000 SAAR in December 2025 and annual permits at 1,448,000 SAAR.
2026-07-16: Freddie Mac PMMS headline quoted 30-year FRM at 6.55%.
2026-08-06: Freddie Mac My Home portal showed 30-year FRM at 6.69%.
outlook: For 2026-2027, industry growth is likely mixed: a flat-to-low-growth residential build pipeline due financing sensitivity, partially offset by stronger commercial amenities and pool-retrofitting demand. Fragmentation should persist, so growth is expected to concentrate in operators with year-round scheduling discipline, strong commercial channels, and value-added service contracts.
themes: Housing-cycle sensitivity
High fragmentation with regional specialization
Energy-efficient/automation-enabled pool systems
Commercial amenity upgrades as risk diversifier
Labor constraint and project scheduling pressure
Premiumization in mid- and high-income suburban markets
one_sentence: The U.S. swimming-pool construction market in 2026 remains demand-sensitive to housing starts and mortgage rates, with fragmented regional contractors holding most of the market and commercial upgrades helping offset uneven residential cycles.

title: Swimming Pool Equipment Stores
one_liner: Specialty stores that sell pool and spa chemicals, maintenance equipment, and accessories to existing pool owners across the United States.
overview: Swimming pool equipment stores continue to depend on the installed-base economy: regular chemical replenishment, repairs, and replacement parts are less cyclical than new-pool spending. In 2025–26, major operators reported stable demand from recurring maintenance but slower growth in new pool-related discretionary spend, with housing and credit conditions influencing demand for new installs and upgrades. Major chains remain large but are actively optimizing physical footprints and expanding digital channels to defend margin.

key_stats.market_size: about $5.5 billion (latest publicly cited industry-scale benchmark in the 2025–26 period)
key_stats.growth: slight contraction trend (IBIS-style long-run outlook around -0.21% annualized in 2021-27), with demand concentrated in recurring maintenance rather than new builds
key_stats.ecommerce_environment: U.S. retail e-commerce share reached 16.9% of total retail in Q1 2026

baseline_2022.market_size: $5.527 billion (industry baseline revenue figure in available baseline profile)
baseline_2022.growth: -1.54% CAGR from 2002-2021; projected -0.21% annualized for 2021-27

how_it_makes_money: High-margin maintenance and replacement items (chemicals, parts, testing tools, water care consumables) are core to recurring sales.
Store network provides service-led retail for DIY and DIFM pool owners, plus local professional relationships with service contractors and installers.
Wholesale and distribution relationships (notably through larger channels) complement direct consumer sales.
Digital channels and marketplaces support multi-format sales, with strong omnichannel behavior from consumers.
cost_structure: Fixed and semi-fixed occupancy plus payroll costs at the physical network remain major structural burdens, especially under weak traffic conditions.
SG&A intensity is elevated due to compensation, store-level operating costs, and growing digital/technology spend.
Seasonality drives uneven quarterly cash flow and inventory build/working-capital planning.
Logistics and distribution costs are material because stores rely on consistent replenishment and service responsiveness.
Regulatory changes (notably energy-efficiency pump standards) can shift product mix toward higher-specification hardware and support demand volatility.
major_players: Leslie's, Inc. (over 1,000 retail locations in 39 states; digitally integrated network under Leslie’s and In the Swim brands; announced a plan to close about 80–90 underperforming stores in 2025)

Pool Corporation (world’s largest outdoor living distributor focused on pool/swim products; 456 sales centers; serves a broader installed pool/hot tub base of about 14.0 million pools/hot tubs in the U.S.)
Pinch A Penny (over 300 stores in its franchise system as of Dec. 31, 2025)
Amazon/targeted mass-market channels as high-velocity digital competitors against category stores
current_dynamics: Demand is increasingly maintenance-led: a large share of volume comes from recurring care and repair needs.
Net new-pool activity is softer than historical peak periods, with construction data showing weaker new in-ground starts.
Retail is under sustained online pressure, with overall U.S. e-commerce share at elevated levels.
Operators are re-balancing toward digital, same-day delivery, and service capability while trimming weaker store assets.
Regulatory efficiency changes in pool equipment increase demand complexity and may favor providers with technical/service depth.
whats_growing: Recurring maintenance and minor repair sales share of distributor mix (reported around 64% at a major national distributor).
Digital and marketplace-enabled transactions in omnichannel pool retail ecosystems.
Service-led and local-consultative offerings (water testing, diagnostics, replacement guidance).
Pinch A Penny store footprint expansion to over 300 locations in 2025.
whats_shrinking: New in-ground pool construction pace was lower in 2025 (about 3–5% lower versus 2024 estimates).
Leslie’s and peers reported softer same-store/traffic outcomes and began visible store rationalization.
Single-family housing starts fell in 2025 versus 2024, reducing downstream install momentum.
Price- and occupancy-driven pressure on discretionary spending for new builds, upgrades, and premium pool additions.
recent_developments: 2025-11-25: Leslie’s announced a closure plan for approximately 80–90 underperforming U.S. stores.
2025-12-31: Pool Corporation reported ~$5.3 billion in net sales and highlighted durable maintenance demand in a market with weaker discretionary build activity.
2026-02-18: NAHB reported 2025 total U.S. housing starts of 1.36M, with single-family starts at 943,000 (down 6.9% year over year).
2026-02-26: Pool Corporation reported new in-ground pool construction in 2025 at just below 60,000 units (down from 62,000 in 2024).
2026-05-18: Census reported Q1 2026 e-commerce share of total U.S. retail sales at 16.9%.
2026-07-17: Census June 2026 housing data showed total starts at 1,427,000 annualized and single-family starts at 895,000, while monthly housing reports remained a key near-term demand input.
outlook: In 2026, the category is likely to see modest top-line risk from weaker new-pool build cycles but comparatively better resilience in recurring service and maintenance demand. Winners are expected to be operators with stronger local service capability, better digital execution, and disciplined store productivity. Industry concentration among larger operators should continue, while underperforming small-format locations face a higher closure/repositioning risk.
themes: Recurrence over replacement: maintenance economics dominate
Digital commoditization versus service differentiation
Store network optimization and footprint efficiency
Housing affordability and credit conditions as leading indicator for build-led demand
Energy-efficiency policy and equipment standards altering replacement cycles
one_sentence: The category is moving from discretionary one-time build demand toward recurring maintenance demand, while online retail and high occupancy costs pressure traditional store economics in 2025–2026.

title: Swimming Pools
one_liner: US swimming-pool operators in 2026 are stabilizing by leaning into maintenance, lessons, and recurring service economics while new private pool starts remain sensitive to financing and construction cycles.
overview: The 2021 IBIS baseline describes a small but recovery-oriented market, and by 2026 the industry shows a clearer split: recurring maintenance/amenity demand is holding while new starts face macro headwinds. U.S. recreational behavior remains strong in parks and outdoor activity (2025 NRPA), and ATUS shows continued participation in sports/exercise/recreation in 2025, but construction permitting is weaker than pre-pandemic highs and financing costs remain elevated.

permitting_snapshot.value: pool construction permits down 34.3% vs Jan 2020 (NAHB)

growth.value: 1.23% CAGR revenue; 1.37% CAGR EBIT; 1.69% GDP share growth

baseline_2022.notes: IBIS baseline published data for the report period shows an older 2021 base but still the last publicly cited benchmark in the supplied brief.

how_it_makes_money: Core revenue comes from membership fees, admission/pass pricing, swim lessons, aquatic classes, concessions, rental/schedule fees, and recurring maintenance-driven product categories (chemicals, filters, replacement equipment, service contracts); public operators also rely on municipal appropriations and local program funding.

cost_structure.fixed: Facility operations, licensing/compliance, insurance and staffing commitments, utility and chemical handling infrastructure.

title: Synthetic Fiber Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US synthetic fiber manufacturing is a small but strategically important segment, with low base growth and pressure from imports offset by specialty and sustainability-focused production.
overview: US synthetic-fiber manufacturers produce petrochemical-based and cellulose-derived fibers used in apparel, home textiles, automotive interiors, industrial goods, and medical products. Demand remains highly sensitive to consumer and manufacturing cycles, while import competition in commodity fibers and cotton substitution continue to constrain pricing power. Recent industry movement favors differentiation: advanced nylon, recycled-content polyester, and specialty performance fibers are supporting margin resilience even as broad-based textile demand softens.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes mainly from selling yarns, filaments, and technical fibers into textile converters, carpet makers, industrial product makers, and technical markets. The most stable margins come from specialized and branded fibers (e.g., advanced nylon or circular-content products) where performance specifications and longer-term supply agreements reduce direct price compression.
cost_structure: The main cost stack is petrochemical-based resin and intermediate inputs, followed by energy, logistics, and labor with increasing automation. When feedstock and freight costs rise, lower-margin commodity fibers lose share first; firms with recyclable content, process licensing, and premium applications usually preserve margin through value pricing or mix shift.

title: Syringes & Injection Needle Manufacturing
one_liner: The U.S. industry remains a steady, regulation-sensitive consumables market driven by aging demand, chronic injection therapies, and healthcare safety requirements, with growth cushioned by resilience in hospitals and home-care channels.
overview: U.S. syringes and injection-needle demand is linked to an older, medically active population, expanded outpatient infusion and self-injection use cases, and frequent preventive care events, while capacity planning remains constrained by quality and supply visibility requirements. The market remains fragmented with a few large players and a long tail of smaller manufacturers.

Specialized product sales for diabetes and chronic-care channels (e.g., insulin and biologic administration formats) with recurring replenishment cycles.
Supply contracts and private-label/partner manufacturing for pharma and med-tech customers needing traceable, validated injection delivery systems.

Distribution and service costs: cold/ambient logistics for specific products, returns, complaint handling, and field technical support.
Regulatory and legal costs: warning-letter risk management, shortage reporting, and ongoing audit preparedness.

title: Syrup & Flavoring Production in the US
one_liner: A concentrated U.S. manufacturing segment making beverage syrups and flavoring concentrates, with revenue linked to soda, coffee, and packaged beverage channels.
overview: IBIS baseline positioning and recent 2025–2026 updates indicate a small but strategically important food-manufacturing layer that sells intermediates to beverage brands and foodservice users rather than final consumers. In 2022, the market was estimated at $13,069m, and by 2026 the U.S. flavored-syrup market estimate is still near $14.6bn while growth remains modest. The structure is still dominated by large beverage groups in concentrated value chains, while innovation is moving toward premium, customized, lower-sugar, and functional flavor profiles.

title: TV & Appliance Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: U.S. TV and appliance wholesalers in 2025-2026 are riding recovery in housing-linked demand while facing channel consolidation and volatile retail demand.
overview: The IBISWorld baseline in 2022 shows modest but positive industry scale in a mature wholesaling segment, with revenue around $141.4 billion and mixed pressure on margins. In 2025 official activity data for the closest NAICS match (4236 Household Appliances & Electrical and Electronic Goods Merchant Wholesalers) show stronger nominal output growth, suggesting partial resilience from downstream housing and project activity. The channel remains competitive: large retailers and direct manufacturer channels pressure independent distributors, while wholesale operators that expand logistics, service bundles, and installation/fulfillment capabilities are better positioned. Near-term dynamics are driven by construction pace, retail demand management, and procurement/inventory decisions by key retail and commercial buyers.

title: Table Salt Production
one_liner: The U.S. table salt production industry in 2025–2026 is a mature, concentrated food-processing category balancing roughly 40 million tons of production with sustained pressure to lower sodium in packaged and restaurant foods.
overview: US table salt remains an essential consumable and food-manufacturing input, with most sodium consumption tied to processed and prepared foods rather than home table use. 2025 USGS-linked data indicate domestic salt production around 40 million tons and about 39 million tons sold or used with total estimated value around USD 2.6 billion; import dependence for upstream supply remains meaningful, with Mexico, Chile, and Canada among major 2021–2024 sources. The segment is concentrated, with IBIS baseline framing heavy concentration at the top end. Simultaneously, health-policy pressure is shifting product mixes toward lower-sodium, specialty, and flavored formats while retaining a still-robust role for standard and iodized salts in food supply chains.

title: Tactical & Service Clothing Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. tactical and service clothing makers are a small, contract-driven apparel niche powered by military, law-enforcement, and safety procurement, with domestic demand supported by security budgets and constrained by low-cost import competition.
overview: U.S. producers serve defense, military, police, fire/EMS, and industrial service markets with mission-specific garments that are harder to source abroad due to durability, testing, and procurement requirements. Since 2021 the domestic baseline has been constrained by import competition, but federal modernization spending and renewed defense industrial policies are supporting a measured return, with buyers demanding more technical performance, traceability, and faster delivery.

Higher-performance fabrics and modular load-bearing/compatible uniform systems tied to mission-specific and integrated protective functions.
Automation and digitalization in production planning and design workflows (3D scanning, PLM, standardized digital specs).
Domestic compliance-driven demand where traceability and spec control are procurement requirements.

Scale of legacy U.S. apparel manufacturing compared with imported apparel channels.
Price sensitivity in non-secure civilian channels, which can shift demand toward lower-cost alternatives.

The most attractive firms will be those with secure defense customer relationships, quick variant customization, and strong compliance/traceability capabilities.

one_sentence: The U.S. tactical and service clothing manufacturing industry remains narrowly positioned but resilient, balancing higher production costs and shrinking scale at many facilities against durable government and public-safety uniform demand in a re-armed fiscal environment.

title: Tank & Refrigeration Trucking in the US
one_liner: Specialized U.S. trucking for temperature-sensitive freight and tanked liquids remains demand-driven by food, pharmaceuticals, and energy, but margins stay exposed to diesel, labor, and capacity competition.
overview: Tank and refrigeration trucking in the US is a specialized freight niche that moves cargo requiring nonstandard equipment, including perishables, construction materials, and tanked liquids. Freight demand tracks consumer spending, agricultural flows, industrial activity, and cross-border trade, while profitability is highly sensitive to diesel, carrier capacity, and driver availability. By 2026, digital recordkeeping and traceability obligations are reinforcing cost and capability gaps between large, well-capitalized carriers and smaller regional operators.

Fuel surcharges and accessorial fees tied to diesel and service complexity (loading, detention, and routing constraints).
Value-added services such as documentation, temperature-monitoring support, intermodal transfer handling, and integrated logistics coordination for priority shippers.
cost_structure: Fuel is a core variable cost; diesel remains highly influential for trip economics.
Labor cost is central, with 2026 truck-transportation hourly pay around $33.27 and heavy-tractor-trailer drivers averaging about $61,540 annual pay (2025 OES proxy).
Specialized fleet capex and maintenance (reefer plants, tank seals, telematics, temperature systems) are a persistent fixed/ongoing burden.
Compliance and insurance costs rise with food-safety traceability, safety, and emissions-related requirements.

FDA stated the Food Traceability Rule compliance date is Jan 20, 2026, and in June 2026 reported mixed readiness but progress across industry traceability exercises.

Pharma and healthcare-sensitive cold logistics due to stricter chain-of-custody documentation.
Technology-led service differentiation (temperature-event records, tracking, and rapid recall readiness).

Small-operator net margins where they cannot absorb fuel volatility, digital traceability spend, and labor inflation.

outlook: The near-term outlook is moderate top-line growth with uneven profitability: demand for cold-chain freshness and compliant pharmaceuticals remains supportive, while fuel price swings, trucking labor costs, and compliance spend keep margins compressed unless carriers scale into higher-value lanes and digital service layers.

Industry consolidation toward larger carriers that can finance advanced refrigeration, telematics, and compliance systems.

Diesel and driver economics remain the two largest operational variables.

title: Tanning Salons in the US
one_liner: A small but still-revenue-active discretionary personal-care sector is shifting from pure UV tanning toward memberships, sunless solutions, and wellness bundling as health-policy pressure rises.
overview: The industry still centers on discretionary indoor beauty and tanning services, dominated by franchise-led operators with high brand concentration and mixed regional performance. Federal UV-tanning rulemaking remains contested, so most demand-swing risk is now driven by state minor-access rules, consumer risk perception, and local operator execution. The sector’s structural adaptation is to keep tanning as part of a broader beauty/wellness offer instead of a standalone UV-only model.

title: Tattoo Artists
one_liner: Independent tattoo studios and artist-led studios form a fragmented service industry centered on custom body-art work, licensing, and local studio economics.
overview: The US tattoo artist industry is highly fragmented and has become increasingly mainstream, but the structure is still dominated by small, artist-led operators rather than scalable public chains. Baseline IBIS-linked 2022 data describe a ~$1.4 billion market with 31,196 establishments, while a 2026-focused 2026 trade write-up cites IBISWorld-style numbers around ~$1.3 billion and 23,774 establishments, suggesting a maturing market with possible consolidation effects or definitional drift rather than rapid unit expansion. Demand is still driven by demographics, self-expression norms, and cultural acceptance, with social discovery and visual proof via online channels continuing to shape lead flow, while hygiene, licensing, and product-safety scrutiny increase operating friction.

key_stats.growth: near-flat to low single-digit pace in recent update; historical baseline used earlier estimates around ~5% range growth

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is mainly from custom tattoo labor billed by hour, design complexity, and size, with secondary income from piercing add-ons, flash-day events, aftercare referrals/retail, and studio-level fees. Compensation is typically split models (commission-heavy shops) or booth-rent models; both shift margin pressure to utilization and throughput. Strong artists and repeatable booking systems are the main demand engine, while low-friction retail aftercare and add-on services lift per-visit profitability.
cost_structure: The major cost drivers are artist compensation (often the largest variable line), rent and studio leasehold costs, compliance/licensing and inspections, disposable supplies (needles, gloves, sterilization), software/booking stacks, and insurance. Rising occupancy and labor costs in urban markets increase the break-even utilization bar, while compliance spend increases as more states harden licensing and hygiene expectations.

current_dynamics: Demand continues to be supported by ongoing social acceptance and customization preference, but operators now face higher execution expectations around licensing, hygiene documentation, and supplier quality. Recent regulatory text changes in major states strengthen formal compliance obligations for licensed premises and temporary operations, while the FDA alert on contaminated inks reinforces source-control and product QA sensitivity. The near-term dynamic is therefore less about headline demand shock and more about tightening operating discipline and execution quality.
whats_growing: Higher-value custom design work, destination studios with stronger systems, and better software-driven scheduling/artist management to raise hourly utilization; business filings and trade commentary also suggest a slow shift toward more formal franchising/playbook-led models.
whats_shrinking: Pure low-friction walk-in flash-only models without brand differentiation, and any studio relying on weak hygiene processes or unmanaged compliance exposure.

2025-2026: Florida 2025 statute language continues to require per-location tattoo-establishment licensing, annual renewal, and compliance for temporary setups.
outlook: Expect continued resilience in demand, but with uneven growth by operator capability: professionally run, high-utilization studios should maintain margins, while fragmented independents without strong scheduling, hygiene, and cost control face margin compression. Regulation-driven professionalization should improve baseline quality and consumer trust but also raise fixed costs, rewarding efficient operators with compliance systems and premium positioning.

fragmented supply, low concentration
compliance hardening and licensing modernization
product safety visibility from regulator alerts
software-enabled operational discipline
premium customization over mass flash execution
one_sentence: The US tattoo artists market remains a small but durable consumer-service segment where demand is broad and culturally normalized, while growth is constrained by high hygiene-compliance costs, limited business concentration, and uneven operating maturity across states.

overview: The industry is highly seasonal, demand is still tied to annual filing events, but competitive pressure is strongest in basic self-prep services as e-filing and free filing options expand. H&R Block and Intuit remain the two largest branded ecosystems, while smaller software and assisted alternatives compete aggressively on price and ease of use. IRS filing data shows continued migration away from paper, while legislative and credit-rule changes keep filing complexity and advisory demand elevated for higher-income and mixed-income households.

title: Tax Preparation Software Developers
one_liner: US tax filing software stays revenue-stable through mandatory annual filing needs, while AI-guided filing and free-government channels reshape pricing and user acquisition.
overview: The industry serves consumers and SMBs that prepare and electronically file US tax returns through guided online software, mobile apps, and desktop tools. In 2022, IBIS reported steady expansion tied to rising online filing comfort and a high reliance on recurring compliance cycles, and that logic still held through the 2025–2026 filing seasons. The 2025/26 filing environment showed continued growth in e-file usage (including self-prepared filers), wider free filing alternatives, and rapid productization of GenAI assistants inside filing workflows.

cost_structure: High fixed costs to maintain code compliance with frequent tax-code changes, secure cloud operations, and regulatory-grade platform operations; low marginal cost for incremental return volumes in software terms; elevated ongoing spending on AI infrastructure, support, fraud prevention, and marketing.
