one_sentence: The U.S. taxi-and-limousine industry has shifted from conventional dispatch to platform-mediated service, while employment is volatile and city-level licensing and labor rules are becoming the key margin battleground.

title: Tea Production in the US
one_liner: US tea production (blending, packaging, and branding) remains a small but resilient packaged food and beverage manufacturing niche driven by wellness positioning and higher-margin specialty formats.
overview: IBIS World’s 2022 baseline puts industry revenue at $1.682 billion, with strong emphasis on bagged black and green tea and an increasing shift to premiumized and specialty offerings. A 2024 Tea Association report shows US-wide tea sales near $13.9 billion across traditional, ready-to-drink, foodservice, and specialty channels, while 2025 trade monitoring points to resilient total import volumes despite tariff turbulence and channel rebalancing toward non-commodity formats.

key_stats.market_size: $1.682B (2022, US Tea Production industry definition, IBIS world); $13.9B (2024 estimate, total US tea market by segment)
key_stats.growth: 1.49% CAGR from 2002 to 2022; 1.33% annual growth projected from 2022 onward (IBIS) and 2.6% growth in 2022; US total tea sales moved from $13.6B (2023) to $13.9B estimate (2024)
key_stats.imports: 230 million lb tea imports in 2023 (201-year period cited in TUSA) and 103,179 MT through Nov 2025 (trade monitor) with Black tea ~83% of that volume.
key_stats.market_structure: Mature but competitive; medium barriers to entry and medium competition intensity in official profile; product concentration remains high in core formats

baseline_2022.growth: 1.49% CAGR (2002-2022); 2.6% industry growth in 2022; 10.6% margin in 2022

how_it_makes_money: Purchase/sourcing of raw tea leaves (primarily imported black and green tea) and package/brand into blended finished products.
Brand-led packaging and distribution through grocery/drug chains, mass merchandisers, foodservice, and online channels.
Premiumization via single-serve, flavored blends, functional positioning, and specialty/organic segments with higher unit economics.
Margin expansion from proprietary recipes, flavoring, and packaging formats with stronger shelf conversion.
cost_structure: Leaf sourcing is the largest variable cost component (quality/grade-driven, origin-sensitive).
Import and logistics costs are highly sensitive to tariff rates, transport, and currency movements.
Packaging and fulfillment costs (bags, pouches, sachets, single-serve containers) are a key fixed-to-variable mix.
Labor and R&D (blending, formulation, sensory quality, and compliance) support differentiation and regulatory quality assurance.
Marketing/sales support is increasingly needed to defend premium positions against mass commodity alternatives.
major_players: Tetley/other multi-category tea brand owners under major CPG groups
current_dynamics: 2023: Tea Association data cites nearly 86 billion servings in the US and a continued consumer shift toward perceived health benefits.
2025: A trade-monitoring recap reports 103,179 MT of US tea imports through November 2025, with black tea still dominant (about 86,096 MT, 83% share).
2025: Black tea imports were largely led by Argentina (~43% of black imports), while green tea growth included higher shares from China and faster growth from Japan-related trade.
2025: Tariff volatility affected import timing; reported Chinese-tea tariff rates were noted as peaking and then easing by year-end in industry monitoring.
2024-2026: Association and trade commentary emphasizes health-focused product stories, specialty positioning, and under-penetrated foodservice trial growth as a near-term demand lever.
whats_growing: Specialty/functional teas and wellness-oriented blends are gaining share in premium channels.
Matcha and green tea segments showed above-trend import demand dynamics in 2025 trade monitoring.
Foodservice experimentation and menu innovation remain cited as a route to higher-volume growth.
Organic and sustainably positioned SKUs are increasingly important in brand strategy, especially in higher-income and health-aware cohorts.
whats_shrinking: Commodity-style black tea faces stronger price sensitivity and origin substitution pressure.
Ready-to-drink tea volume growth has been uneven despite dollar growth in 2023.
Greenhouse from some origins is volatile due tariff-driven swings and inventory balancing after 2025 tariff shocks.
Net margin upside from undifferentiated blends is weaker than for premium and niche formats.
recent_developments: 2025-03-10: A US tea-market recap reports 103,179 MT of US tea imports through Nov 2025 and black tea dominance at 83%.
2025-11-14: U.S. White House agricultural-product tariff modification included coffee and tea as products no longer subject to reciprocal tariffs under the announced scope changes.
2025-11: Chinese black tea export-to-US flow remained weak in October while green tea remained resilient in import mix.
2025-12-01: USITC notes 2025 full trade statistics availability for official analysis (DataWeb release).
2026-01-02: Tea Association leadership transition in the US industry body, signaling continuity focus on policy and member coordination.
2026-03-10: Industry commentary highlights sustained consumer demand but ongoing tariff instability and a stronger emphasis on differentiated tea formats.
outlook: Near-term growth is expected to remain moderate rather than explosive, with upside concentrated in premium, specialty, and health-positioned SKUs and downside risk concentrated in trade-cost shocks; by 2026-2027, resilience depends on stable tariff posture, supply chain continuity, and successful category expansion into foodservice and functional at-home channels.
themes: Health/Wellness Consumption
Premiumization & Single-Serve
Import-Dependent Cost Volatility
Tariff Governance and Trade Policy
Foodservice Relevance and Channel Expansion
Sustainability and Transparency

title: Telecommunications Resellers in the US
one_liner: US telecommunications resellers buy carrier capacity and resell fixed/mobile communication services, typically at lower-cost bundles for consumers and SMBs.
overview: The telecom resale model in the US remains a niche layer under wholesale-to-retail connectivity, with traffic density and connection growth keeping demand resilient while differentiation increasingly depends on service quality and niche positioning. A 2025 research summary of the same IBIS-style industry shows revenue moving toward about US$24.0bn with a 0.9% CAGR path and near-26% operating profit ratio, while broader MVNO market evidence still points to scale expansion in 5G-enabled demand channels and low-cost alternatives.

key_stats.growth: 0.9% annualized (2021-2026, industry-definition aligned)

baseline_2022.growth: 1.4% annualized (to 2021 in the pre-2022 baseline framing)

how_it_makes_money: The core margin comes from arbitrage and bundling: resellers buy bulk/mobile network access at wholesale and repackage it as retail plans plus value-added services (support, usage-based billing options, service bundles, and niche packages). In this cycle, 2025–2026 growth is increasingly tied to retention economics in prepaid and SMB segments rather than pure take-rate expansion.
cost_structure: Main cost blocks are wholesale access charges (largest), network usage settlement, customer acquisition, platform/billing costs, support and retention operations, and distribution/channel friction; gross margin is highly sensitive to access-rate shifts and subsidy or device-financing strategy.
major_players: Verizon Communications (including Visible, TracFone, Total Wireless)
T-Mobile US (Metro by T-Mobile, Mint Mobile)
Dish Network / Boost Mobile / Gen Mobile
current_dynamics: 2025 CTIA data showed 579M U.S. wireless connections, with 5G devices materially expanding at roughly 259M units in 2025.
AT&T’s 2025 filings showed 120M mobility subscribers and 11M users served via resale channels (reseller category), confirming continued downstream dependence on wholesale channels.
Dish’s 2026 10-Q filed its hybrid operating transition in late 2025 while reporting 7.527M wireless subscribers, highlighting network-sharing as a structural strategy.
T-Mobile’s 2025 Q4 update showed 142.4M total customers and 2.4M Q4 net additions, indicating continued subscriber gravity despite a saturated US market.
Carrier competition is increasingly overlapping with MVNO value propositions, especially through prepaid/low-cost and 5G-enabled broadband add-ons.
whats_growing: 5G usage intensity and broadband demand, especially fixed wireless/home connections and multi-device use.
Niche enterprise bundles and B2B/MVNO partnerships in regulated and value-sensitive segments.
Cloud-native onboarding, digital-first sales, and eSIM-enabled low-friction activation models.
Operators offering differentiated service layers on top of standardized connectivity (speed-based or feature-based offers).
whats_shrinking: Commodity-style differentiation in basic voice/text/data bundles.
Reliance on legacy fixed-line resell mix relative to mobile-first and 5G-led demand.
High-margin room from simple price-only competition as MNOs launch lower-tier alternatives.
Standalone premium pricing power in crowded prepaid and discount segments.
recent_developments: 2025-09-: CTIA 2025 Annual Survey reported 579M U.S. wireless connections and near-1.7 connections per person, with 5G devices at 259M.
2025-11-14: GSMA Intelligence’s MVNO trends update (2025 edition) highlighted eSIM, 5G-based differentiation, cloud-native MVNO models, and enterprise/IoT expansion.
2025-11-15: Dish disclosed in 2026 filings that it transitioned to a hybrid MNO model with AT&T network reliance and continued MVNO operations.
2026-02-05: T-Mobile Q4 2025 and full-year 2025 customer results showed 142.4M total customers and 2.4M Q4 net additions.

2026-07-01: FCC Universal Service Monitoring Report (2025 data year) published, including 608 wireless carriers reporting and noting telecom resellers tracked separately in Census-related classification.
outlook: A low-to-mid single-digit demand backdrop is expected to persist into 2026, but competitive pressure from host carriers and substitute channels suggests headline revenue growth stays modest. Resellers that win on service quality, SMB niche design, and 5G-enabled use cases should outperform pure-price challengers; weak operators face continuing margin squeeze.
themes: 5G-led demand density over commodity pricing
eSIM and digital-first distribution lowering entry and service-launch cost
Cloud-native MVNO operating models
SMB and household value positioning vs. MNO overlap
Reseller-versus-carrier substitution risk in prepaid and low-cost segments
one_sentence: The sector is mature and slow-growing in 2026, with demand supported by near-universal connectivity but profitability pressured by aggressive pricing from major carriers and in-market MVNO competition.

title: Telehealth Services
one_liner: Telehealth in the U.S. is now a durable care channel, with 2026 federal extensions keeping home-based and non-geographic access in place while growth shifts toward behavioral health, chronic disease management, and hybrid care.
overview: The U.S. telehealth industry has progressed from emergency deployment to a normalized operating model, supported by sustained Medicare access rules and ongoing payer adoption. Baseline IBISWorld data show 2022 revenue at USD 16.57 billion. By 2025, U.S. telemedicine estimates are around USD 41.71 billion, with projected medium-term growth of 16.1% CAGR through 2030. Current policy direction extends major flexibility terms through 2027-12-31, with selected provisions tapering after 2028-01-01.

core_revenue: Virtual visit and consultation fees (video/phone/remote care sessions)
Care-management and remote monitoring program contracts with payers, employers, and health systems
Platform access subscriptions and licensing for providers and enterprise clinical networks
Add-on service revenues for diagnostics support, behavioral health pathways, and care coordination
pricing_behavior: Reimbursement parity and policy flexibility determine service mix and volume by line of business
Payer carve-outs and quality outcomes increasingly influence utilization and service design

major_costs: Clinical workforce compensation (virtual providers, behavioral health clinicians, specialist hours)
Technology stack costs (HIPAA-compliant platforms, EHR integration, remote monitoring, security, AI tools)
Provider network onboarding, credentialing, licensure compliance, and payer admin
Acquisition and retention spend for users, referrals, and enterprise contracts
margin_pressure: Rising clinician and acquisition costs as provider competition increases
Regulatory and coding compliance complexity in telehealth reimbursement
Dependence on payment policy changes and claim-processing rules

current_dynamics: 2026 policy continuity is keeping telehealth demand elevated: CMS and HHS pages confirm home-based non-behavioral access and reduced geography limits through 2027-12-31. At the same time, utilization is no longer surging at 2020-2021 velocity; industry behavior is shifting to ongoing managed care channels, behavioral health, and monitored chronic care.
whats_growing: Policy-supported continuation of telehealth access options through 2027-12-31 is sustaining demand
Tele-mental health and behavioral care continuity remains a high-volume segment
Remote care for chronic conditions and post-acute follow-up is growing as value-based care expands
Provider-side workflow tools (supervision, telemonitoring, virtual visits) are broadening service capacity
whats_shrinking: Growth in provider-level telemedicine adoption among office-based physicians cooled, with use reported at 80.0% in 2024 versus 86.5% in 2021
Purely episodic first-wave demand (pandemic-era surge behavior) is normalizing into hybrid care models
recent_developments: 2025-11-20: AHA tracked CMS updated guidance on Medicare telehealth services (U.S. telehealth policy tracking page).
2025-12-30: AHA-linked updates note telemedicine waivers were extended through 2026, with repeated risk of post-waiver contraction if not made permanent.
2026-02-05: HHS telehealth policy updates list Medicare telehealth flexibilities through 2027-12-31 for home origin, geographic access, and audio-only in non-behavioral services.
2026-02-26: CMS published updated Telehealth FAQ confirming 2027-12-31 access windows and 2028-01-01 transition rules.
2026-07-01: CMS CY 2026 Physician Fee Schedule communications confirm continued payment and supervision updates for telehealth workflows and G2025 billing through 2027-12-31.
2026-07-31: ATA reported federal policy and AI-governance activity in virtual care as a live industry theme.
outlook: Outlook for 2026-2028 is positive but more selective: demand is expected to stay elevated with policy support, while growth leaders focus on integrated behavioral health, remote monitoring, and care-team efficiency. Competitive pressure remains high, so operator profitability should continue to depend on workflow scale, reimbursement optimization, and platform differentiation.
themes: Hybrid care is replacing replacement-only virtual care
Behavioral health as a primary telehealth vertical
Rural access and broadband constraints remain policy-lifted growth bottlenecks
AI-assisted triage, documentation, and care orchestration are increasing differentiation
one_sentence: By 2026, telehealth utilization remains above pre-pandemic levels, but industry momentum is moving from one-time pandemic surge toward sustained reimbursement-driven expansion and care-delivery redesign.

title: Telemarketing & Call Centers in the US
one_liner: US telemarketing and call-center operators are stabilizing in a mature support-services market where AI-driven self-service, e-commerce demand, and tighter robocall controls are reshaping service mix and pricing.
overview: The industry provides inbound and outbound telemarketing, technical support, customer care, and related outsourced communications services for corporate clients, with inbound services still dominant. Demand is concentrated in retail, telecom, and financial services customers that need continuous front-line customer interaction, while automation, cloud-based routing, and AI copilots increasingly handle routine calls and routing. At the same time, federal enforcement and caller-authentication rules are increasing compliance complexity and service costs for legitimate providers.

key_stats.market_size: USD 30.7B (2026, derived from IBIS 2022 base and 3.0% CAGR trajectory)
key_stats.growth: 3.0% annualized (IBIS 2022–2028 forecast)

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn mainly from long-term client contracts for call handling, customer service outsourcing, outbound telemarketing, debt collection support, and upsell/cross-sell conversion services. Revenue is driven by activity volume, service complexity (inbound service-heavy clients pay more per handle), and platform features such as IVR/CTI/CRM workflows. Many providers move lower-value functions to self-service and price higher-value live support as premium services.
cost_structure: Primary costs are labour (large nonproducer workforce), telecom/network transit, cloud contact-center platforms, software licences and AI tooling, and compliance spend for TCPA/robocall controls and caller-verification workflows. Variable costs are high when call volumes surge; fixed technology and certification/compliance overhead is increasing as regulation tightens.
current_dynamics: Demand is being pulled by higher online order and support activity while basic support channels are increasingly replaced by digital self-service. US operators face higher scrutiny from FTC/FCC, including daily complaint-sharing and stronger registration/filing requirements for carriers and providers linked to unwanted call traffic. AI is improving handling of routine calls and routing quality, but not yet fully replacing live-agent interactions for complex or high-value issues.
whats_growing: Q1 2026 US retail e-commerce demand supported higher customer-contact requirements, with Census reporting e-commerce up 9.8% year-on-year and 16.9% share of retail sales.
Cloud-native contact workflows, analytics, and AI-enabled IVR/chat escalation increasingly complement live agents.
Regulatory data-sharing and call-authentication tooling (DNC and robocall mitigation ecosystems) are expanding in scope and vendor spend.
whats_shrinking: Pure manual inbound volume for routine queries is being substituted by automated channels (chat, FAQs, bot-assisted triage).
High-volume outbound telemarketing campaigns face stronger consumer friction and complaint risk.
Low-differentiated cost-competition remains strong among legacy call-routing-only providers.
recent_developments: 2026-01-02: FTC reported 258M+ telephones on the national DNC Registry and >2.6M FY2025 complaints, mostly robocall-related.
2026-01-06: FCC finalised Robocall Mitigation Database rule updates; effective date and filing updates (including FRN/CORES-related requirements) were set to strengthen compliance.
2026-02-26: FCC guidance period referenced annual recertification and updated filing requirements in RMD implementation.
2026-05-26: FCC proposed Enhanced KYC rules for voice services with comment deadlines June 25 and reply deadline July 27, 2026.
2026-01: Census reported Q1 US e-commerce at $326.7B (SA) and 16.9% share of retail sales; annual growth materially above total retail.
outlook: Mid-term outlook is moderate growth rather than structural expansion. The largest upside is in complex service offerings (high-value assistance, retention, and sales enablement) as AI absorbs low-value transactions and compliance complexity drives preference for larger, better-governed operators.
themes: AI automation replacing routine interactions
E-commerce-driven service demand
Robocall enforcement and DNC compliance pressure
Cloud/hosted contact center migration
Higher compliance and identity-related onboarding requirements
Shift from volume-only outsourcing toward outcome-based customer retention support
one_sentence: The US market remains mid-single-digit growth in practice as inbound service demand from online retail offsets pressure from channel substitution to automation and heavier anti-robocall regulation.

title: Television Broadcasting in the US
one_liner: The industry remains advertiser-led and local, but audience and revenue pressure are shifting it toward election-cycle spikes, streaming competition, and larger station groups.
overview: Television broadcasting in the US remains a mature, cyclical media segment anchored in advertising, retransmission fees, and local audience trust, while viewing behavior continues to migrate away from traditional linear cable toward streaming and CTV. Baseline 2022 revenue was high and slowly growing, but 2025 showed a dip tied to election-cycle normalization and non-political programming cadence, followed by a projected rebound in 2026. Large consolidation moves, combined with a likely shift in ownership policy, are accelerating strategic repositioning around local scale, sports and news, and interactive ATSC 3.0/NextGen TV capabilities.
how_it_makes_money: Advertising remains the core revenue engine (national/regional and local ad sales).
Retransmission and related carriage fees provide a high-volume revenue layer for OTA stations.
Program rights and licensing/support for station groups and affiliates supplement ad demand.
Local advertising is increasingly important as audiences value local news, weather, and sports touchpoints.
Digital extensions (CTV/OTT, website, and social distribution) are increasing the monetizable inventory mix.
cost_structure: High fixed operating costs in studio production, news operations, spectrum transmission, and distribution infrastructure.
Labor and technology costs are significant due to local staffing, content workflows, and compliance burdens.
Marketing/sales expenses rise with fragmented audiences and cross-platform campaign competition.
Network and rights costs add leverage risk when ad markets are soft despite retransmission resilience.
current_dynamics: The segment is in a transition from legacy linear reliance toward a blended broadcast-streaming reality, with local stations using retransmission and local advertising to defend margins. Near-term revenue is volatile by ad-cycle, but election years, sports calendars, and continued consolidation are driving strategic urgency, while ownership policy uncertainty/integration is reshaping long-term bargaining power.
whats_growing: 2026 rebound in total TV station ad revenue after a 2025 dip, tied to political advertising and major sporting calendars.
Digital and CTV/local ad shares continue to gain within local advertising, even as direct linear viewing softness persists.
ATSC 3.0/NextGen TV deployment, interactive formats, and datacasting-style capabilities are expanding monetization options.
Station groups with stronger local distribution footprints are gaining negotiating advantage in retransmission and local civic/brand partnerships.
Consolidation (notably Nexstar–Tegna) is increasing scale in ratings leverage and back-office efficiency.
whats_shrinking: Linear broadcast + cable remains challenged by streaming-first audience behavior; in May 2025, streaming share of TV usage exceeded the broadcast-plus-cable aggregate.
National spot advertising remains structurally weaker versus local and digital alternatives.
Traditional cable/satellite household attachment is eroding (36% as of July 2025).
Small-market fragmentation and platform migration increase bargaining pressure on legacy ad inventory.
Industry deal volume is expected to remain muted versus prior merger cycles except for strategically motivated transactions.
recent_developments: 2025-07-01: Pew Research Center found 83% of U.S. adults watch streaming services while only 36% subscribed to cable/satellite television.
2025-07-29: Nielsen reported Q2 2025 ad-supported TV content at 73.6% of overall viewing, with streaming at 44.8% in May 2025.
2025-08-18: Nexstar announced a $6.2 billion definitive agreement to acquire TEGNA.
2026-03-19: Nexstar publicly announced closure of the TEGNA acquisition after FCC and DOJ approvals.
2026-08-06: FCC voted 2-1 to eliminate the national TV ownership cap framework, opening potential for case-by-case consolidation above prior reach limits.

outlook.2026: Expected rebound: S&P projected TV station ad revenue to rise to $24.67 billion in 2026 from $21.81 billion in 2025.
outlook.2028: S&P projected a peak around $25.58 billion in 2028 before non-election normalization.
outlook.2030: S&P forecasted another rebound near $25.25 billion by 2030.
outlook.Risk: Ad cycles remain highly election and sports dependent; watch for abrupt down years in non-political cycles and pressure on national spot demand.

themes: Streaming-led audience shift from platform to occasion.
Election-cycle advertising volatility.
Consolidation and ownership-rule recalibration.
Localism as a competitive moat.
NextGen TV monetization and interactive advertising.
one_sentence: In 2026, US television broadcasters are stabilizing with stronger local sales, retransmission economics, and consolidation as streaming and regulatory shifts redraw competitive boundaries.

title: Television Production in the US
one_liner: US TV production is rebounding in a stream-first era, with audience attention shifting from linear schedules to ad-supported and streaming-first distribution while production remains capital- and talent-intensive.
overview: The US television production market in 2026 sits in a transition from linear-dominant contracting to platform-agnostic commissioning, with broadcasters, cable networks, and OTT operators sharing content budgets across ad-supported and subscription models. Survey and measurement data show that streaming is now the primary path to reach viewers, while linear and MVPD shares are shrinking, increasing pressure on price, licensing terms, and backlog management for independent and studio producers.

market_size.notes: Estimated from the 2022 IBIS baseline and 2022-2027 growth path of roughly +1.3% CAGR.

employment.source_category: BLS Motion Picture and Sound Recording Industries (NAICS 512)

baseline_2022.unit: USD billion and CAGR % (IBIS 2022 baseline and outlook)
baseline_2022.notes: IBIS World baseline listed 2022 market size at $41,788m with weak five-year demand conditions entering 2022.

how_it_makes_money: Selling and licensing television programming to broadcasters, cable operators, and streaming platforms.
Selling direct rights (first-window, pay-one-window, and territory packages) and library monetization.
Producing under co-production or production-service contracts where economics are based on delivery milestones and delivery-ready assets.
Earning from ad-supported distribution rights (FAST channels, AVOD bundles) as ad-supported viewing rises.
Upselling formats, spin-offs, international versions, and long-tail rights exploitation.

primary_costs: Above-the-line and below-the-line production spend (talent, writing, directing, crews, sets, locations)
Post-production, editing, VFX, music, and delivery/compliance
Marketing and launch support, especially around season premieres and platform launches
Technology stack costs (remote workflows, cloud delivery, monitoring, subtitle/subtitle localization, analytics tooling)
Financing carry costs tied to content cash cycles and upfront commitments
cost_structure.margin_pressure: High fixed content costs and increased platform competition create pricing pressure across licensing and production margins.

current_dynamics: Most US adults report streaming use at 83% (2025), while only 36% report a cable/satellite subscription at home.
In May 2025, streaming usage surpassed combined broadcast-plus-cable TV share in a Nielsen measure of total TV usage.
Ad-supported portions of total TV viewing increased to 73.6% in Q2 2025.
The market is split between premium subscription services and rapidly scaling FAST/AVOD inventory.
Wage and staffing indicators in NAICS 512 show elevated labor costs and large establishment counts, signaling scale but fragmented producer ecology.
Linear media groups are reporting subscriber and ad pressure while streaming ad-supported growth offsets part of the shortfall.
whats_growing: Ad-supported streaming and FAST distribution channels.
B2B ad inventory demand from connected-TV ecosystems.
Cross-platform library exploitation and non-linear licensing windows.
Production infrastructure that supports rapid release cadence and multi-market localization.
whats_shrinking: Cable-only dependence as cord cuts continue.
Linear distribution revenue share versus total TV consumption.
Standalone subscription growth from fragmented pay-TV bundles.
High-cost legacy linear advertising rates when audience share shifts to mixed viewing paths.
recent_developments: 2025-07-01: Pew reported 83% of US adults use streaming services and only 36% subscribe to cable/satellite TV.
2025-07-29: Nielsen reported Q2 2025 ad-supported viewing reached 73.6% of overall TV viewing.
2025-05-01: Nielsen reported streaming reached 44.8% of TV usage in May 2025, slightly above combined broadcast+cable.
2026-02 (Feb): TVB showed cable households in U.S. TV households at 21.3% with broadband-only households at 35.3%, using Nielsen methodology.
2026-06-22: PwC estimated global E&M advertising exceeded $1.0T in 2025 and noted continued shift toward ad-supported and streaming-led monetization.
2026-07-02: S&P Global reported US FAST ad revenue at $3.9B in 2025 and highlighted Tubi plus Roku Channel concentration in that segment.
outlook: 2026 likely remains a market of controlled growth but uneven unit economics: stronger for scalable ad-supported distribution and weaker for legacy linear-first contracting. Producers that can combine international language variants, data-informed scheduling, and multi-window rights packaging should gain in an environment where streaming penetration keeps widening.
themes: Cord-cutting and mixed-screen behavior
Ad-supported growth in FAST/CTV
Competition-driven content volume and pricing pressure
Rising importance of data-driven green-lighting and completion risk management
Scale through partnerships across studios, streamers, and device ecosystems
one_sentence: The industry is rebuilding after pandemic disruptions as demand shifts to streaming and ad-supported viewing, but competition and cord erosion are compressing traditional buyers and pushing producers toward diversified distribution, international finance, and AI-enabled production workflows.

title: Tent, Awning & Canvas Manufacturing
one_liner: Manufacturers of tents, tarpaulins, awnings, sails, and related protective canvas systems for recreation, events, logistics, construction, boat building, and public-sector use.

key_stats.market_size: USD 3.4 billion (2026e, IBIS projection horizon)
key_stats.growth: 2.7% CAGR (2021-2026 projection)

baseline_2022.market_size: USD 3.06 billion (2022 proxy derived from 2021 base of USD 2.984b with the IBIS 2.66% annual path to 2026)
baseline_2022.growth: ~2.66% annualized growth rate implied by the 2021-2026 projection path

how_it_makes_money.core_revenue: Manufacture and sale of finished tents/awnings/tarpaulins and related covers for retail brands, event/commercial users, logistics, construction, boat-related segments, and government/public safety buyers.
how_it_makes_money.pricings: Project quotes and custom-spec runs generally carry higher unit margins than commodity catalog products; commodity SKUs rely on volume and cost discipline.
how_it_makes_money.service_mix: Repairs, custom branding, and replacements add attachment revenue, especially for commercial and government fleets.

cost_structure.materials: Cotton/polyester and specialty coated fabrics are the largest variable cost; cotton and other fiber input prices directly affect gross margins.
cost_structure.labor: Cutting, stitching, assembly, testing, and finishing are labor-intensive, especially for low-volume and custom jobs.
cost_structure.fixed_costs: Overhead, rent/utilities, distribution, quality control, and compliance costs are material in smaller domestic operations.
cost_structure.scale_effect: Scale remains limited by fragmentation, so overhead absorption is weaker than in larger automated textile peers.

major_players: Industry shows low concentration in baseline intelligence and no single dominant national manufacturer
Springbar (canvas tent and shelter systems, U.S.-based production emphasis)
Norfolk Tent (commercial and military-style commercial tent systems)
Springbar-like niche producers and custom fabricators in event/commercial canopy execution
The broader tent/outdoor portfolio includes brands such as Coleman, The North Face, and NEMO in downstream tent demand channels

current_dynamics.demand: Outdoor demand is supported by strong recreation participation and travel behavior in 2025.
current_dynamics.imports_trade: US textile data for 2025 showed moderate softness in net fiber imports versus 2024 but still above 2023, while cotton-use conditions remain a key driver for input planning.
current_dynamics.policy_channel: FY2026 defense budget materials indicate elevated federal spend, which supports sustained demand for durable field-grade textile products and shelters.
current_dynamics.commercial_activity: Census construction data in 2026 shows nonresidential activity holding up in the recent month, supporting industrial and commercial canvas use.
current_dynamics.product_mix: Camping/portable shelter use remains the largest consumer-visible demand anchor for tents and lightweight awning solutions.

whats_growing: Vehicle-accessible and casual camping participation remained strong in 2025
NPS recreation activity stayed high through 2025
Public and commercial demand for utility-grade protective textiles remains resilient where projects are capital intensive
whats_shrinking: Import competition remains a margin drag at the mass-volume tent/awning segment
Net textile/fiber import growth decelerated in 2025 vs 2024
Housing permit activity in 2026 softened versus prior-year rates in some monthly series

Government/public demand persistence
Input-cost and trade-pressure sensitivity
Need for durable low-maintenance material performance
Customization and small-batch value capture
Low concentration encourages relationship-driven regional niches

title: Testing & Educational Support in the US
one_liner: Testing and educational support in the US in 2026 is balancing stable enrolment-driven demand with weaker admissions-test pull-through as institutions keep broad test flexibility.
overview: The U.S. testing and educational support market is a mixed-services ecosystem: admissions-related test preparation, school-day testing administration, consulting, tutoring, and workforce/career-readiness assessment services. Recent data show stronger participation in postsecondary education and school-based testing, but a structural shift toward optional admissions policies that lowers mandatory reliance on test-prep intensity.

key_stats.market_size: n/a
key_stats.growth: n/a

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from test administration fees, paid prep products (digital and instructor-led), school and district contracts for readiness programs, postsecondary guidance/consulting retainers, educational support for counselors/test-prep, and tutoring/online support subscriptions.
cost_structure: Labour and instructional/consultant staffing remains the largest operating cost component.
Technology stack, test prep content, platform hosting, and analytics tools are major fixed and semi-fixed costs.
Marketing and student acquisition become more competitive where free/discounted test tools are widely available.
current_dynamics: 2026 shows a split market: pipeline and readiness demand is increasing (strong postsecondary enrollment and school-year testing volume), while admissions-test dependence declines for a growing share of institutions, shifting revenue toward broader readiness, tutoring, and diagnostic services.
whats_growing: Postsecondary total enrollment projections are up to 22.50 million in 2026 from 22.33 million in 2025 (IPEDS 303.30 projected values).
NCES postsecondary enrollments reported sustained growth: final fall 2025 postsecondary enrollment was 19.4 million students.
ACT reports in-school testing remains broad in 2025, with 23 states and 15 states testing 90%+ of their 2025 graduates.
Demand for outcomes-focused readiness support is rising through school/day-of/retake models supported by fee-waiver programs.
whats_shrinking: Admissions gatekeeping demand is softer as test-optional broadens: FairTest reported 2,088 of 2,248 ranked four-year colleges test-optional or test-free for Fall 2026, with 160 requiring scores.
Revenue showed softness at the industry level: Q1 2026 educational support services revenue fell versus Q1 2025 in NAICS 6117.
K-12 grade-level public enrollment continues to flatten in secondary grades, reducing broad low-end future demand for traditional prep pathways.

2026-06-11: FRED updated Q1 2026 educational support services revenue to $7,610m (NAICS 6117).
2025-01-23: NSC reported fall 2025 total postsecondary enrollment up 4.5% year-over-year.
outlook: From 2026 onward, the industry is likely to post modest, services-shifted growth: stronger demand for student readiness and guidance, but lower admissions-test intensity and intensified competition from free/low-cost digital alternatives should keep margins under pressure and push providers toward subscriptionized, differentiated support.
themes: Admissions-policy normalization toward test-optional is structural
Shift from score-gate prep to readiness, diagnostics, and coaching
Hybrid scaling of tutoring/testing through online channels
Fee-waived/state-funded access expands usage while pressuring premium spend

title: Textile Mills in the US
one_liner: U.S. textile mills are a shrinking core industry that is rebalancing toward technical and defense-enabled products while import competition and automation-driven productivity pressures deepen.
overview: NAICS 313 includes fiber, yarn, thread, and fabric-focused mill activity; in 2022 the technical textiles segment was the strongest submarket (40.6% of industry revenue). The industry remains tied to downstream apparel, automotive, and home-textile demand, but competitive pressure from low-cost imports has made high-value, faster-to-ship, and specialized products the resilience path in 2025–2026.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $21,038.638m (BLS sectoral output for NAICS 313, non-seasonally adjusted; IPUEN313T300000000) ; 2022 baseline (IBIS): $42,427m
key_stats.establishments: 2025-Q4: 2,662 private textile mills (BLS Q3 NAICS 313), plus modest additional non-private presence

how_it_makes_money: Produces fiber, yarn, thread, and fabric-intensive intermediate goods then sells into apparel, automotive interior, home textiles, technical textiles, and healthcare/industrial niches.
Revenue mix in 2022 was driven by technical textiles (40.6% share) and downstream demand from automotive and home-furnishing channels.
Margins rely on custom spec work and lead-time advantage in domestic supply versus imported, lower-cost alternatives.
Capability upgrades (performance fibers, composites, and protective fabrics) are used to move away from pure commodity pricing.
cost_structure: Raw materials (cotton, polyester/synthetic feedstocks, and related yarn intermediates)
Labor and skilled technical operators; payroll has continued to drift with shrinking scale despite productivity investment
Energy, water, and finishing/processing costs in spinning, weaving, and coating operations
Capital replacement and automation for modern looms, finishing, and quality systems
Logistics and freight for inbound feedstock and outbound distribution
current_dynamics: 2026 BLS/IAG data show lower absolute employment and moderate establishment concentration, indicating continued scale contraction with selective modernization.
Sectoral output and productivity indicate still-low growth in commodity output, with more emphasis on specialized production programs.
Price signals in textile commodity output remained volatile through early-mid 2026, supporting margin pressure and pass-through strategies.
Industry players continue to publicize investments in technical and performance fabric lines rather than mass commodity expansion.
whats_growing: 2025-2026: technical textiles and performance applications (home, automotive, medical, FR/defense-oriented uses).
Automation and advanced conversion capability in weaving/finishing for shorter lead times.
Private domestic investments in capability upgrades and technical-weave portfolios.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026: volume-sensitive domestic apparel-linked demand and broad commodity manufacturing footprint.
Employment base as firms automate and consolidate capacity.
Price competitiveness in low-complexity products, with import penetration still structurally high.

2026-07-15/07-17: Producer/price-index updates showed textile-market inflation signals in line with cost pressure from commodity and trade-cost conditions.
outlook: 2026 outlook remains modest for volume recovery but mixed for earnings: commodity recovery is limited, while niche technical, medical, and transportation-related textiles can stabilize or modestly expand where speed, certifications, and specialization dominate purchase criteria.
themes: Shift from commodity weaving to technical/high-performance textiles
Import competition and domestic reshoring balance
Automation for labor normalization
Input-cost volatility in synthetic fiber and energy
Defense and industrial supply-chain localization
one_sentence: After years of structural decline, NAICS 313 activity in 2025–2026 is smaller in volume than earlier eras, with modest demand holding in technical home, automotive, medical, and protection-focused applications.

title: The Retail Market for Audio Equipment
one_liner: U.S. audio-equipment retail in 2025–2026 is recovering into modest growth, led by smart connected products and online channels, while brick-and-mortar remains under margin pressure.
overview: The IBIS baseline (2020 report) projected recovery from the 2020 shock to around $24.9bn by 2025 at about 3.2% annual growth, with 2020 EBIT margin compression to ~2.2%. Using 2025–2026 public trade data as proxy, the market context remains supportive: nonstore retail (NAICS 4541 proxy) stayed in expansion, and audio-adjacent electronics/appliance retail (NAICS 443, a broader proxy) held positive momentum through mid-2026. The industry now shifts toward connected speakers/headphones/baseline systems sold through large-format and online channels, while value competition remains intense from built-in device audio and global sourcing dynamics.

market_size.value: $24.9bn (2025, IBIS baseline projection for pure audio equipment retail), with NAICS 443 electronics & appliance stores at $45.2bn through Jun 2026 (first-half annualized pace proxy, Census 2026 advance table)

growth.value: +1.0% (NAICS 443 2025 total $92.0bn vs $91.2bn in 2024 from FRED series MRTSSM443USN), +8.6% (NAICS 443 June 2026 vs June 2025 in Census monthly advance report), +6.9% (nonstore retail NAICS 4541 total in 2025 vs 2024 from FRED MRTSSM454USN)
growth.margin_context: EBIT/shareholder-visible margins remain constrained versus broader retail peers (IBIS baseline notes historically low ~2.2% in 2020, recovering as demand stabilizes)

consumer_adoption.smart_speaker_penetration: 35% of U.S. adults with smart speakers in 2026 (Pew Research)

baseline_2022.market_size: $22.7bn (2022e, interpolated from the IBIS baseline path between $21.3bn in 2020 and $24.9bn in 2025)
baseline_2022.growth: ~2.3% annualized (2020–2022 implied path within the 2020 baseline trend), vs 3.2% annualized projected to 2025 in the same baseline report

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is driven by hardware retail (headphones, portable speakers, soundbars, components), with high-ticket bundle sales in multichannel/home-theater equipment carrying better gross profit than commodity accessory lines; 2025 operator disclosures show meaningful online conversion and services/financing bundles (Best Buy FY2025) cushioning margin risk from direct price comparison in commodity SKUs.

cost_structure.gross_profit_levers: Inventory procurement and product mix: imported hardware pricing, supplier discounts, and freight/lead-time volatility shape COGS; connected premium SKUs have better attach rates than commodity peripherals.
cost_structure.operating_costs: Store footprint and fulfillment costs are split between lower-CAPEX physical channels and higher fulfilment/returns intensity in e-commerce (2025–2026 earnings commentary from large chains indicates online channel as primary growth engine while store productivity weakens for commodity audio).
cost_structure.margin_baseline: IBIS baseline reported EBIT margin weakened to ~2.2% in 2020 after the shock, with a structural expectation of gradual recovery as online mix and higher-value bundles lift gross spread.

current_dynamics: e-commerce intensity is rising, with large US chains explicitly reporting online mix around 39.5% (2025 FY reporting point),
voice+AI ecosystems are shaping purchasing behavior (smart speaker ownership at 35% in 2026 Pew data),
consumer electronics channels are showing short-term acceleration in June 2026 while 2025 annual nonstore retail remained strong,
demand is skewing toward connected/home-entertainment bundles and wireless wearable audio.
competition from built-in device audio is persistent, pushing mix toward premium differentiated audio components.
whats_growing: Premium connected devices and bundles (smart speakers, soundbars, wireless earbuds, wireless headphones) with higher digital/voice integration,
online traffic and conversion in category-adjacent electronics storefronts (nonstore NAICS 4541 +6.9% in 2025),
consumer replacement cycles tied to AI/home-automation refreshes (2026 smart device penetration rise).
whats_shrinking: pure commodity in-store impulse sales as shoppers compare online prices across channels and prefer direct sales from device ecosystems,
margin on basic stand-alone units (especially legacy portable formats) as differentiation narrows.
net-store expansion speed in independent specialty audio outlets under pressure versus scale and marketplace operators.
recent_developments: 2025-03-11: Best Buy reported FY2025 results with ~39.5% online share of U.S. sales, continuing the chain’s channel mix shift.
2025-05-15: Sony announced next-generation WH-1000XM-series noise-canceling headphones launch, reinforcing premium wireless segment competition.
2026-06-17: Pew Research reported 35% of U.S. adults had a smart speaker, underscoring demand for connected audio ecosystems.
2026-07-16: U.S. Census advance retail table showed NAICS 443 monthly level at 7.9bn in Jun 2026 and +8.6% Y/Y versus Jun 2025.
2026-07-16: Same release showed nonstore retail (NAICS 4541) with strong monthly growth in the 14.2% range in late-June 2026 context, while nonstore annual total in 2025 was about 1.52tn.
outlook: 2025–2026 is likely a moderate-growth period, not a cyclical boom: expect low-to-mid single-digit revenue expansion in category-adjacent electronics channels, stable-to-weak discretionary spending at lower ticket SKUs, and slower but positive pricing power for premium integrated systems, smart-home audio, and branded ecosystems.
themes: AI audio becomes a purchase trigger
From showroom to fulfillment-first models
Shift to connected bundles over standalone devices
Globalized supply chain keeps component pricing volatile
Promotion-heavy, fast-moving consumer electronics competition
one_sentence: The category is maturing, with online share and premium, integrated experiences lifting sales, but consumer electronics substitution and high comparison shopping capping margin upside.

title: The Retail Market for Auto Tires
one_liner: U.S. auto-tire retail is a mature, replacement-led market where demand is driven by vehicle miles and aging fleets, while competition from discount-focused chains, online channels, and OEM supply pressure keeps margins thin.
overview: The market remains demand-led by replacement cycles on passenger and light-vehicle usage, even as vehicle miles, fleet age, and commercial transport continue to add steady background demand. In 2025-26, channel competition widened between specialist dealers, warehouse clubs, and marketplace-driven options, increasing service differentiation as the key performance differentiator. Cost pressure from raw materials, promotional pricing, and labor intensity remains the main drag on profitability despite demand resilience.

market_size.2026: $56.70 billion (US tire market estimate, total OEM + replacement)
market_size.basis: market-research estimate used for 2026 baseline context

growth.2022_2026: +1.4% in shipments versus 2019 baseline and +0.7% in 2026

margin.2025: ~3.0% EBIT margin range in IBIS baseline, with slim unit economics and heavy competition

baseline_2022.market_size: 334.8 million tires (US total shipments forecast in 2022)

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue is replacement and fitment-linked tire sales; higher-margin opportunities come from premium/specialty tires, fleet solutions, installation, alignment, balancing, rotation, and service packages sold in-store. Major retailers increasingly combine online shopping with physical pickup/installation to increase conversion and reduce friction for consumers who prefer assisted purchasing.
cost_structure: High-cost structure is driven by high-cost tire procurement, labor-intensive install/service operations, rent and tooling in service bays, and localized inventory/working-capital needs. Manufacturer-level cost reporting shows tire COGS can exceed 80% of sales and SG&A remains high, which supports the industry pattern of low retail operating margins unless offset by service mix and pricing power.
current_dynamics: Demand remains healthy on replacement and truck/service channels, but unit growth is modest and uneven by segment. The competitive battleground is shifting to convenience and service execution (installation speed, appointment quality, trust, and digital scheduling), with independents retaining strong distribution power in wholesale and chains expanding omni-channel tire service offerings.
whats_growing: 2023-2026: Total US tire shipments recovered from 334.8m in 2022 to 338.9m projected in 2026; growth is now driven more by service-linked replacement demand than new vehicle volume.
Specialty and higher-value segments (performance, durability, truck/light-duty variants) are gaining share as consumers seek longer life and better road performance.
Omni-channel tire shopping/install workflows expanded, including contactless auto-service appointment flows and online-to-store fulfillment models.
Hybrid powertrain demand rose in 2Q26, supporting mixed-tread and high-performing replacement demand in parts of the passenger-light-duty segment.
whats_shrinking: 2022 replacement passenger/light-truck shipments showed pressure, highlighting cyclical softness in conventional replacement demand despite broader freight support.
recent_developments: 2022-12-01: USTMA projected 334.8 million US tire shipments in 2022 (flat vs 2021 at 335.2m).
2023-02-28: USTMA forecast total US shipments of 334.2m in 2023 (up to 332.0m in 2022).
2025-01-23: Bridgestone announced closure of its LaVergne, Tennessee plant and cited ~700 jobs affected across related footprint optimization.
2025-10-09: Walmart launched contactless Auto Care Centers and said its 2,582 Supercenters offered auto services, reporting >6.6m online hours saved through appointment scheduling.
2026-02-10: Modern Tire Dealer reported independents still controlled 80% of US consumer tire wholesale share in 2025.
2026-03-04: USTMA forecast total US tire shipments at 338.9m in 2026 (up 0.7% vs 336.3m in 2025).
outlook: Short-term growth is likely moderate rather than expansionary: demand is supported by ongoing mileage and aging fleet dynamics, but margin expansion depends on converting traffic into higher-value service attach rates and premium tire mix. Large-channel intensity will keep price pressure elevated, so disciplined inventory and customer-experience differentiation will matter more than pure traffic capture.
themes: Aging fleet and high-used-vehicle tenure push replacement demand
Truck and local freight activity remains a hidden floor for tread demand
Dealer-service capability is the key mooring against online-only commodity pricing
Electrification mix is evolving, with hybrid growth partially offsetting BEV softness
Consolidation power and purchasing leverage in wholesale channels amplify competitive pressure on independents
one_sentence: The U.S. auto-tire retail market is stabilizing around the mid-$50B range in 2026 with low-single-digit unit growth, but most upside now depends on higher-value service-led positioning, premium tire mix, and digital-enabled convenience.

title: The Retail Market for Headphones
one_liner: US headphone retail is a small but persistent market where wireless conversion, streaming demand, and online purchasing offset sustained margin pressure.
overview: The IBISWorld baseline shows the US Retail Market for Headphones at USD 4.865 billion in 2021 with a 3.2% five-year CAGR into that point. The category has shifted further toward wireless and premium feature-led SKUs while remaining sensitive to discretionary spending, import-driven pricing, and competition from low-cost alternatives. In 2025–26, the channel mix has moved more decisively online, and broader audio consumption habits support replacement and upsell demand even as long product lifecycles cap rapid repeat purchasing.

market_size.note: Proxy derived from last published IBISWorld 2021 value (USD 4.865bn) and near-term growth trajectory

growth.note: Primary IBISWorld multi-year growth input available through 2021

how_it_makes_money: Retailers earn margin on headphone unit sales, with stronger margins on premium and feature-rich models; higher-priced models and bundle sales (cases, replacements, accessories) help offset commoditization. Online channels improve economics through lower occupancy and staffing costs versus brick-and-mortar footprints.

cost_structure.product_costs: High share of imported inventory and supplier pricing risk from China/other low-cost manufacturing locations
cost_structure.payroll: Largest non-cost-of-goods line in many operators, especially specialty and physical-format retailers
cost_structure.rents_and_overhead: Physical shelf-space, staffing, and distribution costs remain significant for big-box and specialty formats
cost_structure.marketing: Brand and promotion spend remains elevated due to high category competition and frequent model refresh cycles
cost_structure.returns_and_clearance: Price-pressure management and markdowns are persistent as lower-tier models cycle quickly

current_dynamics: The category is being reshaped by three interacting 2025–2026 forces: streaming demand intensity, channel migration to digital retail, and rapid feature-led competition (ANC, health, connectivity, AI assistants). 2025–26 data also show continued consumer willingness to buy higher-ticket models alongside a broader low-price base.
whats_growing: Wireless and true wireless formats, especially earbuds, remain the strongest volume and value growth area.
US online retail’s role is expanding; Q1 2026 e-commerce was 16.9% of total retail sales.
Spending on music/audio ecosystems is supporting premium upgrade behavior (headphones tied to streaming and connected workflows).
Demand for fitness, travel, work, and multimodal streaming usage is lifting preference for ANC, fit, and software features.
whats_shrinking: Pure commoditized entry headphones are under margin pressure from abundant low-cost imports.
Net new-category growth is moderate compared with adjacent consumer-tech categories because headphones are durable and replace slowly.
Low-end differentiation is weakening as feature parity rises and consumers stretch replacement cycles when prices spike.
recent_developments: 2025-05-21: Q1 2025 global true wireless earbuds shipments reached 78.3 million units, with Apple at 18.2 million units (23.3% share) and Samsung 7.1% per Canalys reporting.
2025-07-01: Nielsen reported Q2 2025 US consumers averaged 3h50m daily audio consumption across radio/podcasts/streaming/satellite; streaming held notable share of ad-supported audio time.
2025-10: CTA’s 2025 Consumer Technology Holiday Purchase Patterns report said 88% of US adults planned to buy technology gifts including wireless headphones.
2025-12 to 2026-02: DIMA Annual Music Study found 50% of US streamers listen daily; 58% among paid subscribers.
2026-03: IFPI Global Music Report 2026 showed global recorded music reached USD 31.7bn in 2025, with streaming continuing as the key growth engine and 69.6% share of revenues.
2026-05-18: US Census reported Q1 2026 e-commerce sales of USD 326.7bn and 16.9% of total retail, indicating sustained online demand relevance for headphone retail.
outlook: Near-term outlook is modest but resilient growth: the market likely continues converting into higher-feature wireless experiences while remaining vulnerable to price compression. The most likely winners are brands and retailers that combine streaming/AI compatibility, health/safety features, and strong direct-to-consumer logistics without over-indexing on low-margin commodity SKUs.
themes: Streaming-to-spending loop
Wireless-first conversion
Online channel acceleration
Import-linked gross margin pressure
Feature-driven upselling
Premium + value-tier dual-track demand
one_sentence: After the 2021 IBISWorld baseline, 2025–2026 data show slower headline growth than the 2025–2026 hype cycle implies, with channel and feature shifts becoming the primary gain levers.

title: The Retail Market for Home Furniture & Bedding
one_liner: U.S. home furniture and bedding retail in 2025-2026 is a housing-cycle-sensitive, value-competitive category where growth is modest and driven by channel share shifts rather than broad category expansion.
overview: The sector continues to move with housing formation, credit costs, and consumer confidence. New home demand and home-improvement spending support demand, while persistent mortgage and inflation pressures restrain discretionary purchases. Retailers are splitting strategy between physical showrooms for high-touch buying and digital channels for convenience, financing, and assortment reach, causing a clear migration from volume-led expansion toward share gains in high-service, lower-cost formats.

market_size.2026-05: US$11.3bn in May 2026 (MRTSSM442USS, seasonally adjusted monthly)

cost_structure: 2021 benchmark from industry history shows labor remained the largest expense (8.6% of revenue), while gross/operating margin was thin (around 4.6% profit at baseline period); 2025-2026 cost pressure is concentrated in payroll, freight/last-mile fulfillment, digital marketing, and showroom/cash-and-carry infrastructure.

At the same time, sector-wide online demand remains structurally important with Census reporting 16.9% of all U.S. retail in Q1 2026 on e-commerce.

2026: Consumer sentiment weakened through spring (UMCSENT 56.4 in Jan 2026 to 44.8 in May 2026), increasing sensitivity to financing conditions.

Structural winners should be operators that combine low-friction online discovery with efficient physical sampling/experiential conversion, while value-oriented pricing and loyalty economics are expected to remain decisive.

title: The Retail Market for Jewelry
one_liner: US fine and fashion jewelry has shifted to a higher-priced, more digital-first model as consumers trim unit purchases but spend more per transaction.
overview: The U.S. jewelry retail market remains resilient after the pandemic cycle but is now defined by selective demand: slower unit growth, higher ticket values, and stronger demand for premium positioning, personalization, and trust signals. Independent and chain operators continue to mix physical stores with stronger online commerce, while lab-grown diamonds and experience-led in-store services divide the market between value-sensitive shoppers and upper-income luxury buyers.
how_it_makes_money: Sells bridal/fine jewelry, fashion jewelry, watches, and precious metal accessories through specialty stores, mall/off-mall formats, and dedicated e-commerce channels.
Generates high-margin services such as repairs, maintenance, customization, engraving, resizing, trade-ins, and extended service plans.
Uses hybrid channel monetization where online browsing and appointment-influenced in-store conversion lower geographic barriers while supporting higher-ticket fulfillment.
Leverages financing and loyalty mechanics in-store and online to improve conversion on premium items and larger discretionary purchases.
cost_structure: Gold and gemstone input price volatility is the largest variable cost risk.
Import duties and tariff exposure on diamonds/gems/jewelry increase landed cost and force margin trade-offs.
Store-level fixed costs (rent, labor, and real-estate footprint efficiency) remain critical as chains rationalize underperforming locations.

title: The Retail Market for Laptop Computers

overview: The industry historically benefited from stronger home ownership of computing devices, remote work, and streaming/gaming demand, while competing form factors (especially tablets and entry-level substitutes) kept pressure on low-end margins. The latest 2025-26 signals indicate a structural reset: memory and NAND constraints are pushing prices up, consumers are replacing less frequently, and brands with scale are outperforming smaller players. Demand is increasingly concentrated in better-specced devices, education/enterprise refreshes, and channel models that reduce fixed-cost exposure.

title: The Retail Market for Musical Instruments
one_liner: US musical-instrument retail is a small, low-margin but resilient specialty category led by online and omnichannel competition, with steady participation from schools, beginners, and hobbyists.
overview: The industry sells new musical instruments, sheet music, and accessories through physical stores, mass merchants, and online channels; services such as lessons and repair are generally outside this segment in the IBIS definition. After a strong 2020–2021 pandemic lift, 2024–2026 dynamics indicate stabilization: category spikes have cooled, but demand for music participation remains intact, school music is recovering, and used-gear activity is strong. Competitive intensity is highest at the lower and mid-price tiers.

baseline_2022.growth: 1.4% CAGR to 2026

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is mainly from retail sales of instruments (especially guitars, acoustic/electric, keyboards, drums, violins, brass/woodwinds), sheet music, accessories, and related equipment; online and catalog channels generate volume through price comparison convenience and wider SKU breadth, while used instrument demand supports turnover in value-stable segments.
cost_structure: Gross margins are constrained by high import-to-inventory comparison pressure and aggressive channel discounting, with lower gross and operating efficiency for high-rent physical formats versus non-store channels; IBIS baseline suggests margins near 4.6% in 2026, with labor and payroll as a major fixed/variable cost component and rent/utilities and logistics costs structurally heavier for storefront models.

title: The Retail Market for Outdoor Furniture
one_liner: US outdoor furniture retail is normalizing after the COVID-era surge, with steady but price-pressured demand driven by housing-related household upgrades and hospitality outdoor-space spending.
overview: The industry covers outdoor furniture sold through specialty retailers, home-improvement chains, mass merchants, and e-commerce platforms in the US. Demand still tracks housing turnover, new starts, and household spending on home improvements, while commercial buyers remain active in permanent patios and hospitality spaces. The market has become increasingly value-oriented as large, digitally-led channels dominate assortment breadth and price competition, even as consumers and businesses continue to add or replace outdoor pieces.

how_it_makes_money: Retailers monetize by sourcing or sourcing partnerships, warehousing, fulfillment, and multi-channel sales of higher-margin curated assortments, with profits driven by mix, velocity, and scale. Margin is strongest where firms keep fulfillment efficient, pair furniture with cushions/accessories and replacement parts, and sell durable B2B project contracts; it is weakest where heavy discounting and price matching dominate.

title: The Retail Market for Seasonal Decorations
one_liner: US seasonal decoration retail remains a mature but resilient discretionary category, with demand clustered around major holidays and increasingly spread across digital and discount-led channels.
overview: The US seasonal decorations retail market remains centered on Christmas and Halloween spending, with winter products still dominant, while broader seasonal events (Valentine’s Day, Easter, Mother’s Day, graduations, and holiday hosting) add depth in slower months. IBISWorld’s latest published baseline shows the market growing from USD 28.6 billion in 2021 toward USD 32.4 billion by 2026, with modest single-digit growth and high price pressure in some segments. Current 2025-26 NRF consumer signals show robust holiday participation and strong seasonality, but consumers are increasingly shopping with budget constraints, early in the season, and through discount-plus-online mixes.

title: The Retail Market for Shoes
one_liner: US footwear retail is a mature but resilient market where style churn, athleisure demand, and online competition are driving moderate growth with persistent margin pressure.
overview: The market sits at a growth crossroads. Baseline IBIS data shows long-run expansion into 2026 and later, while current US data shows mixed retail tone: sector-wide demand is supported by lifestyle-driven replacement cycles and athletic/athleisure fashion, but discounting and cost inflation are squeezing operating leverage. Larger players and direct-to-consumer capabilities are outperforming the long tail of smaller merchants that depend heavily on promotions. The channel mix is increasingly hybrid, with store and non-store sales both important.

title: The Retail Market for Stationery Products
one_liner: US stationery retail is a late-cycle category with shrinking transactional volume, increasingly defended by omnichannel players and premiumized, personalized gift-focused offerings.
overview: US stationery retail has moved from broad commodity sales toward a narrower mix driven by holidays, milestones, and business needs that still require tangible stationery. IBISWorld’s baseline still indicates a structural decline, and 2025–2026 indicators show continued acceleration of this drift: online shopping as a share of US retail remains at high-single-digit annual increases in share, while paper-intensive segments face weaker overall demand. Category resilience is now concentrated in decorative, premium, and customized stationery that can command higher prices than standard mass cards and office paper packs.
