baseline_2022.growth: -1.2% annualized
baseline_2022.notes: Computed proxy using IBISWorld 2021 baseline of $5.996 billion and the 2021–2026 decline path.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from sales of writing materials, greeting and note cards, invitations, folders, envelopes, journals, and related stationery, sold through supermarkets, warehouse clubs, dollar retailers, specialty stores, and online marketplaces. Demand shifts to higher-ticket occasions (weddings, holidays, personalized gifts) improve average order value; low-price high-volume items face substitution by email, messaging, and e-cards. Margin recovery in 2026 is expected mainly from assortment upgrades (handcrafted, customizable, premium) and reduced overhead.
cost_structure: Primary costs are paper, printing components, and labor-intensive fulfillment at physical and e-commerce channels. Baseline IBISWorld economics highlight paper as a major input, and AF&PA supply data show weak print-writing paper demand context (printing-writing capacity -13.9% in 2025), which pressures volumes in legacy assortments. Retailers also face fixed-cost pressure from rent and distribution as low-margin store traffic declines and digital/order-fulfillment costs rise.
current_dynamics: 2025–2026 has reinforced two opposing vectors: substitution to digital communication continues to reduce commodity stationery volume, while digital-to-physical hybrid gifting ecosystems and premiumization sustain revenue in niches. The category is being redistributed toward large omnichannel retailers and digital-enabled greeting brands rather than traditional standalone stationery storefronts.
whats_growing: Digital and hybrid greeting solutions (card + e-gift or card + digital add-ons), shown by major brand launches and platform expansion in 2025.
Premiumization, personalization, and seasonal/luxury stationery with higher unit economics.
B2B-adjacent categories sold through office-supply networks as traditional consumer traffic weakens.
whats_shrinking: Traditional commodity stationery and low-value mass formats, especially where digital substitutes are acceptable.
Physical retail footprint in smaller office-stationery-heavy stores (ODP reported fewer operated stores and lower retail traffic in 2025).
White-space demand for paper-writing products in consumer channels versus digital-first communication.
recent_developments: 2026-03-10: US Census reported total retail e-commerce at $316.1B in Q4 2025 (16.6% share) and total 2025 e-commerce sales up 5.4% at $1,233.7B.
2025-11-05: ODP Q3 2025 results showed total sales of $1.6B, down 9%; Office Depot division sales were $749M, down 13%, with 63 fewer locations versus prior year.
2025-12-10: Atlas Holdings completed acquisition of ODP, transitioning Office Depot/OfficeMax to a private structure and emphasizing focus on core retail plus B2B operations.
2025-02-05: American Greetings expanded digital gifting features, adding value-added digital gift capabilities to its e-cards.
2026-05-29: AF&PA reported 2025 US paper and paperboard production down 3.7% to 66.3M tons; printing-writing capacity fell 13.9% to 7.7M tons.
2026-06-23: Hallmark announced 2026 online fan-exclusive seasonal merchandise, indicating continued multichannel investment in greeting/seasonal stationery demand.
outlook: Near-term outlook remains mildly negative for broad volume with another structurally pressured phase likely through 2027, but top-line downside should be cushioned where retailers shift toward emotional/seasonal gifting, personalization, and digital-enhanced physical products. Operators with strong online conversion, custom production, and compact assortment strategies should outperform slower legacy formats.
themes: Digital substitution pressure
Niche premiumization and personalization
Consolidation of fragmented store footprints
Hybrid physical-digital gifting
Age cohort substitution (older buyers hold legacy demand, younger buyers need differentiated value)
one_sentence: The market is expected to continue declining in volume as digital communication grows, while physical sales increasingly shift toward higher-margin occasion, personalization, and gift-pairing formats.

title: The Retail Market for Toys
one_liner: U.S. toy retail returned to growth in 2025 and accelerated in early 2026, with licensed, collectible, and mid-to-premium demand replacing broad volume-led growth.
overview: The US retail market for toys remains a discretionary but resilient category where channel power has shifted toward mass online-capable retailers and large superstore chains. 2025 data show clear pull from licensing, fandom-driven franchises, and higher-ticket play products, while legacy low-ticket and some weather-sensitive categories lost steam. 2019-to-2026 pressure from digital substitutes persisted, but 2025-26 rebound has been supported by family gifting, adult recipients, and social commerce discovery.

key_stats.market_size: $30.3 billion in U.S. toy retail sales in 2025 (Circana via The Toy Association).
key_stats.growth: 2024→2025: +6.0%; 2026 Jan–Apr: +13.0% versus Jan–Apr 2025; 2025→2026 early trend shows value-led recovery plus premiuming.
key_stats.2025_category_leader: Games & Puzzles reached $4.9 billion in 2025 and became the largest supercategory.
key_stats.seasonality: 13.7% of hobby, toy and game store sales occurred in December 2024 (Census holiday season snapshot).
key_stats.peak_month_sales_2025: December 2025 monthly toy/club-sales index point was 3,318 million (FRED MRTSSM45112USN).

baseline_2022.market_size: $30.6 billion in U.S. toy retail sales (Circana all supercategories).
baseline_2022.growth: +0.7% vs 2021 (Circana table); 2019→2025 in the older IBIS baseline era was near-flat with 0.08% projected annual growth.

how_it_makes_money: Gross margin from sale of toys, games, collectibles, and branded experiences sold through stores and marketplaces.
Revenue concentration in promotional placement, seasonal event spikes, and licensed property-driven merchandising cycles.
Additional margin from full-line distribution relationships with major brands and manufacturers, including velocity-driven assortments and private-label mix.

largest_costs: Inventory purchase costs from concentrated branded suppliers and licensing-linked assortment requirements.
Fulfillment and logistics for omnichannel distribution, especially fast-growing online demand.
Labor, including seasonal workforce scaling during holidays and higher-skilled digital operations.
Marketing and commerce-engineering costs (search, social, marketplace placement, and creator-driven demand generation).

current_dynamics: 2025: six of 11 toy supercategories posted dollar growth, with Games & Puzzles and Building Sets leading (Circana 2025 update).
2025: Pokémon posted $2.5 billion and was the top property, up 87% year-over-year.
2026: through April, toy industry sales accelerated to +13.0% with units +5.0% and average selling prices +7.0%.
2026: social-led discovery rose in relevance, with squishy sensory toys showing triple-digit growth through April and TikTok becoming a major category placement channel for toys/hobbies.
Seasonality remains high, with mid-to-high holiday concentration in toy and game stores.
whats_growing: Games & Puzzles (+37% in 2025), Building Sets (+15% in 2025), Explorative & Other Toys (+20% in 2025).
Higher-priced SKUs and collectible-driven categories (especially adult-directed and fandom-linked SKUs).
Licensed content lines tied to sports, gaming, and media properties.
Social commerce-to-first-customer journeys, especially for novelty and collectible formats.
whats_shrinking: Outdoor & Sports Toys (-6% in 2025).
Dolls (-7% in 2025).
Low-price SKU segments (<$5 and $15–$19.99 bands) under pressure versus premium tiers.
Smaller specialty-only channels face margin pressure versus large-format and omnichannel competitors.
recent_developments: 2025-08-05: Circana reported first-half 2025 toy sales up 6%, units up 3%, and ASP up 3% per month-over-month tracked period.
2026-02-03: Toy Association press release on Circana data said U.S. toy sales were +6% in 2025 and total toy industry value up 16% from 2020.
2026-06-15: Circana reported 2026 momentum at +13% through April and identified rapid growth in social/commercially driven sensory and collectible segments.
2025-12-16: Census Holiday Season briefing reported 13.7% of 2024 hobby, toy and game sales occurring in December.
2025-12 to 2026-05: FRED MRTSSM45112USN monthly toy/store-channel series shows strong seasonality and record 2025 holiday-month sales compared with prior-year trough periods.
outlook: 2026 appears to favor licensed, experiential, and digital-discovery-driven demand, with growth likely to remain above low-single digits at full-year pace if supply chains and inflation/consumer spending remain manageable. 2027 pressure points are likely to be premium-price elasticity, concentration risk in top retailers, and category volatility in trend-led franchises.
themes: Fandom and licensing as the structural demand engine
Premiumization and margin protection versus low-ticket softness
E-commerce plus social discovery replacing purely store-led discovery
Weather- and cycle-sensitive children’s segments versus adult-led gifting resilience
one_sentence: In 2025, U.S. toy retail sales climbed 6.0% to $30.3 billion while total industry strength came from higher average prices, and through April 2026 retail toy demand was up 13.0% year-over-year.

title: Thermometer Manufacturing
one_liner: US thermometer manufacturing is a small but durable niche where healthcare, industrial automation, and safety monitoring keep demand steady while margins remain exposed to input-cost and import competition.
overview: The US thermometer manufacturing base was modest in 2022 and continues to be dominated by medical, industrial, and food-use segments with stable underlying demand from hospitals, process plants, and workplaces. The 2020s shift to sustained fever screening and remote/self-health monitoring left a clear up-tier in demand quality and encouraged continued revenue despite fewer domestic entrants. 2025-2026 web-evidenced market reporting still shows continued expansion in medical thermometer demand (with different global estimates), while US industrial production and healthcare spending conditions also support underlying demand for manufacturing and hospital-facing thermometry.

baseline_2022.growth: -4.8% annualized decline over five years to 2022; long-run CAGR 1.71% (2005-2022)
baseline_2022.notes: IBISWorld baseline indicates a shrinking number of enterprises and continued competitiveness pressure despite demand resilience.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell temperature-measurement devices (digital and non-contact thermometers, clinical thermometers, industrial process sensors, food thermometers) through healthcare wholesalers, industrial channels, and direct B2B buyers. Because demand is broadly distributed across downstream sectors, revenue shifts are driven mostly by product mix and price adjustments rather than abrupt volume swings. Companies retain pricing power when demand is sticky and input costs rise.

main_cost_items: Plastics and resin content in enclosures and components
Calibration, metrology, QA testing, and compliance documentation
Skilled labor for assembly, calibration, and accuracy validation
cost_pressure_signals: US Producer Price Index for plastics and materials remains a persistent input-cost driver (WPS066; June 2026 level 308.753, index 1982=100).
Commodity volatility raises pressure on gross margin management and can force periodic repricing.

major_players: Johnson Controls International (historical participant with reduced domestic footprint)
current_dynamics: In 2025-2026, demand support remains linked to healthcare workflow needs and infection-control routines rather than a singular pandemic shock, while US industrial activity data show manufacturing output stabilization and modest growth. Regulatory clarity around clinical thermograph standards is improving, and firms with strong validation/QMS and connected-device portfolios are positioned to capture premium pricing. At the same time, global supply competition and the low-setup-cost profile of commodity categories keep margins under pressure in commoditized thermometer lines.
whats_growing: Non-contact and connected clinical thermometers used in fever screening and remote monitoring workflows
Mercury-free home and clinical thermometer formats versus older mercury-based styles
Industrial thermometer demand tied to process reliability in manufacturing and temperature-sensitive operations
Quality-focused contracts with hospitals, clinics, and industrial process customers that can absorb validated accuracy improvements
whats_shrinking: Mercury-based thermometer formats
Domestic enterprise count and standalone mid-size operators as concentration increases
High-volume low-spec commodity segments facing import-backed price pressure from China
recent_developments: 2025-06-18: FDA exempted certain clinical electronic non-contact thermometers from premarket notification requirements.
2025-05-26: FDA recognized updated IEC 80601-2-59 screening-thermograph guidance for screening thermometers, with conformity transition period references through 2028.

2026-07-17: Federal Reserve G.17 release showed US total industrial production index at 102.6 (2017=100) with manufacturing +1.1% year-over-year in June 2026; Q2 manufacturing output growth supported by broader production demand.
2026-07-15: FRED/WPS066 shows U.S. plastic resins and materials PPI at 308.753 (1982=100), indicating input-cost sensitivity for molded thermometer bodies and components.
2026: OECD health-at-a-glance context confirms high US healthcare spending intensity (~USD 14,885 per capita and 17.2% of GDP in 2025 data), supporting persistent clinical thermometry demand.
outlook: Base case is low-single to high-single-digit growth in value through 2027 as healthcare and industrial monitoring remain structurally supportive while the market remains mature and import-competitive. Winners are expected to be firms with stronger clinical validation, connected offerings, and lower-cost, higher-precision manufacturing.
themes: post-pandemic infection-control persistence
precision + compliance over commodity price competition
connected/home health expansion
input-cost hedging via pricing
industry consolidation and global sourcing pressure
one_sentence: The industry is mature but resilient, with clinical and industrial temperature-monitoring demand offsetting shrinking factory participation and rising pressure from global price competition.

title: Third-Party Administrators & Insurance Claims Adjusters in the US
one_liner: U.S. insurers and employers keep outsourcing claims processing, benefit-plan administration, and loss-management work to specialist TPAs and claims-adjusting firms that are paid mainly through claim- and service-based fees.
overview: US TPAs and claims administrators sit directly behind insurers, self-insured employers, and benefit plans, monetizing claim intake, adjudication, medical management, subrogation, and compliance. IBIS-style long-term data still frames the industry as steady, while 2025-26 signals show a mixed operating environment: high administrative complexity, increased AI-enabled process change, and weather/injury-pattern swings. Employer-sponsored coverage remains broad (2025: 60% of under-65s with ESI), and insurers’ premium base stayed high (2025: NAIC P&C direct premiums written up 4.6%), sustaining outsourceable volume, even as some carriers internalize routine work.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: US$322.3bn (Third Party Administration of Insurance and Pension Funds, Kentley); 2025: NAIC P&C direct premiums written proxy base US$1,105.3bn; 2022: IBIS World US market US$274.2bn
key_stats.growth: 2025: 9.3% annual growth over prior three years in the Kentley-defined subsegment; 2022: 3.3% annual growth and 3.76% CAGR over 2003-2022 (IBIS baseline); 2022 projected: 1.48% CAGR to 2028
key_stats.claims_adjuster_occupation: 2024-2034: BLS projects -5% employment change for claims adjusters (from 2024 baseline)

baseline_2022.growth: 2022: +3.3% annual increase; 3.76% CAGR from 2003-2022; IBIS projected 1.48% CAGR through 2028

how_it_makes_money: Firms earn primarily on transaction-processing and service contracts: per-claim fees, fixed-fee claims programs, and administrative fees for health-plan, workers-comp, pension, liability, and disability management. Larger providers combine high-touch labor-intensive loss adjustment with lower-margin network/platform products; broad service mix can smooth revenue while individual segments fluctuate with accident, weather, and litigation activity.
cost_structure: Labor is the core fixed cost because claims resolution remains specialist-intensive; human-capital exposure is high (CorVel fiscal-2025 workforce 5,075 and 91% remote/hybrid staff). Technology spend is rising sharply (AI-enabled claim summarization, underwriting-risk modeling, workflow automation), while cybersecurity and regulatory-compliance costs rise with AI and data-use scrutiny. Weather and catastrophe cycles shift utilization across segments, forcing flexible staffing and cost-control discipline.
current_dynamics: Demand continues from employer-paid health and benefit administration (2025: 60% of U.S. population under 65 had employer-sponsored insurance) and large downstream insurers, while the claims mix is bifurcating between routine claim intake (more automated) and high-touch medical-management/compliance services. Carriers’ and large TPAs’ investment in AI, analytics, and fraud/risk controls is accelerating as they seek to preserve margin as claims handling complexity rises.
whats_growing: 2025: Employers increasingly use self-funded and hybrid benefit structures, increasing TPA scope for medical management and compliance support.
2025: AI-assisted workflow adoption in claims escalates (e.g., Sedgwick’s February 2025 GenAI claims summary launch).

2025: Self-funded and specialty benefit administration volume remains resilient, including higher revenue contribution from medical-management-intensive lines (Crawford 2025 full-year Broadspire growth).
2025-2026: Employer-based insurance coverage stayed broadly stable, supporting claim volume base.
whats_shrinking: 2025: benign U.S. weather/catastrophe claims conditions lowered claims activity in some catastrophe-sensitive platform/services areas.
2025: Traditional commodity manual claims handling is being displaced by automation and structured digital triage workflows.
2025: Workers’ compensation private-carrier weather-sensitive growth remains muted while frequency pressure in line items is moderate and severity remains elevated, capping easy volume expansion.
recent_developments: 2025-02-27: Sedgwick launched an AI-generated claims summary feature in viaOne to speed claim review and decision support.
2025-03-31: CorVel’s 2025 filing disclosed 5,075 employees and 91% hybrid/remote workforce arrangement.
2025-10-08: NCCI published CY2024/early-CY2025 workers’ compensation update: CY2024 private-carrier NWP was US$41.6bn and CY2025 AY frequencies/ severities showed mixed but manageable pressure.
2026-03-03: Crawford held a conference call for 2025 results after reporting US$1,265.7m revenues before reimbursements and record Broadspire/International segment growth.
2026-04-01: NHTSA reported 2025 U.S. traffic fatalities at 36,640, a 6.7% drop from 2024.
2026-05: CDC NHIS early release estimated 2025 uninsured rate at 8.3% (28.0m people) and 11.6% adult private coverage share at 69.4% in 2025.
outlook: Near-term outlook (2026-2027) is moderate expansion with stronger dispersion: high-friction service lines and compliance-heavy administration should hold up, while price-sensitive or low-complexity claim handling faces margin pressure from automation and volume volatility. Operators that pair AI adoption with labor productivity and weather-cycle management should gain share.
themes: Automation and AI as productivity drivers
Catastrophe/weather-cycle sensitivity
Coverage-driven claim admin demand
AI governance, cyber risk, and regulatory scrutiny
Talent normalization with higher hybrid work and specialized skill needs
Industry concentration in top providers
one_sentence: The industry remains a mature but strategically important outsourcing layer with stable demand, stronger digitalization, and profitability sensitive to claim-activity volatility.

title: Third-Party Logistics
one_liner: US third-party logistics operators are growing through e-commerce fulfillment, cold-chain specialization, and AI-led network execution, while competitive pricing keeps margins tight.
overview: Third-party logistics providers coordinate transportation, warehousing, customs, and visibility services for shippers that outsource distribution and supply-chain execution. The market has shifted toward hybrid and integrated models that combine digital brokerage with controlled capacity to deliver reliable service in volatile lanes. Demand remains tied to freight volumes, consumer spending, cross-border flows, and ecommerce order complexity, while operators win by adding value-added services and software-enabled visibility.

key_stats.profitability: EBIT margin about 8.7% in 2022 (industry average, IBIS baseline)

baseline_2022.growth: 5.7% in 2022 and about 5.3% annualized in the IBIS baseline build-up

how_it_makes_money: Charging service fees and margins on freight brokerage, dedicated transportation, and intermodal forwarding
Taking managed warehouse and distribution fees for storage, picking/packing, returns, and reverse logistics
Capturing software and optimization value through visibility platforms, load matching, and visibility/reporting subscriptions
Earning contract-based premiums by bundling transportation with compliance and value-added handling

major_cost_drivers: Fuel-linked transportation costs and fuel-surcharge pass-through volatility
Labor and staffing costs across warehouse, transportation coordination, and local operations
Technology and automation spend to sustain pricing discipline and service reliability
Network operating costs: cross-border support, compliance, insurance, and carrier capacity management
cost_structure.margin_context: Competition remains high in transaction-based logistics, pushing operators toward integrated service portfolios to defend margin

current_dynamics: The US 3PL baseline remains positive, but operators are under pressure to invest in AI and automation while preserving service reliability.
Demand from ecommerce and healthcare/regulated supply chains is lifting value-added warehousing and reverse logistics requirements.
Cross-border complexity and customs-heavy flows are increasing need for integrated nearshoring and trade-compliant service design.
whats_growing: E-commerce fulfillment demand as small-pack, high-frequency shipping keeps increasing
Life sciences and healthcare cold-chain and traceability services
Hybrid digital + controlled-capacity models over pure spot brokerage
M&A-driven scaling among mid-market 3PLs to expand technology, footprint, and compliance capabilities
whats_shrinking: Low-touch, transaction-only brokerage without long-cycle service lock-in
Pure asset-light offerings that cannot differentiate on resilience, compliance, or visibility
Long-distance services with thin execution differentiation and limited analytics depth
recent_developments: 2025-05-06: DHL Supply Chain announced acquisition of IDS Fulfillment, adding over 1.3 million sq ft and expanding multi-customer ecommerce fulfillment capacity.
2026-01-21: Echo announced definitive acquisition of ITS Logistics, projecting a combined 2025 revenue platform around USD 5.4 billion.
2026-02-24: FMCSA announced Motus rollout Phase I (Dec 2025) and planned Phase II availability to all regulated entities in Q2 2026.
2026-03-10: US Census reported Q4 2025 retail e-commerce sales of USD 316.1 billion (seasonally adjusted), up 1.7% quarter-on-quarter.
2026-03-25: Echo completed the ITS Logistics acquisition, citing a combined 2025 revenue context of about USD 5.2 billion.
2026-06-22: C.H. Robinson acquired DeSpir Logistics to expand high-value and security-sensitive cargo services.
outlook: US 3PL demand is supported by continuing ecommerce growth and complex, security- and compliance-heavy supply chains; the market is expected to grow into the USD 272.74 billion range by 2031, but margin expansion is unlikely without stronger value capture from software-enabled, service-integrated portfolios.
themes: AI-driven freight planning and visibility
Cold-chain and life-sciences specialization
Nearshoring and cross-border service orchestration
Consolidation and capability-focused M&A
Fuel and labor-cost resilience
State freight planning and multimodal infrastructure integration
one_sentence: The US 3PL industry is at a moderate-growth, high-competition phase with resilient demand from e-commerce and trade, but margin pressure from fuel, labor, and capacity costs.

title: Thrift Stores
one_liner: U.S. thrift stores are moving from a value-necessity niche into mainstream resale demand, pressured by inflation and competition from rapidly scaling online resale platforms.
overview: U.S. thrift stores are nonprofit-affiliated used-goods retailers that sell donated merchandise and generally do not share resale proceeds with donors. The segment is still smaller than broader used-merchandise retail, but thrift and resale behaviors have become mainstream: a 2026 Bain survey reported 42% of U.S. consumers bought secondhand clothing or accessories at least once over the past year, and ThredUp’s 2025 results and The RealReal’s 2025 growth indicate strong scaling of organized resale ecosystems.

market_size.scope: NAICS 4533 used merchandise stores (sectoral output, includes broader used retail mix)

baseline_2022.notes: IBIS baseline projection context for the thrift Stores industry in 2022.
baseline_2022.growth: n/a

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue comes from resale of donated goods through store and, increasingly, online channels; pricing is low-to-mid price point based on inventory quality and category mix. Larger operators improve margin with higher throughput, better assortment sorting, and stronger online conversion, while non-profit stores also capture mission-related support flows (not direct operating margin substitute).
cost_structure: High-volume donation intake and sorting labor, store rent and utilities, loss/waste from unsellable inventory, cleaning/processing costs, digital marketplace and payment technology, fulfillment for online orders, and marketing/community acquisition.
current_dynamics: Demand is supported by both value shopping and circularity motives; used-merchandise sector output rebounded strongly into 2025 and BLS now treats secondhand apparel as a formal price-measured market segment for CPI methodology. For-profit and platform-led resale are gaining share through scale, authentication tooling, and digital discovery, while thrift stores remain anchors for lower-price and community segments.
whats_growing: Resale ubiquity is increasing: online resale sales and authenticated consignment are expanding fastest; 2026 survey and company reporting show active buyer growth, while broader fashion retailers face substitution toward cheaper resale options.
whats_shrinking: Purely local, low-differentiation thrift formats face pressure on foot-traffic-only models and higher-income discretionary spend shifting to higher-value channels or premium online alternatives.
recent_developments: 2025-07-2026: FRED updated NAICS 4533 sector output at $27,825.604M for 2025 (annual), with 12.1% year-over-year growth.
2025-2025: Bain reported 42% of U.S. consumers bought secondhand clothing or accessories at least once over the past year in its July 2026 consumer research release.
2026-02-26: The RealReal reported 2025 full-year revenue of $693M (+15% YoY), GMV of $2.13B (+16% YoY), and full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $765M–$780M.
2026-03-02: ThredUp reported 2025 full-year revenue of $310.8M (+20% YoY) and guided 2026 full-year revenue of $349M–$355M.
2026-04-24: Fortune cited U.S. March resale strength, with secondhand transactions up 22% year over year and strong growth at both discount and luxury resale channels.
2026-06-03: BLS-linked FRED methodology notes used-merchandise data remain elevated from prior years, supporting an above-trend trajectory versus 2024.
outlook: Base case is steady positive growth as value sensitivity and reuse norms deepen, but growth is likely uneven: faster in organized online and authenticated resale, slower in uninvested local formats unless they digitize or specialize.
themes: Value-led consumption
Circular fashion habits
Digital resale acceleration
Platform-led category premiumization
Cross-channel pressure between thrift and online consignment
one_sentence: Demand in 2025–2026 is rising on affordability and sustainability, while channel competition and margin pressure remain structural.

title: Tile & Marble Stores
one_liner: Specialty tile and stone retailers in the U.S. are holding up in 2025-2026 on resilient remodeling demand, but growth is increasingly concentrated in high-margin natural stone and design-led projects while big-box competition and higher costs intensify.
overview: Tile and marble stores sell ceramic, porcelain, marble, granite, limestone and related accessories for residential and commercial projects, with demand driven by remodeling activity and new construction specifications. The segment remains highly competitive versus broad home-improvement retailers, especially in DIY-oriented buying, and is increasingly differentiated by product mix, in-store expertise, and fulfillment speed. The industry is shifting toward higher-value premium surfaces and stronger service integration as lower-value transaction growth slows.

baseline_2022.baseline_as_of: 2021 (latest historical figure in provided baseline and used as pre-2025 starting reference)
baseline_2022.note: Industry was projecting 2.3% annualized to reach about 10.0bn by 2026 in the legacy forecast.

revenue_mix: Tile and stone sales (ceramic, concrete, marble, granite and mosaic/terrazzo tile)
Natural stone premium lines (higher ticket and higher margin)
Ancillary products: grout, adhesives, tools, edges, accessories
Design and specification support for DIY and pro customers
Sales to pros and contractors for remodeling and commercial projects
how_it_makes_money.pricing_model: Higher margins on premium and project-intensive categories; lower margins on commodity line replacements and volume trade sales.

cost_structure: Store rent and fixed overhead at regional showroom locations
Inventory carrying cost for bulky SKUs and material handling
Freight, trucking, and distribution center operating cost
Skilled sales/design labor and installation handoff support
Sourcing volatility, tariff pass-through limits, and input-cost inflation risk
major_players: {'name': 'Floor & Decor', 'evidence': '270 warehouse-format stores by Dec. 25 2025; opened 20 stores in fiscal 2025'}
{'name': 'The Home Depot', 'evidence': 'Large national home-improvement chain with dedicated Flooring and Kitchens & Bath merchandising and broad tile category competition'}
{'name': "Lowe's", 'evidence': 'Retail home-improvement operator with store-level flooring assortment and strong omnichannel/pro-installation integration'}
{'name': 'The Tile Shop', 'evidence': 'Tiered 2025 performance reference in IBIS baseline and long-standing presence in premium tile retail'}
current_dynamics: Demand is resilient in remodeling channels, supported by home equity and aging-housing retrofit spending.
Home-improvement mega-retailers continue to absorb discretionary volume, pushing specialty chains to specialize and compete on assortment, service, and convenience.
Housing conditions in 2025-2026 are uneven: weaker single-family activity but stabilizing pockets and stronger nonresidential sectors in selected geographies.
Material cost and trade-flow complexity remain inflationary, while domestic labor and installation demand constraints dampen project conversion speed.
whats_growing: Premium natural stone, high-touch bath/kitchen projects in 2025-2026 remodelling.
Regional specialization and cluster expansion by large specialty chains (for example, 20 new stores in FY2025 at a leading chain).
Nonresidential renovation demand where healthcare, institutional and selective commercial segments sustain finishes spend.
Installers and pro-market demand for reliable project-ready supply in one-stop formats.
whats_shrinking: Commodity-style standalone local operators without scale or differentiated assortment.
Comparable-store momentum in soft-demand periods where existing-home-sales cycles weaken tile purchase frequency.
Price-sensitive discretionary demand for luxury stone when mortgage and construction financing conditions remain tight.
Purely physical-only distribution models versus omnichannel and assisted-design formats.
recent_developments: 2026-01-15: NAHB reported RMI reading at 64, indicating continued moderate improvement in remodeling activity into 2026.
2026-02-18: NAHB reported overall 2025 housing starts at 1.36m with single-family starts at 943k and softness versus 2024 context.
2026-03-00: NAHB noted March 2026 stabilization in starts, but total permits remained low (about 1.37m annualized rate; single-family permits down 3.8% y/y).
2026-06-00: NAHB HBGI showed single-family declines across most geographies in Q1 2026, while multifamily expanded broadly outside rural pockets.
2026-07-20: AIA forecast said nonresidential building spending fell 2% in 2025 to about USD 846bn and adjusted to 2026 consensus near 0.3% decline.
2025-12-25: Floor & Decor reported 20 new warehouse stores in FY2025, ending with 270 stores and five design studios.
outlook: For 2026, the segment is likely to grow modestly overall with resilience in remodeling offsetting uneven residential construction. The most probable winners are differentiated chains with design expertise and multi-channel fulfillment, while weaker standalone operators face further market share pressure.
themes: Shift from bulk volume to high-margin design and stone-led projects
Consolidation and local strategic partnering among specialty operators
Competition pressure from national home-improvement ecosystems
Cost management through better logistics and pro-channel servicing
Geographic rebalancing of demand toward outlying and multifamily-driven pockets
one_sentence: The U.S. tile and marble market is a moderate-growth, mature specialty retail segment where 2025 activity sits around USD 11.1 billion, sustained by kitchen and bath upgrades even as construction affordability and single-family softness limit upside.

title: Tile Installers in the US
one_liner: Tile installation remains a cyclical, labor-intensive trades market where demand tracks housing and commercial construction, with remodel spending and nonresidential projects helping offset weaker single-family affordability.
overview: Tile installers install ceramic, stone, marble, mosaic, and concrete tile in residential and commercial projects. The market is fragmented and still dominated by small private crews, while larger builders and contractors absorb tile work through broader construction programs. In 2022 the sector was near-flat; in 2026, demand is split across slower single-family construction and more resilient remodeling/commercial activity.

key_stats.market_size: 12,701 USD million (2022); no publicly released standalone 2025-2026 industry revenue series found in accessible official sources.
key_stats.growth: IBIS baseline: 2003-2022 CAGR 0.20% on revenue; 2022-2028 projected CAGR 0.15%; 2026 proxy indicators show muted construction demand in parts of the market.
key_stats.employment: 97,250 industry workers in 2022 baseline; broader BLS occupancy family shows 112,300 flooring installers and tile/stone-related workers in 2024 with strong replacement demand.
key_stats.revenue_dynamics: Census June 2026 total construction spending was 2,166.5 USD billion SAAR, while private construction was 1,622.5 USD billion SAAR.

baseline_2022.growth: Revenue was largely flat-to-slow: 2022 rise of 0.70% in the latest year of baseline period; CAGR 0.20% across 2003-2022 and 0.15% projected to 2028.
baseline_2022.profit: 622 USD million, with 4.90% margin in 2022 (IBIS baseline)

how_it_makes_money: Installers earn through labor and job-level pricing (residential, commercial, and repair/renovation scopes), typically per square foot or full-package project bids. Revenue is influenced by material sourcing, job complexity, travel, and turnaround guarantees in occupied buildings.

cost_structure.labor: High share: specialized installers and helper layers; wage pressure is persistent.
cost_structure.materials: Tile products, adhesives, grout, underlayment, specialty tools, and transport costs are major variable expenses.
cost_structure.tools: Specialized layout and cutting equipment raises fixed costs for smaller operators.
cost_structure.insurance_and_compliance: Safety, liability, and workers’ comp add fixed overhead and can materially erode margin in smaller firms.

major_players: Independent local tile installers and small private firms (highly fragmented base)
Large home builders and general contractors packaging tile scope into broader construction programs
Retail-linked installation channels tied to large improvement ecosystems (e.g., Lowe’s installation ecosystem and Home Depot-linked installer networks)
current_dynamics: Residential new-build is constrained by high borrowing costs, while nonresidential and multifamily segments and remodel spending are supporting job flow in 2026, creating a split demand environment rather than a broad expansion trend.
whats_growing: Residential and commercial remodeling in kitchens/bathrooms remained resilient relative to new home pace.
Nonresidential and multifamily activity improved in 2026, supporting commercial tile scope.
Long-term occupational demand for tile/floor installers is projected to grow (BLS Employment Projections +6% for 2024-2034).
whats_shrinking: Single-family starts weakened versus prior year in 2026, reducing builder-driven new home tile demand.
Homebuyer affordability remained a constraint in 2026 as mortgage rates stayed elevated.
Profitability remains pressured by elevated material, labor, and financing costs.
recent_developments: 2026-08-06: MORTGAGE30US = 6.69% (30-year fixed PMMS rate).
2026-08-04: DFF effective federal funds rate = 3.63%.
2026-08-03: Census June 2026 total construction spending = 2,166.5 USD billion SAAR, 0.1% below revised June 2026 estimate and 3.2% below June 2025.
2026-08-03: June 2026 private construction = 1,622.5 USD billion SAAR; residential = 877.1 USD billion; nonresidential = 745.3 USD billion.
2026-07-17: NAHB reported overall starts at 1.43 million SAAR in June, with single-family starts down 3.2% vs June 2025 and multifamily up 17.2% vs June 2025.
2026-07-16: NAHB HMI for newly built single-family homes fell to 34, below 40 for the 15th consecutive month.
outlook: 2026–2027 likely remains a low-moderate growth environment for the sector: new home demand is constrained by rates, while retrofit and commercial activity provide a stabilizing floor. Market performance should improve only if financing conditions ease and construction material volatility normalizes.
themes: Housing affordability and financing are now central demand determinants for tile installers.
Remodeling intensity remains the strongest buffer against new-build weakness.
Labor remains tight in skilled finishing trades, sustaining wage pressure.
Commercial and multifamily growth is becoming a larger share of tile opportunity than before.
one_sentence: Tile installers are low-barrier, high-skill service providers whose margins are pulled by materials, labor, and financing-cost pressure in the 2025–2026 construction cycle.

title: Timber Services in the US
one_liner: Timber services remains a housing- and manufacturing-input service business where 2025-26 demand is constrained by housing-softening and paper-market shifts, while timberland portfolio concentration continues.
overview: Timber services sells standing timber access and harvest rights through timber tract operations, with demand primarily linked to downstream wood product conversion. In 2025-26, U.S. residential housing demand and multifamily cycles moved unevenly, while downstream paper/packaging markets showed mixed signal strength, keeping pricing leverage limited and margins pressured for service providers.

key_stats.market_size: 2025-26 proxy: AFH value-added proxy reached 2025 Q4 at $262.0B SAAR (VAAFH) and weakened to 2026 Q1 at $235.3B SAAR (BEA via FRED); forestry-fishing-related GDP was $53,856M in 2024 (USFRSTFISHNGSP, annual).
key_stats.growth: 2025 Q4→2026 Q1 AFH value-added slowed to 235.3B from 262.0B SAAR (about -10.2% quarter-to-quarter on that basis); 2024→2025 forestry/fishing/related activities value increased from $46,978M to $53,856M (+14.7%).

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 baseline context (from baseline Timber Services IBIS file): around US$1.2B in sector revenue, anchored to 2021 revenue-level reporting.
baseline_2022.growth: IBIS baseline (2022 snapshot): 2021–2026 projected CAGR of -0.38%; historical 2004–2021 CAGR of -1.09%.

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue is from sale of standing timber rights (lump-sum tract transactions and/or per-unit stumpage sales) into downstream sawmills, wood product plants, and pulp/board chains. Revenue timing is sensitive to downstream conversion volumes, especially U.S. homebuilding and packaging demand, because harvestability and buyer conversion activity affect pace and pricing.
cost_structure: Land and asset management costs (site access, regeneration/silviculture, stewardship)
Safety, compliance, and liability management in forestry operations
Labor and contract labor tied to logging, site prep, equipment operators, and transport support
Operating costs influenced by fuels and machinery; BLS 2025 logging-occupation wage benchmarks: logging equipment operators median $24.44/hour and $50,840 annual
Seasonal risk management and fire-risk mitigation expenses during high-fire years
major_players: Weyerhaeuser (NY: WY): announced 117,000-acre timberland acquisition in 2025 and continues portfolio optimization actions through late 2025
Rayonier (NYSE: RYN): reported 2.0M acres of US timberland-related holdings at 12/31/2025 in its annual reporting package
BTG Pactual Timberland Investment Group (TIMG): 2026 acquisition expansion activity in Virginia increasing U.S. timberland management footprint

current_dynamics.housing: NAHB/Demographics and starts remained volatile in 2025-26; Jan–Jul 2025 and May–Jul 2026 readings show demand oscillating with elevated housing finance costs.
current_dynamics.pricing: Softwood lumber PPI remained elevated but volatile: FRED WPS0811 reported June 2026 at 286.523 (1982=100) versus May 2026 at 280.370.
current_dynamics.policy_and_risk: Federal wildfire policy integration (USWFS) and severe 2025 fire impacts (5.1m acres burned) increased focus on fuel mitigation and firefighting resource coordination.
current_dynamics.industry_structure: Industry productivity and employment structures still show broad forestry-sector stress, but timber-tract operations hours worked rose to 10.375 million in 2025 and employment structure in 2025 remained highly cyclical by occupation.

whats_growing: 2025-2026: FRED WPS0811 showed softwood lumber index increase in June 2026 (286.523) versus May 2026 (280.370)
2025: BLS forestry/wage data show logging-operations labor remains above many adjacent segment averages and supports operational resilience in contracted harvesting windows
2025/2026: Weyerhaeuser disclosed continued timberland optimization and acquisition activity, indicating active capital allocation by major owners
whats_shrinking: 2026-01: AFH value-added proxy fell to 235.3B SAAR from 262.0B SAAR in 2025 Q4 (same series basis)
2026-06: NAHB reported total starts of 1.18M with SF at 882,000 and single-family softness versus prior stronger months
2025: overall 2025 U.S. housing starts were below 2024 pace in many official NAHB releases, reducing long-cycle timber demand support
recent_developments: 2025-05-22: Weyerhaeuser announced acquisition of approximately 117,000 acres in NC/VA for $375 million.
2025-12-01: NAHB’s annual review showed 2025 total housing starts at 1.36M, below 2024 and flagged near-term softening.
2026-02-01: NAHB reported 2025 total starts at 1.36M, down 0.6% from 1.37M in 2024.
2026-05-16: NAHB reported May 2026 total starts at 1.18M with single-family 882,000 and continued affordability-driven weakness.
2026-06-25: 2025 wildfires context and federal wildfire unification policy work remained active in federal reorganization planning for suppression and fuel mitigation.
outlook: For 2026-2027, the industry is likely to trend lower in revenue visibility due to continued housing-market softness and persistent downstream substitution, partially offset by productivity-improving REIT-led timberland management and selective acreage repositioning. The near-term path is best seen as uneven: cyclical downside risk from construction and trade pressures, with localized upside if housing starts reaccelerate while input prices stabilize.
themes: Housing-led demand cyclicality persists
Timberland ownership increasingly concentrated in large REIT and institutional structures
Downstream paper/packaging demand remains mixed versus historical highs
Wildfire and climate-related land risk is rising
Labor and machinery productivity are now central to margin protection
one_sentence: The industry’s current cycle is defined by uneven end-market demand, volatile lumber pricing, and a faster shift toward timberland consolidation among publicly traded timber REITs.

title: Tire & Rubber Recycling
one_liner: The U.S. tire-and-rubber-recycling industry turns end-of-life tires into fuel, aggregates, and reclaimed rubber products, with near-term demand tied to tire throughput, industrial fuel demand, and public policy on tire waste.
overview: U.S. tire recycling is still a policy-sensitive, infrastructure-dependent industry centered on collecting, processing, and monetizing end-of-life tires through tire-derived fuel (TDF), tire-derived aggregate (TDA), crumb rubber, and steel/rubber coproducts. Federal reporting and recent trade-group forecasts suggest continued volume growth from higher tire shipments while alternative outlets (construction, industrial combustion, and specialty rubber products) remain the key demand engines. Market data from 2025 appears to place U.S. tire-recycling revenue around USD 1,594.0 million, with a medium-growth outlook versus a still relatively concentrated and capital-intensive operator base. Legacy baseline data still shows a much smaller 2020 value point (USD 1,061.0 million), indicating the industry has been growing incrementally rather than experiencing disruptive expansion.

managed_share.unit: percent of end-of-life tires managed for recycling or fuel

market_size.methodology: reconstructed from baseline trajectory using IBIS figures around USD 1,061m in 2020 and low-single-digit growth

how_it_makes_money: Collection and processing service fees from scrap-tire operators, municipalities, tire retailers, and fleet/transport channels.
Sales of tire-derived fuel (TDF) to industrial users such as cement and pulp/paper sectors.
Sales of tire-derived aggregate, crumb rubber, and recovered steel/rubber byproducts into construction, asphalt, sound barrier, and manufacturing applications.

major_costs: Collection logistics and handling of dispersed waste streams
Sorting, shredding, and grinding/capture systems
Labor and wages (historically a high share and rising pressure)
Regulatory compliance, transport manifests, and waste handling requirements
cost_structure.cost_structure_trend: In 2026-era filings and announcements, operators continue to emphasize automation and integration to counter higher labor and compliance burdens while raising throughput.

current_dynamics: USTMA 2026 forecast shows stronger tire replacement and OE demand versus 2025, with total U.S. tire shipments at 338.9 million units in 2026 versus 336.3 million in 2025.
EPA source data indicates 264 million end-of-life tires were generated in 2023, with 207 million (79%) managed through recycling or use as fuel.
EPA’s 2026 proposed rule removes friction for certain scrap tire combustibility pathways by treating recovered scrap tires in cement kilns as nonwaste fuel when appropriately managed.
State policy remains active: New York advanced a tire extended producer responsibility bill, signaling additional producer-level compliance and collection obligations in at least some large markets.
Industry consolidation and scale investments are continuing, with large North American operators adding facilities and automation.
whats_growing: Recovery scale tied to higher tire generation from 2025-2026 shipment growth.
Industrial fuel substitution and TDF-related demand where facilities and permitting conditions improve.
Regulated diversion infrastructure that channels more end-of-life tires into managed recovery channels (with 2023 measured at 79% managed).
Consolidation and technology upgrades by large operators (e.g., automation, multi-stream processing, expanded footprint).
whats_shrinking: Unmanaged tire stockpiles have declined substantially versus prior decades (EPA references show reduction to about 48 million stranded scrap as of 2023).
High-margin white-space growth from simple expansion is harder as management and processing standards converge and market channels mature.
Smaller operators face pressure on margins and bargaining power relative to larger integrated players.
recent_developments: 2026-03-23: EPA proposed rule to treat certain recovered scrap tires used in cement kilns as nonwaste fuel and expand eligible collections for abandonment recovery.
2026-03-04: USTMA forecast projected 2026 U.S. tire shipments at 338.9 million units versus 336.3 million in 2025.
2026-03-25: New York Senate bill 2025-S7553 (tire EPR framework) reported to finance, marking active legislative progress.
2026-08-03: Grand View Research posted a refreshed U.S. tire recycling outlook showing USD 1,594.0m revenue in 2025 and 4.55% CAGR through 2033.
2025-10-14: Liberty Tire Recycling announced acquisition activity (I Squared to acquire Liberty), reinforcing vertical integration and capital-backed expansion in U.S. tire recycling.
outlook: By 2026-2028 the industry is likely to see steady but non-accelerating growth: stronger tire throughput and construction-linked recovery demand support top-line gains, while market saturation in collection channels, rising costs, and policy complexity limit upside unless new profitable outputs (especially higher-value materials and advanced pyrolysis pathways) scale faster.
themes: Circular economy for end-of-life tires
Industrial symbiosis through TDF and recycled aggregate
State-level policy harmonization pressure (EPR, disposal stewardship)
Consolidation plus automation in a capital-leaning logistics chain
Low-carbon substitute materials for road and infrastructure applications
one_sentence: After pandemic-era pressure eased, the industry is growing at a modest pace in 2026, but returns remain constrained by high logistics and processing costs and by a maturing recovery market.

title: Tire Dealers in the US
one_liner: Tire dealers in the US are a thin-margin, service-heavy retail channel where replacement demand is increasingly supported by an older vehicle fleet and larger dealers are consolidating rapidly.
overview: IBIS estimates put the U.S. tire dealer industry at $35.2 billion in 2022, with a 2022 revenue drawdown of 2.4% in a still-demanding recovery phase, while independent tire retailers continue to dominate local market share despite rising competitive pressure. In 2026, supplier/wholesaler structure and dealer concentration indicators point to scale advantages for the largest networks: the 2026 MTD 100 reports 12,083 tire dealership locations total and the top three dealers controlling 6,181 of them. New data also show replacement demand and vehicle usage remaining supported by high mileage and truck activity, while strategy activity (M&A, PE-backed expansion, strategic alternatives reviews) has accelerated.

how_it_makes_money.2026_model: Revenue comes from tire and tube sales plus high-touch installation and related maintenance services; dealers protect margin by bundling tire fitment with alignments, brake work, suspension/rotation services, and inspection packages.
how_it_makes_money.revenue_mix_2026_behavior: Gross sales are more durable in service lines than pure tire merchandising due to online price comparison in the pure tire product channel.
how_it_makes_money.customer_segments_2026: Consumer vehicles, fleet/light commercial operators, and local replacement customers; commercial truck demand remains tied to freight demand.

cost_structure.tire_inventory_and_product_costs: Primary cost variable tied to manufacturer pricing, wholesale terms, and commodity pressure from rubber and related inputs.
cost_structure.labor: Labor is the largest service-side variable, especially in installation and diagnostic workflows.
cost_structure.fixed_costs: Facility rent, technician equipment, lifts/aligners, parking/yard capacity, and compliance-related overhead.
cost_structure.distribution_and_funding: Inventory carrying, payment handling, and capital tied to working inventory and real estate footprint.
cost_structure.margin_pressure: High-price competition from warehouse clubs, e-commerce channels, and national retailers compresses gross and operating spreads.

major_players: Mavis Tire Express Services Corp. — 3,639 locations (2026 MTD 100)
Sun Auto Tire & Service — 591 locations (2026 MTD 100)
Gills Point S Tire & Auto Service — 135 locations (2026 MTD 100)
Great Water — ~160 stores after late-2025 acquisition activity (MTD 50 coverage)
current_dynamics: 2025-2026 consolidation is active: multiple chains grew footprint through acquisitions and continued greenfield openings.
2026 MTD 100 data show top 100 dealers at 12,083 locations, with top 3 dealers at 6,181, and private-equity-backed players concentrated among largest operators.
Modern Tire Dealer’s 2026 Facts Issue indicates independents held roughly 80% of U.S. consumer tire wholesale volume in 2025.
USTMA shipment mix shows replacement segments rising while some OE replacement categories shifted unevenly in 2025.
2025 NADA retail benchmarks show repair/service remain structurally important to the broader automotive after-market spend environment.
whats_growing: Demand for tire replacement and service tied to older fleets: S&P Global reports U.S. light-vehicle average age at 12.8 years in 2025.
Replacement and commercial tire demand remain supported by stable vehicle-mile activity and freight/truck travel trends.
Large dealer roll-ups and private-equity-backed operators are adding scale and service footprint.
Service-led revenue (installations, alignments, maintenance bundles) is more resilient than standalone commodity tire sales.
Freight-linked commercial tire and downtime-reduction service demand remains a growth niche as heavy transport volumes stabilize.
whats_shrinking: Pure price-based tire merchandising margins remain weak due to disciplined online and big-box comparison alternatives.
Dealer-level market entry remains easy, keeping competitive intensity high despite location concentration.
Some OEM/vehicle-production-related timing shifts can temporarily dampen replacement urgency.
Higher labor intensity and real-time inventory obligations increase operational drag for smaller independents.
recent_developments: 2025-06-16: Mavis Tire completed the Midas acquisition, lifting its network to more than 3,500 U.S.-Canada locations.
2025-08-07: USTMA projected total U.S. tire shipments at 340.2 million units versus 337.3 million in 2024.
2025-??: MTD 100 coverage reports Discount Tire added 45 locations in 2025 and 11 more by early 2026.
2026-02-10: MTD’s 2026 Facts Issue documents independents still controlling about 80% of U.S. consumer tire wholesale.
2026-05-27: Monro announced a strategic alternatives review including acquisitions, refinancing, and potential sale options.
outlook: By 2026–27, the industry is likely to remain moderate-growth to stable in revenue with a stronger bias toward service and consolidation than pure tire product margin capture. Fleet age and travel demand support replacement cycles, while competitive pressure from e-commerce and value-driven shoppers keeps margin gains limited; scale, location density, and disciplined operations should separate winners.
themes: Fleet aging and replacement-cycle support
Consolidation and private-equity participation
Service-led differentiation vs. commoditized tire sales
Wholesale dependency on independent distributors
one_sentence: The sector remains mature in 2026, but consolidation, a record-aging fleet, and resilient road usage are reshaping pricing power toward service-led and multi-location operators.

title: Tire Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US tire manufacturing in 2026 is operating on near-record shipment levels while facing higher raw-material and input tariff costs, with modest demand growth concentrated in replacement and OE channels.
overview: US tire manufacturing continues to sit at a moderate growth phase after pandemic recovery, with 2025 forecast shipments at 340.4 million units and 2026 forecast at 338.9 million units. Demand remains tied to vehicle replacement cycles and downstream vehicle output, while cost pressure from rubber and steel-intensive inputs remains the main profit risk. USTMA’s member footprint and tariff environment indicate ongoing structural pressure to secure domestic supply chains and stabilize costs.

key_stats.market_size: US tire shipments 2025: 340.4 million units; US tire shipments 2026: 338.9 million units; USTMA estimates the industry’s annual economic footprint at $259.5 billion (2026 member page)
key_stats.growth: 2024 to 2025 (forecast): +0.9%; 2025 to 2026 (forecast): +0.7% in total shipments; replacement+OE segment-level shipment growth is positive within the same forecasts

baseline_2022.market_size: US tire manufacturing revenue: $22,215 million in 2022 (IBIS baseline) ; profit margin: 3.1% in 2022
baseline_2022.growth: IBIS baseline 2005-2022 CAGR: -0.23% revenue; projected 2005-2028 CAGR revision context from baseline remains below 2% and indicates mature-cycle behavior

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is mainly split between OE supply (new vehicles, including passenger, light truck, and truck/touring segments) and replacement sales; these remain the two anchors of the business model. Margin expansion in any given year depends on managing fixed cost absorption and input pass-through, while avoiding share loss from low-cost imports.
cost_structure: Purchases and input costs were the largest cost component (45.3% of revenue in 2022 baseline), with raw materials and commodities the most volatile driver. Goodyear’s 2025 filing shows direct sensitivity: higher raw material costs, conversion costs, and tariff/transportation costs all reduced operating income materially.
current_dynamics: Current activity is shaped by modest domestic demand growth, stronger policy risk around metals and trade barriers, and ongoing capacity reconfiguration by major players. In 2026, shipment expectations remain above 2024 levels but only slightly so, while cost inflation and tariff uncertainty keep profit outlook uneven across operators.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 USTMA shipment trend is slightly higher than 2024; OE and replacement categories continue to post positive shipment revisions despite uneven regional outcomes; USTMA member firms still emphasize advanced tire technologies and connected/safety innovations.
whats_shrinking: Mid- and low-tier replacement replacement demand is under pressure in parts of the market, while price competition and input inflation remain constraints; major firms are still restructuring production footprints, suggesting continuing rationalization and possible capacity exits.
recent_developments: 2025-03-06: USTMA forecast total US tire shipments at 340.4 million units versus 337.3 million in 2024.
2025-01-23: Bridgestone Americas announced planned closure of its LaVergne, Tennessee truck-and-bus radial tire plant (effective 2025-07-31).
2025-03-12: US steel tariff proclamation changes reinstated broad steel coverage, removing broad exclusion pathways and keeping US metals exposure high for downstream users.
2025: Goodyear reported Americas replacement tire volume down 2.9 million units (-4.3%) and higher raw-material-related costs in 2025 filings.
2026-03-04: USTMA updated its 2026 projection to 338.9 million units, up 0.7% versus 2025.
2026-04-02: White House Proclamation 11021 imposed strengthened Section 232 rates (50% on qualifying full-value metal products; 25% on derivatives, temporary 15% subset).
outlook: Near-term growth remains moderate rather than re-accelerating, with demand supported by continued vehicle-use demand and replacement needs. The near-term winner scenario is cost discipline and efficiency at plants that can offset material and logistics volatility; downside risk is sustained raw-material inflation and tariff complexity raising pricing frictions.
themes: Mild volume growth with mature-cycle dynamics
Input-cost and tariff-led margin compression risk
Footprint optimization and selective capacity consolidation
Safety, sustainability, and tire-health innovation
Technology-enabled tire performance differentiation (smart/connected tire systems)

one_sentence: The industry remains mature but resilient, with 2025-26 USTMA shipment forecasts showing only low-single-digit growth in a cost-pressured environment.

title: Tire Retreading & Recapping
one_liner: U.S. tire retreaders extend heavy-duty tire life by replacing worn tread, with demand driven by freight intensity and total-cost pressure in trucking.
overview: The U.S. tire retreading industry remains focused on commercial and trucking applications, where cost savings versus new tires are the main commercial driver. Baseline IBIS coverage (last updated Aug 16, 2021) showed a USD 1.545B industry with a projected gradual recovery to above USD 1.7B by 2026 and a pre-cure process mix still dominant. The current 2025-2026 signal set strengthens this thesis: BTS freight indicators did not collapse in late 2025, and industry policy activity increased around federal fleet procurement reform and domestic adoption incentives.

market_size.note: estimated baseline from 2021 base plus published 2021-2026 growth trend

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue comes from re-manufactured truck tire sales (mainly pre-cure products) and associated inspection, sorting, recapping labor, and warranty/service support sold to fleet operators and independent tire-service channels; profitability improves with high utilization of casings, longer life-cycle contracts, and pre-cure process efficiency.
cost_structure: Rubber and tread materials (primary variable cost linked to raw-material volatility)
Energy and oil exposure in cure operations
Skilled labor and quality-control labor intensity
Casing acquisition and recovery logistics
Curing, buffing, and testing equipment (capital-heavy process controls)
current_dynamics: Environmental economics remain strong: TRIB states retreading uses about 7 gallons of oil versus about 22 gallons for a comparable new medium truck tire.
Freight demand stayed positive in late 2025 on the Truck-Rail Freight and general freight indices, supporting retread replacement cycles.
Policy advocacy intensified in 2025-2026 for procurement incentives and federal preference frameworks for retreaded tires.
Cost competitiveness versus new tires is structurally favored when oil and raw-material prices rise, strengthening retread positioning for fleets.
whats_growing: 2026 policy-backed demand for circular/economic fleet supply chains (federal procurement and tax-credit discussion around S.2790/H.R.3401).
2010s-era and newer fleet-mileage-driven replacement demand linked to persistent freight activity.
Pre-cure share in commercial fleet service as the lower-cost/high-volume method.
Safety/traceability investments, including more formalized process and sourcing discipline through dealer networks.
whats_shrinking: Consumer-passenger and light-vehicle retread penetration, where perception and convenience still limit growth versus new tires.
Independent vendor count due to high capital and quality-control barriers in a concentrated US market.
Potential margin share in segments exposed to intense price competition and import pressure.
recent_developments: 2025-10-29: TRIB and TIA public update highlighted continued advocacy and industry employment/environmental framing for retreading in policy circles.
2026-07-16: TIA/TRIB delegation renewed Capitol Hill advocacy for S.2790/H.R.3401 (retread procurement and tax credit framework).
2026-02-11: BTS reported December 2025 Freight Transportation Services Index fell 0.6% from November but rose 0.4% from December 2024.
2026-02-02: Truck-Rail Freight TSI rose 0.2% in Dec 2025 and was 0.2% above Dec 2024.
2025-12-01: ATA reported Dec 2025 for-hire truck tonnage improved 0.4% from November after a 0.2% November gain.
outlook: The market outlook is cautiously constructive into 2026: freight indicators remain supportive, and policy visibility is improving; growth likely remains moderate unless broader public procurement and fleet-credit rules materially accelerate adoption, while competitive intensity and consolidation continue.
themes: circular economy
fleet economics
freight activity sensitivity
policy-driven demand expansion
process automation in retread operations
one_sentence: Retreading remains a mature but resilient US manufacturing niche, now supported by circular-economy and federal-fleet procurement momentum as trucking demand stabilizes.

title: Tire Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: U.S. tire wholesalers are recovering on stable vehicle demand and high replacement volume while facing persistent tariff, raw-material, and price-compression pressure.
overview: Industry activity is driven by vehicle mileage and replacement cycles, with USTMA’s 2026 outlook indicating slight overall shipment growth after two years of strong rebound from pandemic weakness. Tire wholesalers continue to compete on service and speed rather than scale pricing, while digital tools and inventory automation increasingly determine retention of independent tire dealers and service shops. At the same time, trade policy and import-cost friction remain a material drag, reinforcing margin discipline as operators push efficiency and selective growth.

growth.vehicle_sales_2025_to_2026: vehicle demand remains elevated (June 2026 total vehicle sales 17.037m SAAR)

core_revenue_streams: Distribution and wholesale resale of passenger, light truck, and truck tires; replacement and OE channels
Inventory and delivery margin on recurring dealer replenishment orders
Private-label/white-label SKUs to improve dealer retention
Service and account support for independent tire dealers and fleet service channels
how_it_makes_money.pricing_model: Wholesale customers increasingly buy across multiple brands with price-sensitive mix shifts toward value SKUs, keeping gross margins tight.

key_cost_drivers: Labor intensity in sales/distribution with partial automation offsets
Raw-material pass-through via price and supplier cost changes
Trade-policy and compliance cost from tariff-documented channels
cost_structure.efficiency_trend: Greater use of internet portals, integrated ERP, and automated order/inventory workflows has reduced manual handling per unit over the midterm.
